lessons.title: What Computer Security Is: Assets, the CIA Triad and Beyond
lessons.content:
Imagine your family keeps its savings, gold and important papers in a steel almirah at home in Khulna. You lock it, you keep the key in a secret place, and only your parents know where it is. Without ever reading a textbook, your family is already doing computer security thinking: there is something valuable (the asset), there are people who might want it (thieves, or a curious cousin), there is a weakness (a cheap lock, a key left on the table), and there are protections (a strong lock, a hidden key, a neighbour who watches the house). Computer security is exactly this way of thinking, applied to data, programs, devices and networks. This course teaches you how attackers think, how defenders think, and how the mathematics of cryptography gives us locks that even the world's fastest computers cannot simply break open.

What computer security is: Computer security is the protection of computer systems and the information they hold against harm, theft, unauthorised access and misuse, while keeping them available to the people who are supposed to use them. That last part matters. A computer buried in concrete is perfectly safe from hackers, but it is also useless. Real security is always a balance: keep the bad things out and let the good things happen. You will also hear the words information security (protecting information in any form, even on paper) and cybersecurity (a popular word for security of networked systems). In this course they overlap heavily and we will not fight about names.

Why it matters today: Twenty years ago most Bangladeshi families had no computer at all. Today a rickshaw puller may receive his daily income on a mobile wallet, a student pays university fees online, a garment factory runs its payroll on software, and hospitals keep patient records in databases. Every one of these depends on computers behaving correctly. If an attacker steals a wallet PIN, changes a salary file, or shuts down a hospital system, real people lose real money, privacy or even health. Security failures are no longer a technical embarrassment; they hurt lives. That is why every software engineer, not only security specialists, needs the basics you will learn here.

Assets: Before protecting anything, we ask: what are we protecting? An asset is anything of value to a person or an organisation. Assets include hardware (laptops, phones, servers), software (the banking app, the operating system), data (customer lists, exam results, medical records, passwords), services (the ability to send money at midnight) and even reputation (people trusting your brand). Different assets need different levels of protection. Your old class notes and your national ID number are both data, but losing the second one is far more dangerous.

The CIA triad: The classic way to describe what security means is three goals, called the CIA triad. This has nothing to do with the American spy agency; the letters stand for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability. Almost every security problem you will ever meet is a failure of at least one of these three. Let us look at each one carefully.

Confidentiality: Confidentiality means information is seen only by those who are allowed to see it. Your exam result before publication, your bank balance, your private chats, a company's secret recipe: all of these need confidentiality. Tools that protect it include encryption (scrambling data so only key holders can read it), access control (deciding who may open which file) and physical protection (a locked server room). A confidentiality failure is often called a data breach or a leak. Example: if a hospital's patient list is posted online, confidentiality is lost. Closely related is privacy, which is about individuals controlling how information about themselves is collected and used.

Integrity: Integrity means information and systems are not changed in unauthorised or undetected ways. Think of a land record at a government office. If someone quietly changes the owner's name from Rahim to Karim, the record still looks fine, but it is now false and dangerous. Integrity covers data integrity (the content is correct and unchanged) and system integrity (the system does what it should and has not been tampered with). Tools include hash functions, message authentication codes, digital signatures, backups and change logs. Note the word "undetected": we cannot always stop someone from changing data, but cryptography can at least make sure the change is noticed.

Availability: Availability means systems and data are usable when authorised people need them. A mobile banking service that is down on Eid day, when everyone is sending salami to family, fails availability even if no data was stolen. Threats to availability include hardware failure, power cuts, floods, software bugs, ransomware that locks files, and denial-of-service attacks that flood a server with junk traffic. Tools include backups, redundant servers, generators, load balancing and DDoS protection. Availability is often forgotten by beginners, but for a business, hours of downtime can be as costly as a theft.

Tension between the three: The goals sometimes pull against each other. If you encrypt everything and lock it behind five passwords, confidentiality goes up but availability may go down when someone forgets a password. If you keep ten copies of a file for availability, you now have ten places from which it could leak. Good security design is about finding the right balance for each asset, not maximising one goal blindly.

Beyond CIA, authenticity: Many textbooks add more goals. Authenticity means being able to verify that something or someone is genuine: that a message really came from the claimed sender, that a website really belongs to your bank, that a software update really came from the vendor. Authentication of people (passwords, fingerprints, OTP codes) and of data (signatures and MACs) both serve authenticity. A phishing site that copies a bank's login page attacks authenticity: it looks real but is not.

Non-repudiation: Non-repudiation means a person cannot later successfully deny an action they performed. If you sign a cheque, you cannot easily say "I never signed that." In the digital world, a digital signature made with a private key that only you hold provides strong evidence that you signed a message. Non-repudiation matters for contracts, money transfers and official documents. Notice that a shared secret key cannot give non-repudiation, because both parties hold the same key and either could have produced the proof. We will see this exact point again when we compare MACs and digital signatures.

Accountability: Accountability means actions can be traced back to the entity that performed them. This needs identification (each user has their own account, not a shared one), authentication, and audit logs that record who did what and when. If ten clerks share one password, accountability is gone, because no log can tell which clerk approved a fraudulent payment. Accountability also deters insiders: people misbehave less when they know actions are recorded.

A tiny worked mapping: Let us map some events to the goals. A thief reads your SMS messages: confidentiality. A virus changes numbers in an Excel salary sheet: integrity. A flood fills the server room with water and the website goes offline: availability. A fake caller claims to be from your bank: authenticity. A customer sends money and later claims he never did, but the bank has his signed request: non-repudiation helps the bank. One event can hit several goals at once. Ransomware, for example, encrypts files (availability lost) and modern gangs also copy the files and threaten to publish them (confidentiality lost).

Security is people, process and technology: Beginners often think security is only about clever software. In reality, it rests on three legs. Technology includes encryption, firewalls and antivirus. Process includes rules such as "every payment above one lakh taka needs two approvals" and "backups are tested every month". People includes training staff to recognise scams and choosing trustworthy employees. A bank can buy the best firewall in the world, but if a staff member gives a password to a caller pretending to be from IT, the firewall does not help. Attackers usually go for the weakest leg, and very often that is the human one.

Security is a process, not a product: Systems change, new bugs are discovered, attackers learn new tricks. A system that was secure last year may be insecure today if it was never updated. That is why real organisations treat security as a continuous cycle: identify assets and risks, protect, detect problems, respond, recover, and learn. You will see this cycle again in the final lesson when we talk about patching, backups and incident response.

The role of cryptography: A big part of this course is cryptography, the science of protecting information using mathematics. Cryptography gives us encryption for confidentiality, hash functions and MACs for integrity, digital signatures for authenticity and non-repudiation, and key exchange so two strangers on the Internet can agree on a secret. But cryptography is not all of security. A perfectly encrypted message is useless if the attacker has installed spyware on your phone and reads it before encryption. So we will study both: the mathematics of crypto, and the wider systems around it such as authentication, access control, software bugs, malware, social engineering and network defences.

Course map: We start with threats, risk and design principles. Then we learn classical ciphers, the one-time pad and modern symmetric ciphers (DES, AES) with modes of operation. Next we build the number theory needed for public-key cryptography: modular arithmetic, Euclid, Fermat, Euler and fast exponentiation. With that we do RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves, then hash functions, MACs, digital signatures, certificates and TLS. The second half moves to systems: authentication, access control, software security, malware, phishing and network security, and finishes with security in practice and a capstone in which we secure a mobile-wallet style app. Some topics you already met: password hashing and web attacks in Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3), TLS basics in Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3), and protection in Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1). We will recap them briefly and go deeper.

What this course is not: We learn attacks only as ideas, so that we can defend. Law, ethics and the Digital Security related laws of Bangladesh belong to Professional Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6). Detailed offensive techniques, forensics and advanced threats belong to Advanced Cyber Security (deep-cse-9-5). Blockchains, which reuse many tools from this course, have their own course (deep-cse-9-2). Remember one rule from day one: testing or attacking systems you do not own, without written permission, is both unethical and illegal.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet: Think of a mobile financial service like bKash, Nagad or Rocket. Confidentiality: your PIN and balance must stay secret, so the app and server use encryption and the PIN is never shown. Integrity: when you send 500 taka, the amount must not become 5,000 on the way, so messages are protected by cryptographic checks and the server validates every transaction. Availability: millions of users send money before Eid, so the service needs many servers and protection against traffic floods. Authenticity: the app must be sure it talks to the real server, and the server must be sure the request came from your phone with your PIN. Non-repudiation and accountability: every transaction is logged with time, sender and receiver, so disputes can be settled.

Real-life example 2, a university result portal: Before results are published, confidentiality protects them from early leaks. Integrity is critical: if a student could change a grade from C to A, the whole degree system loses value, so only authorised teachers may edit, and every change is logged (accountability). On result day thousands of students refresh the page at once; if the server crashes, that is an availability failure. And if a fake portal appears asking students to "log in to see results early", that is an attack on authenticity using social engineering.

Common mistakes: Thinking security means only confidentiality and forgetting integrity and availability. Mixing up authentication (proving who you are) with authorisation (what you are allowed to do). Believing a system is secure because it has encryption, even though passwords are weak or software is unpatched. Treating security as a one-time feature to add at the end. Assuming attackers are always outsiders, when insiders cause a large share of incidents.

What exams ask: Define the CIA triad with one example of a violation of each. Explain authenticity, non-repudiation and accountability and how they differ. Given a scenario (for example, a hacked e-commerce site), identify which goals were violated. Explain why security is a process and why people are often the weakest link. Explain why symmetric keys alone cannot give non-repudiation.

Recap: Security protects assets: hardware, software, data, services and reputation. The core goals are confidentiality (only the right people see it), integrity (no unauthorised or undetected changes) and availability (usable when needed). Authenticity, non-repudiation and accountability extend them. Security rests on people, process and technology, and it is a never-ending cycle. Cryptography is a powerful tool inside security, but not the whole of it. In the next lesson we look at the enemy side: threats, vulnerabilities, attackers and how to measure risk.
key_points: Computer security protects systems and data from harm and misuse while keeping them usable for authorised people.
An asset is anything of value: hardware, software, data, services and reputation.
Confidentiality: only authorised people see information. Integrity: no unauthorised or undetected change. Availability: usable when needed.
Authenticity means verifying something is genuine; non-repudiation means a person cannot deny an action they performed.
Accountability needs individual accounts, authentication and audit logs; shared passwords destroy it.
Security goals can conflict, so design balances them per asset.
Security rests on people, process and technology and is a continuous cycle, not a one-time product.
Cryptography is a key tool of security but not all of it; systems, software and people matter too.
lessons.tip: For every news story about a hack this semester, write one line: which asset was hit and which of C, I, A (or authenticity) failed. You will build a strong instinct fast.
lessons.task: Pick one app you use daily (a mobile wallet, Facebook, your university portal). On paper, write one realistic threat to its confidentiality, one to its integrity and one to its availability, plus one protection for each.

quiz.q: A virus silently changes the numbers in a company's salary spreadsheet. Which security goal is violated most directly?
quiz.explain: The data was modified without authorisation, which is an integrity failure.

quiz.q: A mobile banking service goes offline for six hours on Eid day because of a traffic flood. Which goal failed?
quiz.explain: Authorised users could not use the service when they needed it: availability.

quiz.q: Why can a key shared between two parties not provide non-repudiation?
options: Either party could have produced the proof, so a third party cannot tell who did it
quiz.explain: Both sides hold the same key, so the proof does not point to one specific person.

quiz.q: Ten clerks in an office share one login account. Which property is lost most clearly?
quiz.explain: Logs cannot tell which clerk did an action, so actions cannot be traced to individuals.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes security in practice?
options: It is a product you buy once
It depends on people, process and technology and is a continuous cycle
quiz.explain: Security is ongoing and rests on all three legs; insiders and processes matter as much as tools.

lessons.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Attackers and Risk
lessons.content:
Think of the steel almirah from the last lesson again. A thief exists somewhere in the city: that is a threat. The almirah's lock is cheap and can be opened with a hairpin: that is a vulnerability. One night the thief actually tries the hairpin: that is an attack. And the chance that you lose your gold, multiplied by how bad that loss would be, is the risk. These four words are used loosely in daily talk, but in security they have precise meanings, and mixing them up leads to bad decisions. This lesson gives you the vocabulary every security professional uses, shows you how attackers are modelled, and teaches you to measure risk with simple numbers so you can decide where to spend limited money and time.

Asset, threat, vulnerability: An asset, as we saw, is anything of value. A threat is any potential cause of harm to an asset: a person, a group, an event or a circumstance. Threats can be deliberate (a hacker, a dishonest employee) or accidental (a clerk deleting the wrong folder, a fire, a flood, a power surge). A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat could use: a software bug, a default password never changed, an unlocked server room, a staff member who has never heard of phishing. A threat without a vulnerability cannot do harm, and a vulnerability nobody can reach is less dangerous. Harm happens where the two meet.

Exploit and attack: An exploit is a specific technique or piece of code that takes advantage of a particular vulnerability. An attack is an actual attempt by a threat agent to cause harm, often by using an exploit. A threat agent (or threat actor) is the person or thing carrying out the threat. Security people also use the word control or countermeasure for anything that reduces risk: a firewall, a lock, a backup, a training session, a policy. A useful sentence to remember: a threat agent launches an attack that uses an exploit against a vulnerability to harm an asset, and controls try to stop it.

Zero-day: A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor, or for which no fix exists yet, is called a zero-day, because defenders have had zero days to fix it. Most real attacks, however, use old, well-known vulnerabilities for which patches have existed for months or years. That simple fact is why updating software is one of the most effective security habits.

Attack surface: The attack surface of a system is the total set of points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data: open network ports, web forms, APIs, file uploads, USB ports, staff email inboxes, even the receptionist's phone. A larger surface means more chances for a mistake. A simple defensive rule follows: reduce the attack surface. Turn off services you do not use, close unused ports, remove old test accounts, uninstall unused apps, and expose only what customers truly need.

Passive and active attacks: A classic classification divides attacks into two types. A passive attack only observes: eavesdropping on network traffic, reading unencrypted Wi-Fi packets in a cafe, or traffic analysis (learning who talks to whom and how often, even without reading the content). Passive attacks are hard to detect because nothing changes, so the main defence is prevention, mostly by encryption. An active attack modifies or disrupts: changing messages, replaying old messages, pretending to be someone else, or flooding a service. Active attacks are easier to detect but hard to prevent completely, so we aim to detect them quickly and recover.

Four classic attack types: Another old but useful model looks at the normal flow of information from a source to a destination and lists four ways to disturb it. Interception: an unauthorised party reads the flow, attacking confidentiality (wiretapping). Interruption: the flow is stopped, attacking availability (cutting a cable, a denial-of-service attack). Modification: the attacker changes the content in the middle, attacking integrity (changing the amount in a payment request). Fabrication: the attacker inserts fake messages that seem to come from a real source, attacking authenticity (a fake SMS that looks like it came from your bank). Notice how neatly these map to the goals from lesson 01.

Attacker models, who is the enemy: Defending against "hackers" in general is impossible to plan. Instead we write down an attacker model (also called a threat model): who the attacker is, what they want, what they know, and what resources they have. Outsiders have no legitimate access; insiders such as employees, contractors or ex-employees already have some access and knowledge, which makes them dangerous. By skill and resources, attackers range from unskilled people using ready-made tools (often called script kiddies), to hacktivists with a political message, to organised criminal groups running ransomware as a business, up to state-sponsored groups with large budgets and patience. Motives include money, revenge, fame, ideology, espionage and simple curiosity.

Why the model matters: A small grocery website in Rajshahi does not need to defend against a nation-state, but it certainly must defend against automated bots that scan the whole Internet for weak passwords and unpatched software. A defence ministry must assume a patient, well-funded attacker. Writing down the attacker model keeps defences realistic: not too weak, and not wildly expensive. In cryptography we will meet a very formal version of attacker models: ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext and chosen-ciphertext attacks, which describe what the attacker can see and ask for. A good cipher must survive the strongest of these.

Risk: Risk combines how likely a bad event is with how much damage it would cause. The simplest qualitative formula is risk = likelihood x impact. Organisations often rate each from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high), giving scores from 1 to 25, and draw a coloured risk matrix: green for low scores, yellow for medium, red for high.

Worked risk example: Imagine a small online clothing shop in Dhaka with five staff. They list four risks. Staff fall for phishing emails: likelihood 4, impact 4, risk 16. The single database server's disk fails: likelihood 2, impact 5, risk 10. A stolen office laptop with customer data: likelihood 3, impact 3, risk 9. Website defacement by a bot: likelihood 2, impact 2, risk 4. Sorting by score tells the owner where to start: phishing training and multi-factor authentication first, then backups and a spare disk, then laptop disk encryption, then website patching. The numbers are rough judgements, not exact science, but they turn vague worry into an ordered to-do list.

Quantitative risk, a tiny formula: Some organisations put money values on risk. Single loss expectancy (SLE) = asset value x exposure factor, where exposure factor is the fraction of the asset lost in one incident. Annualised rate of occurrence (ARO) is how many times per year the event is expected. Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE x ARO. Example: a laptop worth 80,000 taka is fully lost when stolen (exposure factor 1.0), and the company expects one theft every four years (ARO 0.25). ALE = 80,000 x 1.0 x 0.25 = 20,000 taka per year. If a control costs less than the yearly loss it removes, it is usually worth buying. Real estimates are uncertain, so treat these as guides.

Risk treatment: Once a risk is measured, there are four classic choices. Reduce (mitigate) it by adding controls: training, patches, encryption, backups. Transfer it to someone else, for example by buying cyber insurance or outsourcing payment processing to a licensed gateway. Avoid it by not doing the risky activity at all, for example not storing card numbers if you do not need them. Accept it when the cost of control is greater than the expected loss, but accept consciously and write it down. The risk that remains after controls is called residual risk; it is never zero.

STRIDE threat modelling: Threat modelling is a structured way to find threats while designing a system, before code is written. A popular checklist from Microsoft is STRIDE, one letter per threat type: Spoofing (pretending to be someone else, breaks authenticity), Tampering (changing data, breaks integrity), Repudiation (denying an action, breaks non-repudiation), Information disclosure (leaks, breaks confidentiality), Denial of service (breaks availability) and Elevation of privilege (gaining rights you should not have, breaks authorisation). You draw a simple diagram of your system, with users, processes, data stores and data flows, and for each part ask the six STRIDE questions.

STRIDE on a tiny example: Take a student fee payment page. Spoofing: could someone pay as another student or pretend to be the payment gateway? Tampering: could the amount be changed in the browser before sending? Repudiation: could a student claim they never paid, and do we have signed records? Information disclosure: could one student see another's receipts by changing an ID in the URL? Denial of service: could bots flood the page on the last day of payment? Elevation of privilege: could a student reach the admin page that marks fees as waived? Each "yes" becomes a design requirement with a control.

Security vs safety: In English, security usually means protection against deliberate attackers, while safety means protection against accidents and nature. Real systems need both, and the risk process handles both kinds of threats. A flood in Sylhet that drowns a server room and a hacker who deletes the database end in the same place: lost availability. That is why risk lists include natural and accidental threats too.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet agent shop: Picture a cash-in and cash-out agent shop in a district town. Assets: the agent's phone and SIM, the e-money balance, cash in the drawer, customer trust. Threats: a thief, a fraudster who calls pretending to be from head office, a dishonest helper. Vulnerabilities: the PIN written on a paper near the phone, no habit of verifying callers, the phone left unlocked. The biggest risk is probably the fake head-office call, with high likelihood and high impact. Controls: never share the PIN, verify calls through an official number, lock the phone, and limit the helper's access.

Real-life example 2, a university lab: A computer lab has 40 PCs shared by hundreds of students. Assets: the PCs, students' files, the lab's network connection. Threats: malware from USB drives, a student installing a keylogger, accidental deletion. Vulnerabilities: everyone logs in as administrator, antivirus out of date, no separate accounts. Treatment: give students normal (non-admin) accounts, reset machines each night from a clean image, keep antivirus and the operating system updated, and accept the small leftover risk of a shared machine.

Common mistakes: Using threat and vulnerability as the same word. Thinking only about outsiders and forgetting insiders and accidents. Trying to fix everything at once instead of ranking by risk. Believing residual risk can be zero. Forgetting that passive attacks leave no trace and must be prevented, not just detected.

What exams ask: Define asset, threat, vulnerability, exploit, attack and control with one example each. Distinguish passive and active attacks. Explain interception, interruption, modification and fabrication with the goal each violates. Compute a risk score or an ALE from given numbers. Apply STRIDE to a small system description. List the four risk treatment options.

Recap: A threat agent attacks an asset by using an exploit against a vulnerability; controls reduce the risk. Attacks are passive (observe) or active (change), and interception, interruption, modification and fabrication map to the security goals. An attacker model states who the enemy is and what they can do. Risk = likelihood x impact, or ALE = SLE x ARO in money terms, and we reduce, transfer, avoid or accept it. STRIDE helps find threats during design. Next lesson: the design principles that make systems hard to attack in the first place.
key_points: Asset: something of value. Threat: potential cause of harm. Vulnerability: a weakness. Exploit: a technique using a weakness. Attack: an actual attempt.
A zero-day is a vulnerability with no fix yet, but most real attacks use old, already-patched bugs.
Reduce the attack surface: fewer open ports, services, accounts and features exposed.
Passive attacks observe and are prevented mainly with encryption; active attacks change or disrupt and must be detected and recovered from.
Interception, interruption, modification and fabrication attack confidentiality, availability, integrity and authenticity.
An attacker model states who the attacker is, their goals, knowledge and resources, including insiders.
Risk = likelihood x impact; ALE = SLE x ARO; treat risk by reducing, transferring, avoiding or accepting it.
STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
lessons.tip: When you read a security news story, try to name the threat agent, the vulnerability and the asset separately. If you can split a story into these three parts, the vocabulary has stuck.
lessons.task: Draw a simple box-and-arrow diagram of an app you use (for example, ordering food from a delivery app). Apply all six STRIDE questions to it and write one possible threat and one control for each letter.

quiz.q: A default admin password that was never changed is best described as a:
quiz.explain: It is a weakness that a threat could use, which is a vulnerability.

quiz.q: An attacker quietly records unencrypted Wi-Fi traffic in a cafe without changing anything. This is:
quiz.explain: It only observes data, so it is passive; it threatens confidentiality.

quiz.q: A shop rates a risk with likelihood 3 and impact 4 on 1-5 scales. What is the risk score?
quiz.explain: Risk = likelihood x impact = 3 x 4 = 12.

quiz.q: A company buys cyber insurance to cover losses from a breach. Which risk treatment is this?
quiz.explain: Insurance shifts the financial impact to another party, which is risk transfer.

quiz.q: In STRIDE, the letter E stands for:
quiz.explain: E is elevation of privilege: gaining rights you should not have.

lessons.title: Security Design Principles: Least Privilege to Defence in Depth
lessons.content:
Think about how an old zamindar house protected its treasury. There was a gate with a guard, then a courtyard, then a locked room, then an iron chest, and the keys were held by different people. The gatekeeper could not open the chest, and the treasurer could not leave the house with the chest without passing the guard. Nobody had a single key to everything. Without any computers, these people were applying security design principles: give each person only the access they need, use several layers, and never let one failure open everything. In 1975 two researchers at MIT, Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder, wrote down a set of design principles for protecting information in computer systems. Almost fifty years later, those principles still guide how operating systems, cloud platforms, banking apps and even smartphones are built. This lesson explains each one with simple examples.

Why principles at all: Attacks change every year, but the mistakes that make attacks possible repeat again and again: too much power given to one account, complicated code nobody understands, a check done once and then forgotten, a secret design that falls apart as soon as someone learns it. Principles are lessons distilled from those repeated mistakes. They do not tell you exactly which tool to use, but they help you judge any design, including designs that do not exist yet.

Least privilege: Every user, program and process should operate with the smallest set of privileges needed to do its job, and only for as long as needed. A cashier needs to record sales, not to change the salary table. A photo-editing app needs your gallery, not your SMS messages. A web server process needs to read the website files, not to install software on the machine. Why it works: if an account or program is compromised, the attacker gets only its limited powers, so the damage is contained. In practice: daily work on a normal account rather than administrator, separate database users for the website (read and insert orders) and for the admin panel, and app permissions on Android or iOS granted only when needed.

Fail-safe defaults: Access should be denied by default, and granted only by explicit permission. Ask "who should be allowed?" rather than "who should be blocked?". If a rule list has a mistake or a missing entry under a deny-by-default design, the result is that someone legitimate is locked out and complains, which is visible and easily fixed. Under an allow-by-default design, the same mistake silently lets an attacker in. A firewall that blocks everything except listed services, and a new employee account that starts with no access until a manager approves it, are fail-safe defaults. The idea also covers failure: if the authentication server crashes, the system should refuse logins, not let everybody in.

Economy of mechanism: Keep the design as simple and small as possible. Security bugs hide in complexity: every extra feature, option and line of code is another place for a mistake. Simple mechanisms can be reviewed, tested and understood completely. This is why security-critical parts, such as the code that checks passwords or the kernel of an operating system, should be small. A short checklist: if you cannot explain how your security check works on one page, it is probably too complex to trust.

Complete mediation: Every access to every object must be checked for authority, every time. It is not enough to check once at login and then trust everything afterwards. Example of a failure: a web app checks that you are logged in, but when you change the order number in the URL from 1001 to 1002, it shows someone else's order without checking that order 1002 belongs to you. You met this as IDOR (insecure direct object reference) in Web Engineering. Caching permissions is risky for the same reason: if a manager removes your access, a system that cached the old permission keeps letting you in.

Open design: The security of a mechanism should not depend on the secrecy of its design. Assume attackers know exactly how your system works; security should rest only on secret keys or passwords, which are small and easy to change. If your design is secret and someone leaks it, you must redesign everything. If only a key leaks, you change the key. Open designs can also be reviewed by many experts, who find flaws before attackers do.

Kerckhoffs's principle: In 1883 the Dutch-born cryptographer Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote that a military cipher should not require secrecy, and that it should not be a problem if it falls into enemy hands. Today we state it as: a cryptosystem should be secure even if everything about the system, except the key, is public. Claude Shannon later put it even more bluntly: the enemy knows the system. That is why the world uses public, heavily analysed algorithms such as AES, RSA and SHA-256 instead of secret home-made ones. A company that advertises "our own secret unbreakable encryption algorithm" is usually showing a warning sign, not a strength.

Security through obscurity: Hiding details, such as running a service on an unusual port or giving the admin page a strange name, is called security through obscurity. On its own it is weak, because secrets of this kind are easily discovered by scanning or leaks. As one extra layer on top of real controls it can slightly slow down casual attackers, but it must never be the main protection. The key test: if the hidden detail becomes known tomorrow, are you still secure? If not, you were relying on obscurity.

Separation of privilege: Where feasible, a protection mechanism that requires two separate keys or conditions is stronger than one requiring a single key. A bank locker that needs both the customer's key and the bank's key, a payment above a limit that needs two officers' approval, and two-factor authentication (password plus a code from your phone) all apply this principle. An attacker must now defeat two independent things. A closely related organisational idea is separation of duties: the person who creates a vendor in the accounts system should not be the same person who approves payments to that vendor.

Least common mechanism: Minimise the amount of mechanism shared by different users, because every shared component is a possible channel for information to leak between users, or for one user to disturb another. Shared temporary folders, shared memory and shared accounts are examples. Modern cloud platforms isolate customers with separate virtual machines or containers partly for this reason. In daily life: a shared family email password means one person's mistake exposes everyone.

Psychological acceptability: Security mechanisms must be easy to use correctly, or people will work around them. If a policy forces a new 16-character password every two weeks, staff write passwords on sticky notes under the keyboard, which is worse than a moderate policy. If a security warning appears on every page, users learn to click "OK" without reading. Good security fits how people really behave: password managers, fingerprint unlock, clear warnings only when something is truly wrong. Saltzer and Schroeder also mentioned two more ideas: work factor (compare the cost of breaking a mechanism with the attacker's resources) and compromise recording (sometimes it is enough to reliably detect and record that a breach happened, like a tamper seal on a medicine bottle).

Defence in depth: Never rely on a single control. Use several independent layers so that when one fails, others still protect the asset. For a web server: a network firewall, then an up-to-date operating system, then a web application firewall, then input validation in the code, then a database user with least privilege, then encrypted backups, then monitoring and alerts. The idea comes from military defence and castles: walls, moat, gates, inner keep. Each layer may be imperfect, but an attacker must defeat all of them, and every layer is another chance to detect them. The layers should be different in kind, because two copies of the same control often fail for the same reason.

Weakest link: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Attackers do not attack your strongest point; they look for the weakest one. If you use AES-256 encryption but the admin password is "admin123", the attacker simply logs in. This is why balanced security across all parts beats extreme strength in one part. The weakest link is very often a person, a forgotten old server, or a third-party supplier with access to your network.

Security vs usability and cost: Every control has costs: money, time, convenience and sometimes performance. A bank vault door on a kitchen cupboard would be absurd. Engineers must decide, using risk from the previous lesson, how much security each asset deserves. Too little and attackers walk in; too much and people bypass controls or the business cannot work. The art is to put strong, easy-to-use controls exactly where risk is high.

Secure by design and by default: Modern guidance adds two practical slogans. Secure by design: think about security from the first diagram, using threat modelling and these principles, instead of patching at the end. Secure by default: ship products with safe settings switched on, such as automatic updates, no default passwords and encryption enabled, so that users who never change any setting are still protected.

Real-life example 1, a bank branch and its software: In a typical bank, a teller can process deposits up to a limit (least privilege). Larger transactions need a manager's approval (separation of privilege). New staff accounts start with no access (fail-safe default). Every transaction screen re-checks the user's rights against the account (complete mediation). The core banking system uses standard published cryptography instead of a secret home-made algorithm (open design). And there are guards, CCTV, vault locks, audit logs and backups (defence in depth).

Real-life example 2, your Android phone: Apps run in separate sandboxes and cannot read each other's data (least common mechanism and least privilege). Apps must ask before using the camera, location or contacts, and you can deny them (fail-safe defaults). Unlock needs a fingerprint or PIN, which is quick enough that people actually use it (psychological acceptability). The operating system, the app store review, Google Play Protect scanning and regular security updates form several layers (defence in depth).

Common mistakes: Giving every developer full production access "to save time". Allow-by-default rules with a block list. Checking authorisation only on the first page of a flow. Inventing a secret encryption scheme. Thinking a hidden URL is protection. Making security so painful that staff share passwords. Building one very strong wall and nothing behind it.

What exams ask: List and explain Saltzer and Schroeder's design principles with an example of each. State Kerckhoffs's principle and explain why open design is preferred over security through obscurity. Explain defence in depth with a layered diagram. Given a scenario (for example, a web app where users can view others' records), identify which principle is violated and suggest a fix.

Recap: Least privilege limits damage. Fail-safe defaults deny unless allowed. Economy of mechanism keeps security code small and simple. Complete mediation checks every access every time. Open design and Kerckhoffs's principle say only the key should be secret. Separation of privilege needs two conditions. Least common mechanism reduces sharing. Psychological acceptability keeps controls usable. Defence in depth stacks different layers, and the weakest link decides real strength. In the next lesson we open the cryptography toolbox, starting with the oldest ciphers.
key_points: Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) listed design principles that still guide secure systems.
Least privilege: give only the rights needed, for only as long as needed, to contain damage.
Fail-safe defaults: deny by default; mistakes then lock people out instead of letting attackers in.
Complete mediation: check authority on every access, not just once at login.
Open design and Kerckhoffs's principle: security should depend only on the secrecy of the key, not the algorithm.
Separation of privilege needs two independent conditions; economy of mechanism keeps security code simple.
Psychological acceptability: controls must be easy to use or people will bypass them.
Defence in depth uses several different layers; attackers look for the weakest link.
lessons.tip: Learn each principle with one everyday example of your own (a bank locker, a hostel gate, your phone). Examples are what examiners want and what you will remember.
lessons.task: Choose one system you know well (your university portal, a family shop's accounts, a WhatsApp group). For each of the eight Saltzer-Schroeder principles, write one sentence on whether the system follows it or breaks it.

quiz.q: A web app checks login only once, then shows any order whose number you type in the URL. Which principle is broken?
quiz.explain: Every access to every object must be checked; here the ownership of each order is never checked.

quiz.q: Kerckhoffs's principle says a cryptosystem should stay secure even if:
options: The attacker has unlimited computing power
The system is used for a very long time
Everything except the key is known to the enemy
quiz.explain: Only the key should need to be secret; the algorithm can be public.

quiz.q: A firewall that blocks all traffic except a short list of allowed services is an example of:
quiz.explain: Denying by default and allowing only explicit exceptions is a fail-safe default.

quiz.q: A bank requires two officers to approve payments above ten lakh taka. Which principle is this?
quiz.explain: Two independent conditions must be met, which is separation of privilege.

quiz.q: Why is security through obscurity weak as the main protection?
options: Once the hidden detail is discovered, no protection remains
quiz.explain: Hidden details are often found by scanning or leaks; then nothing else protects the system.

lessons.title: Cryptography Basics and Substitution Ciphers: Caesar and Frequency Analysis
lessons.content:
When you were in class five, did you and your best friend ever write secret notes by shifting every letter, so that "MEET AT TIFFIN" became something strange that the teacher could not read? If so, you have already used one of the oldest ciphers in history. Two thousand years ago Julius Caesar reportedly did almost exactly the same thing with his military messages. In this lesson we learn the basic words of cryptography, look at how a code-breaker thinks, and then break the Caesar cipher and its bigger cousin, the general substitution cipher, with nothing but counting. Breaking these old ciphers is not just history: it teaches the most important lesson in cryptography, that a large number of keys alone does not make a cipher secure.

The basic vocabulary: Plaintext is the original readable message, for example "SEND 500 TAKA". Ciphertext is the scrambled version that looks like nonsense. Encryption is the process that turns plaintext into ciphertext; decryption turns ciphertext back into plaintext. A cipher is the algorithm (the method) used for encryption and decryption. A key is the secret value that controls the cipher; the same cipher with a different key gives different ciphertext. The set of all possible keys is called the key space. Cryptography is the art and science of designing ciphers; cryptanalysis is the art and science of breaking them; cryptology covers both.

A tiny bit of notation: We write encryption as C = E(K, P), meaning ciphertext C is the encryption of plaintext P under key K, and decryption as P = D(K, C). The basic correctness rule is D(K, E(K, P)) = P: decrypting with the right key always gives back the original message. When the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt, the scheme is called symmetric (or secret-key) cryptography. Later in the course we will meet asymmetric (public-key) cryptography, where one key encrypts and a different key decrypts.

Codes vs ciphers: In everyday speech people say "secret code" for everything, but cryptographers separate the two. A code replaces whole words or phrases with code words from a codebook, for example "the eagle has landed" meaning "the shipment arrived". A cipher works on small units such as letters, bits or bytes, using a fixed rule and a key. Modern cryptography is almost entirely about ciphers, because they work for any message and need only a short key instead of a huge book.

What the attacker can do: Following Kerckhoffs's principle from the previous lesson, we always assume the attacker knows the cipher algorithm, and only the key is secret. Cryptanalysts classify attacks by how much the attacker gets to see. Ciphertext-only attack: the attacker has only ciphertexts, for example intercepted messages. Known-plaintext attack: the attacker also knows some plaintext-ciphertext pairs, for example because every message begins with "Dear Sir". Chosen-plaintext attack: the attacker can get plaintexts of their choice encrypted, for example by sending a message that the victim's system will encrypt. Chosen-ciphertext attack: the attacker can get chosen ciphertexts decrypted, for example by sending modified data to a server and watching its reaction. A modern cipher must stay secure even against chosen-plaintext and chosen-ciphertext attackers. Classical ciphers usually fail already at ciphertext-only.

Brute force: The simplest attack on any cipher is brute force, also called exhaustive key search: try every key until the plaintext makes sense. Its cost depends only on the size of the key space. If there are N keys, an attacker needs N tries in the worst case and about N/2 on average. Security engineers therefore demand that the key space be so large that trying all keys is hopeless. But as we will see, a huge key space is necessary, not sufficient.

Substitution vs transposition: All classical ciphers do one or both of two things. Substitution replaces each letter by another letter or symbol, so the letters change but stay in their places. Transposition keeps the same letters but shuffles their positions. Modern ciphers like AES combine many rounds of both ideas. This lesson covers substitution; the next lesson adds transposition and the stronger polyalphabetic ciphers.

The Caesar cipher: Number the letters A=0, B=1, up to Z=25. Pick a key k between 1 and 25. Encrypt each letter by C = (P + k) mod 26 and decrypt by P = (C - k) mod 26. The "mod 26" means we wrap around after Z, like a clock: with k = 3, X becomes A, Y becomes B and Z becomes C. Caesar is said to have used k = 3.

Caesar worked example: Encrypt HELLO with k = 3. H is 7, and 7 + 3 = 10, which is K. E is 4, and 4 + 3 = 7, which is H. L is 11, and 11 + 3 = 14, which is O, twice. O is 14, and 14 + 3 = 17, which is R. So HELLO becomes KHOOR. Similarly DHAKA becomes GKDND: D(3) to G(6), H(7) to K(10), A(0) to D(3), K(10) to N(13), A to D. To decrypt KHOOR, subtract 3 from each: K(10) - 3 = 7 = H, and so on, giving HELLO back. In pseudo-code: for each letter ch: out += chr((ord(ch) - 65 + k) mod 26 + 65).

Breaking Caesar by brute force: The key space has only 25 useful keys. An attacker simply writes the ciphertext decrypted with k = 1, 2, 3, up to 25 and reads down the list until one line is readable English or Bangla written in Latin letters. On paper this takes ten minutes; on a computer, microseconds. Caesar fails because its key space is tiny.

The general monoalphabetic substitution cipher: To fix the tiny key space, let the key be any arrangement of the alphabet. For example the key might say A becomes Q, B becomes W, C becomes E, and so on, with every letter mapped to a different letter. Each letter of the plaintext is always replaced by the same ciphertext letter, which is why it is called monoalphabetic (one alphabet). How many keys are there? The first letter can go to any of 26 letters, the second to any of the remaining 25, and so on, giving 26! = 26 x 25 x ... x 1, about 4.03 x 10^26 keys, which is roughly 2^88. Even at a trillion (10^12) keys per second, brute force would take around 13 million years. It sounds unbreakable. It is not.

Why it still breaks, frequency analysis: Human languages do not use letters equally. In typical English text the most common letter is E (about 12-13 percent of letters), followed by T, A, O, I and N; the rarest include J, Q, X and Z. Common pairs include TH, HE and IN, and THE is the most common three-letter word. A monoalphabetic cipher replaces each letter by one fixed letter, so it hides which letter is which, but it does not hide how often each letter appears. The most common ciphertext letter very likely stands for E. This method was described by the Arab scholar Al-Kindi in the ninth century, making him one of the first known cryptanalysts.

Frequency analysis worked: Suppose you intercept this ciphertext: TLLA TL ULHY AOL AYLL ILZPKL AOL NYLLU NHAL. It has 35 letters. Count them: L appears 13 times, far more than any other letter; A appears 5 times; Y appears 3 times. Guess that L stands for E. In a Caesar cipher, the shift is then L minus E = 11 - 4 = 7. Decrypt everything with k = 7: T(19) - 7 = 12 = M, L becomes E, A(0) - 7 = -7, and -7 mod 26 = 19 = T. The whole message reads MEET ME NEAR THE TREE BESIDE THE GREEN GATE. One count and one subtraction broke the cipher, no brute force needed. The repeated three-letter word AOL, which decrypts to THE, would have given the same answer.

Breaking a general substitution: For a full substitution key, the attacker does the same thing letter by letter. Map the most common ciphertext letter to E, the next to T or A, then look for a three-letter word that appears often and guess THE, which gives T and H. Look for double letters (LL, EE, SS, OO are common in English), single-letter words (A or I), and word endings like -ING and -TION. Each correct guess makes more words partly readable, and the rest falls like a crossword puzzle. With a few hundred letters of ciphertext, a patient person with pencil and paper can usually recover the whole key. Short messages are harder, because counts are less reliable, but the method still helps.

The big lesson: The monoalphabetic cipher has about 2^88 keys, more than many modern requirements, yet it falls to a schoolchild with a pencil. Why? Because the ciphertext leaks the structure of the plaintext: letter frequencies, repeated words, word lengths and spaces. A secure cipher must make the ciphertext look random, giving the attacker no usable pattern. This idea, hiding statistical patterns, will lead us to the concepts of confusion and diffusion and eventually to AES.

Small improvements and their limits: People tried to fix substitution ciphers by removing spaces, writing in fixed groups of five letters, adding meaningless "null" letters, or giving common letters several possible replacements (homophonic substitution, so E might become any of 7, 23 or 51). These make frequency analysis harder but not impossible, since pairs of letters and other patterns still leak. The real fix, using several alphabets that change from letter to letter, is the topic of the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, puzzle pages and simple apps: Newspaper puzzle pages and many mobile puzzle apps offer "cryptograms", which are exactly monoalphabetic substitution ciphers of a famous quote. People solve them for fun in a few minutes using frequency and word patterns. If a fun puzzle can be solved by hobbyists, it can never protect a bank PIN. Likewise, ROT13 (Caesar with k = 13) is still used on some forums to hide spoilers or puzzle answers, which is fine because it is meant only to stop accidental reading, not attackers.

Real-life example 2, a fake "encrypted" app: Imagine a small Dhaka startup that stores customer phone numbers "encrypted" by replacing each digit with another digit using a fixed table. That is a substitution cipher on digits, with only 10! = 3,628,800 possible keys, which a laptop tries in about a second. Worse, if an attacker knows one customer's real number (a known-plaintext attack), the table is partly revealed at once. The fix is to use a standard modern cipher such as AES from a well-tested library, as Kerckhoffs would advise.

Common mistakes: Calling any scrambling "encryption" even when it has no secret key. Believing a large key space guarantees security. Forgetting the wrap-around in mod 26 (for example, writing -7 instead of 19). Mixing up plaintext and ciphertext alphabets when writing a substitution key. Assuming the attacker does not know the algorithm.

What exams ask: Define plaintext, ciphertext, key, cipher, cryptography and cryptanalysis. Encrypt or decrypt a word with Caesar for a given k. Explain why Caesar falls to brute force. Compute the key space of a monoalphabetic substitution cipher. Show how frequency analysis breaks a given ciphertext. List the four attack models from ciphertext-only to chosen-ciphertext.

Recap: Encryption uses a cipher and a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext; cryptanalysis tries to break it. Attackers know the algorithm and are classified by what they can see: ciphertext-only up to chosen-ciphertext. Caesar shifts letters by k with C = (P + k) mod 26 and breaks with only 25 tries. Monoalphabetic substitution has 26! keys but breaks by frequency analysis because letter statistics leak through. Key space must be large, and ciphertext must also hide patterns. Next we see how Vigenere tried to hide those patterns.
key_points: Plaintext is readable; ciphertext is scrambled; a cipher is the algorithm; the key is the secret; cryptanalysis is breaking ciphers.
Symmetric cryptography uses the same key for encryption and decryption: D(K, E(K, P)) = P.
Attack models: ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext; modern ciphers must resist all of them.
Caesar cipher: C = (P + k) mod 26; with only 25 keys it falls to brute force immediately.
Monoalphabetic substitution has 26! (about 2^88) keys but still breaks easily.
Frequency analysis works because each plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter, so letter statistics leak.
A large key space is necessary but not sufficient; ciphertext must also hide the patterns of the plaintext.
lessons.tip: Do frequency analysis by hand at least once. Counting letters with a pencil makes you truly understand why modern ciphers must make ciphertext look random.
lessons.task: Ask a friend to encrypt a two or three sentence English message with a Caesar shift of their choice. Count the letters of the ciphertext, guess which one is E, compute the shift and decrypt it without asking for the key.

quiz.q: Which of these is the cryptanalyst's job?
options: Breaking ciphers or finding weaknesses in them
quiz.explain: Cryptanalysis is the study of breaking ciphers; cryptography designs them.

quiz.q: What is HELLO encrypted with a Caesar cipher using k = 3?
quiz.explain: Each letter moves 3 forward: H to K, E to H, L to O, L to O, O to R.

quiz.q: How many keys does a general monoalphabetic substitution cipher on 26 letters have?
quiz.explain: Any arrangement of the 26 letters can be a key, giving 26 factorial keys.

quiz.q: In a Caesar ciphertext the most frequent letter is L. If L stands for E, what is the shift k?
An attacker knows that every intercepted message begins with 'Dear Sir' and has the matching ciphertext. This is a:
quiz.explain: The attacker knows some plaintext and its corresponding ciphertext.

lessons.title: Polyalphabetic and Transposition Ciphers: Vigenere, Kasiski and Enigma
lessons.content:
Frequency analysis broke every monoalphabetic cipher because one plaintext letter always became the same ciphertext letter. So cryptographers of the Renaissance asked a clever question: what if the same letter E became K in one place, P in the next and Z after that? Then counting letters would show a flat, boring distribution and the code-breaker would have nothing to hold on to. That idea, using several substitution alphabets in turn, gave the Vigenere cipher, which was called "le chiffre indechiffrable", the indecipherable cipher, for about three hundred years. In this lesson we work through Vigenere by hand, see how it was finally broken, add the second classical trick of transposition, take a quick look at the famous Enigma machine, and collect the lessons that modern cryptography learned from all of them.

Polyalphabetic substitution: A polyalphabetic cipher uses more than one substitution alphabet and switches between them as it moves through the message. The key decides which alphabet is used for each letter. The goal is to flatten letter frequencies: E is still common in the plaintext, but its ciphertext appearances are spread over several different letters, so no single ciphertext letter stands out.

The Vigenere cipher: The best-known polyalphabetic cipher is named after Blaise de Vigenere, a sixteenth-century French diplomat, although a similar method had been described earlier by Giovan Battista Bellaso. The key is a word, for example LEMON. Write the key repeatedly under the plaintext. Each key letter gives a Caesar shift: A means shift 0, B means shift 1, L means shift 11, and so on. Encryption is C_i = (P_i + K_i) mod 26, and decryption is P_i = (C_i - K_i) mod 26, where K_i is the key letter under position i. So Vigenere is simply several Caesar ciphers taking turns.

Vigenere worked example: Encrypt ATTACKATDAWN with key LEMON. Write the key repeating: LEMONLEMONLE. Now add letter by letter using A=0 to Z=25. A(0) + L(11) = 11 = L. T(19) + E(4) = 23 = X. T(19) + M(12) = 31, and 31 mod 26 = 5 = F. A(0) + O(14) = 14 = O. C(2) + N(13) = 15 = P. K(10) + L(11) = 21 = V. A(0) + E(4) = 4 = E. T(19) + M(12) = 31 mod 26 = 5 = F. D(3) + O(14) = 17 = R. A(0) + N(13) = 13 = N. W(22) + L(11) = 33 mod 26 = 7 = H. N(13) + E(4) = 17 = R. The ciphertext is LXFOPVEFRNHR. To decrypt, subtract the same key letters and you get ATTACKATDAWN back.

What the example shows: Look at the two T's at the start of ATTACK: the first became X and the second became F. Meanwhile the four A's in the message became L, O, E and N. The same plaintext letter turns into different ciphertext letters, and different plaintext letters can turn into the same ciphertext letter. A frequency count on this ciphertext shows no obvious E. That is exactly why Vigenere resisted simple frequency analysis for so long. Historically people used a 26 x 26 table called the Vigenere square (tabula recta) to do the additions without arithmetic: find the plaintext letter's column, the key letter's row, and read the cell.

Key space of Vigenere: If the key has m letters, there are 26^m possible keys. For a 5-letter key that is 26^5 = 11,881,376, and for 10 letters about 1.4 x 10^14. Bigger than Caesar, but as with the substitution cipher, the real weakness is not the key count. It is the repetition: the key is reused every m letters.

Breaking Vigenere, the Kasiski idea: In the nineteenth century, Charles Babbage (unpublished) and Friedrich Kasiski (published in 1863) found the crack. If the same plaintext fragment appears twice at positions that are a multiple of the key length apart, it is encrypted with the same key letters and produces the same ciphertext fragment. Example: encrypt THESUNANDTHEMOON with key KEY. The word THE appears at positions 0 and 9; 9 is a multiple of 3, so both copies become DLC, and the ciphertext DLCCYLKRBDLCWSMX shows DLC twice, 9 letters apart. An attacker looks for repeated ciphertext sequences and measures their distances. If repeats occur 15 and 25 letters apart, the key length likely divides both, so the gcd(15, 25) = 5 is a strong candidate.

Finishing the attack: Once the key length m is known, split the ciphertext into m columns: letters 1, m+1, 2m+1 and so on were all shifted by the first key letter, letters 2, m+2, ... by the second key letter, and so on. Each column is just a Caesar cipher, and we already know how to break Caesar with frequency analysis: find the most common letter in each column and assume it is E. With enough ciphertext, the whole key falls out one letter at a time. Later, William Friedman's index of coincidence gave a statistical way to estimate the key length even without repeats. The lesson: a repeating key leaks structure.

What if the key never repeats: If the Vigenere key were truly random and as long as the message, never reused, the Kasiski attack would have nothing to find. That special case is the one-time pad, which is provably unbreakable, and it is the topic of the next lesson. Using a long book passage as a key (a running-key cipher) is not enough, because the key itself is English text with its own frequencies.

Playfair in brief: Another classical idea was to encrypt pairs of letters instead of single letters. The Playfair cipher, invented by Charles Wheatstone in 1854 and promoted by Lord Playfair, puts a keyword and the remaining letters into a 5 x 5 grid (I and J share a cell) and encrypts each pair of letters by rules based on their positions in the grid: same row, same column, or rectangle. Since there are about 600 possible letter pairs instead of 26 letters, frequency analysis is harder, but pair frequencies still leak, and Playfair can be broken with enough text. It was used for tactical messages in wars where it only had to hold for a few hours.

Transposition ciphers: A transposition cipher does not change letters at all; it rearranges them. The ciphertext therefore has exactly the same letter frequencies as normal language, which immediately tells a cryptanalyst that transposition, not substitution, was used. Two classic examples are rail fence and columnar transposition.

Rail fence worked: Write the plaintext in a zigzag over a number of "rails" (rows), then read the rows one after another. Take WEAREDISCOVERED with 3 rails. Going down and up in a zigzag, row 1 gets the letters at positions 1, 5, 9, 13: W, E, C, R. Row 2 gets positions 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14: E, R, D, S, O, E, E. Row 3 gets positions 3, 7, 11, 15: A, I, V, D. Reading rows: WECR + ERDSOEE + AIVD = WECRERDSOEEAIVD. The key is just the number of rails, so brute force over a handful of values breaks it.

Columnar transposition worked: Write the plaintext in rows under a key of column numbers, then read the columns in the key's order. Plaintext ATTACKATDAWN, key 3 1 4 2 (four columns). Rows: ATTA / CKAT / DAWN. Column labelled 1 is the second column: T, K, A. Column 2 is the fourth: A, T, N. Column 3 is the first: A, C, D. Column 4 is the third: T, A, W. Ciphertext: TKA ATN ACD TAW, written together TKAATNACDTAW. A receiver who knows the key writes the columns back in place and reads the rows. Doing two columnar transpositions in a row (double transposition) was much stronger and was used in both world wars.

Combining both tricks, a product cipher: Substitution alone leaks frequencies; transposition alone leaks letters. Combining them, a substitution followed by a transposition, possibly repeated, gives a product cipher that is much stronger than either part. This is the seed of modern block cipher design: AES, which you will meet soon, is essentially many rounds of carefully designed substitution and permutation steps.

Enigma, a brief story: In the twentieth century, cipher machines automated polyalphabetic encryption. The German Enigma machine used rotating wheels (rotors) that changed the substitution alphabet after every key press, plus a plugboard that swapped letter pairs, giving an enormous number of settings. Polish mathematicians led by Marian Rejewski broke early versions in the 1930s, and the British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, built on their work during World War II, using electro-mechanical machines called bombes. Enigma fell not because of brute force over its huge key space but because of design weaknesses (for example, a letter was never encrypted to itself) and operator mistakes such as predictable message beginnings. Again: structure and human habits leak.

Lessons from classical crypto: Several lessons stay true today. A big key space is not enough; the cipher must hide all statistical structure. Reusing keys creates patterns that attackers exploit. Known or guessable plaintext (like "Dear Sir" or weather reports) helps attackers a lot, so a modern cipher must resist known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks. And human procedures matter as much as mathematics.

Real-life example 1, a teaching exercise: Many university security classes in Bangladesh and elsewhere start a lab with a Vigenere challenge: students receive a few hundred letters of ciphertext and must find the key length with Kasiski's method and then break each column. It is a perfect warm-up because it uses only counting, gcd and Caesar, yet it shows exactly how real cryptanalysis works.

Real-life example 2, a home-made app "cipher": Suppose a student project hides saved passwords by adding the letters of a fixed word like DHAKA to every stored password, Vigenere style. Anyone who sees a few stored values and knows that one user's password was "password123" can subtract and recover the key immediately (a known-plaintext attack). The repeating key is the fatal flaw. Real systems should not store passwords encrypted at all, but hashed with salt, as you saw in Web Engineering and as we will study again in the authentication lesson.

Common mistakes: Forgetting mod 26 when the sum passes 25. Misaligning the key under the plaintext after skipping spaces. Thinking Vigenere's 26^m keys make it secure. Confusing transposition (letters move) with substitution (letters change). Assuming a running key from a book is as good as a random one.

What exams ask: Encrypt and decrypt a short message with Vigenere. Explain why Vigenere defeats simple frequency analysis. Explain the Kasiski test and compute a likely key length from repeat distances using gcd. Encrypt with rail fence or columnar transposition. Distinguish substitution and transposition and explain product ciphers.

Recap: Polyalphabetic ciphers like Vigenere use several shifts in turn: C_i = (P_i + K_i) mod 26, so ATTACKATDAWN with LEMON gives LXFOPVEFRNHR. They flatten letter frequencies but the repeating key leaks: Kasiski finds the key length from repeat distances, and each column is then a simple Caesar. Transposition ciphers rearrange letters; rail fence and columnar are classic examples. Combining substitution and transposition gives stronger product ciphers, the ancestors of AES. Next: the only cipher proven unbreakable, and why we almost never use it.
key_points: Polyalphabetic ciphers switch between several substitution alphabets to flatten letter frequencies.
Vigenere: C_i = (P_i + K_i) mod 26 with a repeating key word; ATTACKATDAWN with LEMON gives LXFOPVEFRNHR.
A Vigenere key of m letters gives 26^m keys, but the repeating key is the real weakness.
Kasiski test: repeated ciphertext fragments are usually a multiple of the key length apart; the gcd of distances suggests the length.
Once the key length is known, each column is a Caesar cipher broken by frequency analysis.
Transposition rearranges letters (rail fence, columnar); frequencies stay those of normal language.
Product ciphers combine substitution and transposition and are the ancestors of modern block ciphers.
Enigma fell through design weaknesses and operator habits, not brute force.
lessons.tip: Write the Vigenere square once by hand, or at least a few rows. After that, you will do Vigenere additions quickly and never forget the wrap-around.
lessons.task: Encrypt a 60-80 letter English sentence with Vigenere using a 3-letter key. Swap with a friend, tell each other only that the key has 3 letters, then split the ciphertext into 3 columns and break each column with frequency analysis.

quiz.q: What is the main idea that makes Vigenere stronger than a monoalphabetic cipher?
options: It uses a much longer alphabet
The same plaintext letter can become different ciphertext letters
quiz.explain: Different key letters give different shifts, so letter frequencies are flattened.

quiz.q: Encrypt the letter T with Vigenere key letter M (A=0, ..., Z=25).
Repeated ciphertext fragments are found 12, 18 and 30 letters apart. What is the most likely key length?
quiz.explain: The key length likely divides all distances; gcd(12, 18, 30) = 6.

quiz.q: What is WEAREDISCOVERED encrypted with a 3-rail rail fence cipher?
quiz.explain: Rows of the zigzag are WECR, ERDSOEE and AIVD, read one after another.

quiz.q: How can a cryptanalyst quickly tell that a ciphertext was made by transposition rather than substitution?
options: Its letter frequencies match normal language
quiz.explain: Transposition only moves letters, so the letter counts are the same as ordinary text.

lessons.title: Perfect Secrecy and Stream Ciphers: XOR, the One-Time Pad and CSPRNGs
lessons.content:
In the last lesson we saw that the Vigenere cipher broke because its key repeated. A natural question follows: what if the key never repeats? What if the key is completely random, as long as the message, and used only once and then burned? Surprisingly, this simple idea gives a cipher that is not just hard to break but mathematically impossible to break, no matter how much computing power the attacker has, today or in a thousand years. It is called the one-time pad. In this lesson we learn the XOR operation that modern cryptography uses everywhere, see why the one-time pad is perfect, why almost nobody uses it, and how stream ciphers try to keep its spirit with a short key. We finish with Shannon's ideas of confusion and diffusion, which guide every modern cipher.

XOR, the workhorse of cryptography: XOR (exclusive OR, written as a circled plus or simply "xor") works on bits. The rule: 0 xor 0 = 0, 0 xor 1 = 1, 1 xor 0 = 1, 1 xor 1 = 0. In words, the result is 1 when the two bits are different. Two properties make XOR perfect for ciphers. First, x xor x = 0 and x xor 0 = x. Second, it is its own inverse: if C = P xor K, then C xor K = P xor K xor K = P xor 0 = P. So the same operation with the same key both encrypts and decrypts. XOR is also extremely fast in hardware. Another way to see it: XOR is addition mod 2, the binary version of the mod 26 additions we did with Vigenere.

XOR worked example: The letter H in ASCII is 72, which is 01001000 in binary. Take a random key byte 10110011. Encrypt bit by bit: 0 xor 1 = 1, 1 xor 0 = 1, 0 xor 1 = 1, 0 xor 1 = 1, 1 xor 0 = 1, 0 xor 0 = 0, 0 xor 1 = 1, 0 xor 1 = 1. Ciphertext: 11111011. To decrypt, XOR again with the same key: 11111011 xor 10110011 = 01001000, which is H again. You can check each column yourself.

The one-time pad: The one-time pad (OTP) encrypts a message by XORing it with a key that is truly random, at least as long as the message, kept secret, and never reused, not even partly. With letters instead of bits, it is a Vigenere cipher whose key is a random string of letters as long as the message. The idea goes back to Gilbert Vernam, who in 1917 built a teleprinter that XORed message tape with key tape, and to Joseph Mauborgne, who insisted that the key be random and used only once. In 1949 Claude Shannon proved that this scheme has perfect secrecy.

What perfect secrecy means: A cipher has perfect secrecy if seeing the ciphertext gives the attacker absolutely no information about the plaintext, beyond its length. Formally, the probability of each possible plaintext is the same before and after seeing the ciphertext. Even an attacker with infinite computing power learns nothing, because there is nothing to compute.

Why OTP is perfect, worked: Take the ciphertext byte 11111011 from our example. If the key was 10110011, the plaintext was H. But if the key was 10110101, the plaintext would be 11111011 xor 10110101 = 01001110, which is N. In fact, for every possible plaintext byte there is exactly one key that produces this ciphertext. Since the key was chosen uniformly at random, every plaintext is equally likely. A brute-force attacker who tries all keys will see every possible message appear, including "YES" and "NO", "ATTACK" and "RETREAT", with no way to tell which is right. Compare with Caesar, where only one of 25 decryptions made sense.

The price of perfection: Shannon also proved that perfect secrecy requires the key to be at least as long as the message (more precisely, at least as many possible keys as possible messages). That creates huge practical problems. Key distribution: to send 1 gigabyte securely you must first deliver 1 gigabyte of secret random key to the other side, securely. If you have a secure channel for that, why not send the message through it? Key generation: the key must be truly random, not produced by a simple formula. Key storage and destruction: both sides must store large keys safely and destroy each part after use. Synchronisation: both sides must use exactly the same part of the pad for each message.

No integrity: The one-time pad gives confidentiality, not integrity. If an attacker knows a message is "PAY 100" and flips the right ciphertext bits, the receiver decrypts "PAY 900" without noticing. XOR is malleable: flipping a ciphertext bit flips the same plaintext bit. This is an important general lesson. Encryption alone does not stop tampering; later lessons add MACs and authenticated encryption for that.

The two-time pad disaster: What happens if the same pad is used twice? Suppose C1 = P1 xor K and C2 = P2 xor K. An attacker XORs the two ciphertexts: C1 xor C2 = P1 xor K xor P2 xor K = P1 xor P2. The key disappears completely. What remains is the XOR of two real messages, and since natural language has lots of structure, attackers can guess common words and gradually recover both messages. This is not just theory: in the Venona project, American codebreakers were able to read parts of Soviet messages from the 1940s because some one-time pad pages had been reused. The lesson is permanent: a key or keystream must never be used twice.

Where OTP is used: Because of the key distribution problem, the one-time pad is rare. It has been used for some diplomatic and military hotlines, where couriers could physically carry the key material in advance. For normal Internet traffic, sending as much secret key as data is impossible, so we need something more practical.

Stream ciphers, the practical cousin: A stream cipher keeps the OTP's structure, ciphertext = plaintext xor keystream, but generates a long keystream from a short secret key (say 128 or 256 bits) and a nonce, using a deterministic algorithm. The receiver, who has the same key and nonce, generates the same keystream and XORs to decrypt. We lose perfect secrecy, since the key is now much shorter than the message, but we can still get computational security: no realistic attacker can tell the keystream from true randomness or recover the key with any feasible amount of work.

Random vs pseudorandom: Truly random numbers come from physical processes: electrical noise, timing of keyboard and disk events, radioactive decay. A pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) is an algorithm that expands a small seed into a long sequence that looks random. Ordinary PRNGs, like the ones used in games and simulations (for example linear congruential generators or Python's random module), are not safe for cryptography: seeing a few outputs can let an attacker predict the rest. A cryptographically secure PRNG (CSPRNG) is designed so that, without the seed, nobody can predict the next bit with probability noticeably better than one half. For keys, tokens, OTP codes and password reset links, always use the operating system's CSPRNG, such as /dev/urandom on Linux or Python's secrets module, never random.

The nonce rule: Since a stream cipher with the same key and nonce produces the same keystream, reusing the pair recreates the two-time pad disaster. That is why every stream cipher needs a unique nonce (a "number used once") per message with a given key. The nonce does not have to be secret, only unique. Many real-world breaks came from nonce reuse, for example in some old Wi-Fi systems.

RC4, a cautionary tale: RC4, designed by Ron Rivest in 1987, was for years the most widely used stream cipher: it protected early Wi-Fi (WEP) and a large share of HTTPS traffic. Researchers found statistical biases in its keystream, and WEP used it in a weak way with short, repeating per-packet values, which allowed practical attacks. RC4 was eventually prohibited in TLS (RFC 7465, 2015). It shows that ciphers age, and that a cipher used carelessly can fail even faster.

ChaCha20 today: A widely trusted modern stream cipher is ChaCha20, designed by Daniel J. Bernstein. It uses only additions, rotations and XORs on 32-bit words, so it runs fast in software even on phones without special AES hardware. Combined with the Poly1305 authenticator as ChaCha20-Poly1305, it is one of the cipher suites of TLS 1.3 and is used in many apps and VPNs.
