Another common way to build a stream cipher is to run a block cipher such as AES in counter (CTR) mode, which we will meet in the modes lesson.

Confusion and diffusion: In the same period as his perfect secrecy work, Shannon described two properties a practical cipher should have. Confusion means the relationship between the key and the ciphertext should be as complex as possible, so that each ciphertext bit depends on the key in a complicated way; substitution boxes provide this. Diffusion means each plaintext bit should affect many ciphertext bits, spreading out the statistical structure of the plaintext; permutations and mixing steps provide this. Recall frequency analysis: monoalphabetic ciphers have no diffusion, so letter frequencies pass straight through. Modern block ciphers achieve both by repeating rounds of substitution and permutation, and a good cipher shows the avalanche effect: flipping one input bit changes about half of the output bits.

Real-life example 1, generating OTP codes and tokens: When a mobile banking app sends you a 6-digit verification code, or a website emails you a password reset link, those values must come from a CSPRNG. If a developer uses a predictable generator, for example seeded with the current time, an attacker who knows roughly when the code was made can try the few possible seeds and predict codes. Using the language's secure random library is a one-line change that removes the risk.

Real-life example 2, encrypted chats on a phone: When you chat on an end-to-end encrypted messenger on a budget Android phone in Bangladesh, the phone may not have AES hardware acceleration, and a stream cipher like ChaCha20 keeps encryption fast and battery-friendly. Each message uses a fresh nonce, so the keystream is never reused, and an authentication tag protects integrity. The spirit of the one-time pad survives: plaintext xor keystream, but with a short key that is easy to share using key exchange.

Common mistakes: Thinking a one-time pad is secure if the key is "random-looking" text such as a book passage. Reusing a pad or a stream cipher nonce. Using an ordinary PRNG for keys or tokens. Believing encryption also guarantees integrity. Forgetting that OTP requires a key as long as the message.

What exams ask: Define XOR and show encryption and decryption of a byte. Define perfect secrecy and explain why OTP achieves it. List the practical problems of OTP. Show algebraically why reusing a pad leaks P1 xor P2. Explain how stream ciphers differ from OTP and why nonces must be unique. Define confusion and diffusion with examples.

Recap: XOR is its own inverse, so C = P xor K and P = C xor K. The one-time pad uses a truly random key as long as the message, used once, and has perfect secrecy: the ciphertext reveals nothing. But it needs huge keys, gives no integrity, and collapses if reused, since C1 xor C2 = P1 xor P2. Stream ciphers generate a keystream from a short key and a unique nonce using a CSPRNG-like design; RC4 is broken, ChaCha20 is used today. Shannon's confusion and diffusion guide modern ciphers. Next: block ciphers, Feistel networks and DES.
key_points: XOR is addition mod 2 and its own inverse: if C = P xor K then P = C xor K.
The one-time pad uses a truly random key as long as the message, kept secret and never reused.
Perfect secrecy (Shannon, 1949): the ciphertext gives no information about the plaintext, even to an unlimited attacker.
OTP problems: huge keys to distribute, true randomness needed, no integrity (XOR is malleable).
Reusing a pad gives C1 xor C2 = P1 xor P2, which leaks both messages (the Venona lesson).
Stream ciphers expand a short key and a unique nonce into a keystream; they give computational, not perfect, security.
Use a CSPRNG for keys and tokens; RC4 is broken, ChaCha20 is a modern choice.
Confusion hides the key-ciphertext relationship; diffusion spreads plaintext structure; good ciphers show the avalanche effect.
lessons.tip: Practise XOR on 8-bit numbers until you can do it at a glance. It appears in stream ciphers, block ciphers, modes of operation, hashes and MACs for the rest of this course.
lessons.task: Write your name in ASCII binary (use any online ASCII table). Flip a coin 8 times per letter to make a truly random key, XOR to get the ciphertext, then XOR again to recover your name. Finally, XOR your ciphertext with a friend's ciphertext made with the same key and see what remains.

quiz.q: What is 1011 xor 0110?
quiz.explain: Bit by bit: 1 xor 0 = 1, 0 xor 1 = 1, 1 xor 1 = 0, 1 xor 0 = 1, giving 1101.

quiz.q: Which condition is NOT required for a one-time pad to have perfect secrecy?
options: The key is at least as long as the message
quiz.explain: The OTP algorithm (XOR) is public; only the key must be secret, random, long enough and used once.

quiz.q: If the same pad K encrypts P1 and P2, what does C1 xor C2 equal?
quiz.explain: The key cancels: C1 xor C2 = P1 xor K xor P2 xor K = P1 xor P2.

quiz.q: Which generator should be used to create a password reset token?
options: A linear congruential generator seeded with the time
A cryptographically secure PRNG such as the OS generator
quiz.explain: Tokens must be unpredictable, which needs a CSPRNG.

quiz.q: Which property means one changed plaintext bit should affect many ciphertext bits?
quiz.explain: Diffusion spreads the influence of each plaintext bit across the ciphertext.

lessons.title: Block Ciphers, Feistel Networks and DES
lessons.content:
Think of a big photocopy machine that does not copy but scrambles. You feed in exactly one page at a time, the machine shuffles and substitutes the letters on that page according to a secret setting, and out comes a page of nonsense of exactly the same size. Anyone with the same secret setting can feed the nonsense page into the machine's reverse mode and get the original back. That is a block cipher: it encrypts fixed-size blocks of data, one block at a time, under a secret key. Block ciphers are the backbone of modern symmetric cryptography: they protect your bank's database, your Wi-Fi, your phone's storage and every HTTPS connection. In this lesson we see what a block cipher really is, why the obvious "perfect" design is impossible, how the elegant Feistel structure solves the problem, and how DES, the first public standard cipher, rose, fell and taught us about key length.

Block vs stream: A stream cipher, as we saw, encrypts data bit by bit or byte by byte by XORing it with a keystream. A block cipher takes a whole block of n bits at once, for example 64 or 128 bits, and maps it to an n-bit ciphertext block using a k-bit key. For a fixed key, the block cipher must be a permutation: every possible plaintext block maps to a different ciphertext block, otherwise decryption would be ambiguous. Longer messages are split into blocks and handled by a mode of operation, which is the subject of lesson 09. The two types are not enemies: a block cipher in counter mode becomes a stream cipher.

What we want from a block cipher: We want it to behave like a random permutation chosen by the key. Even an attacker who can ask for encryptions of millions of chosen plaintexts should not be able to tell the cipher apart from a truly random permutation, or recover the key, with less work than brute force. That means strong confusion and diffusion: each output bit should depend on every input bit and every key bit in a complicated way, and changing one bit of input should change about half of the output bits (the avalanche effect).

The ideal block cipher and why it is impossible: The ideal would be a huge secret table that lists, for every possible input block, a random output block. For a toy 4-bit block there are only 16 possible inputs, so the table has 16 entries of 4 bits each, 64 bits in total, and there are 16! (about 2.1 x 10^13) possible tables. That is fine. But for a real 64-bit block, the table would need 2^64 entries of 8 bytes each, about 147 exabytes, as the key. No one can store or share that. So real block ciphers use a short key (56, 128 or 256 bits) and a clever algorithm that imitates a random permutation. The question is how to build such an algorithm that is also easy to invert.

Product ciphers and rounds: Following Shannon, real block ciphers repeat a simple round many times. Each round mixes in key material (a round key or subkey derived from the main key), applies substitution (small lookup tables called S-boxes for confusion) and applies permutation or linear mixing (for diffusion). One round is weak, but after enough rounds every output bit depends on every input and key bit. The procedure that derives round keys from the main key is called the key schedule.

The Feistel structure: Horst Feistel, working at IBM in the early 1970s, found a beautiful way to build an invertible cipher out of a round function that does not need to be invertible. Split the block into a left half L and a right half R. In each round i, with round key K_i: the new left half is the old right half, L_i = R_(i-1), and the new right half is R_i = L_(i-1) xor F(R_(i-1), K_i). Here F can be any function, as complicated and non-invertible as we like. After the last round, the halves are swapped back (implementations differ in this small detail).

Why decryption works: To undo one round, notice we know L_i and R_i. Since L_i = R_(i-1), we already have R_(i-1). Then compute F(R_(i-1), K_i) ourselves, using the same F and key, and XOR: L_(i-1) = R_i xor F(L_i, K_i). XOR cancels itself, so we get the old left half back. We never need to run F backwards. Decryption is the same structure with the round keys used in reverse order, so the same hardware or code can do both, a big advantage in the 1970s.

Feistel worked example: Use an 8-bit block split into two 4-bit halves, two rounds, round keys K1 = 0011 and K2 = 0101, and a toy round function F(R, K) = (R + K) mod 16. Plaintext: L0 = 1011 (11), R0 = 0110 (6). Round 1: L1 = R0 = 0110. F(0110, 0011) = (6 + 3) mod 16 = 9 = 1001, so R1 = L0 xor 1001 = 1011 xor 1001 = 0010. Round 2: L2 = R1 = 0010. F(0010, 0101) = (2 + 5) mod 16 = 7 = 0111, so R2 = L1 xor 0111 = 0110 xor 0111 = 0001. Ciphertext halves: L2 = 0010, R2 = 0001.

Decrypting the example: Go backwards with keys in reverse order. Undo round 2: R1 = L2 = 0010, and L1 = R2 xor F(L2, K2) = 0001 xor 0111 = 0110. Undo round 1: R0 = L1 = 0110, and L0 = R1 xor F(L1, K1) = 0010 xor 1001 = 1011. We are back at L0 = 1011, R0 = 0110. Real ciphers use far more rounds and a much stronger F, but the mechanics are exactly this.

DES, the Data Encryption Standard: In the early 1970s the US National Bureau of Standards (now NIST) asked for a public standard cipher. IBM submitted a design based on its earlier Lucifer cipher, and after changes involving the NSA it was published in 1977 as DES. For more than twenty years DES was the world's most widely used cipher, in banking, ATMs and government systems.

DES at a glance: Block size 64 bits. Key: 64 bits written down, but 8 of them are parity bits, so the effective key is 56 bits. It is a 16-round Feistel cipher. The key schedule produces sixteen 48-bit round keys. The data passes through an initial permutation, then 16 rounds, then the inverse permutation. The round function F takes the 32-bit right half, expands it to 48 bits, XORs it with the 48-bit round key, feeds the result through eight S-boxes that each turn 6 bits into 4 bits (giving 32 bits again), and finally permutes those 32 bits. The S-boxes are the only non-linear part and the heart of its security.

The S-box controversy: The NSA's role and the unexplained design of the S-boxes made many people suspect a hidden backdoor. In 1990, when Eli Biham and Adi Shamir publicly described differential cryptanalysis, it turned out the DES S-boxes were already strengthened against it, suggesting the designers knew this attack years earlier. The bigger real weakness was not hidden in the S-boxes; it was in plain sight: the 56-bit key was short.

Brute force against DES: A 56-bit key means 2^56, about 7.2 x 10^16, possible keys, and about 2^55 tries on average. At one billion keys per second, a single machine needs on average roughly one year. But special hardware changes everything. In 1998 the Electronic Frontier Foundation built a machine called Deep Crack for about 250,000 US dollars that found a DES key in 56 hours. In 1999, combined with thousands of volunteers' computers, a key was found in about 22 hours. DES was officially dead as a secure cipher, not because of a clever mathematical attack, but because computers had become fast enough to try every key.

Double DES and meet-in-the-middle: Why not encrypt twice with two keys, C = E(K2, E(K1, P)), for 112 bits of key? Because of the meet-in-the-middle attack. Given one known plaintext-ciphertext pair, the attacker encrypts P under all 2^56 values of K1 and stores the results in a table. Then the attacker decrypts C under all 2^56 values of K2 and looks each result up in the table. A match gives candidate keys, checked with a second pair. The work is about 2 x 2^56 = 2^57 operations plus a big table, not 2^112. Double encryption barely helps.

Triple DES: The practical fix was 3DES (Triple DES), which uses encrypt-decrypt-encrypt: C = E(K3, D(K2, E(K1, P))). With three independent keys, meet-in-the-middle still applies, so the effective strength is about 112 bits, not 168. The middle decryption allows compatibility: if K1 = K2 = K3, it reduces to single DES. 3DES kept old banking systems going for years, but it is slow (three DES operations per block) and its 64-bit block causes problems when huge amounts of data are encrypted with one key. NIST has deprecated it and no longer allows it for new encryption. Its successor, AES, is the next lesson.

Block size matters too: A 64-bit block can take only 2^64 values. By the birthday effect (lesson 15), after about 2^32 blocks, around 32 gigabytes, encrypted under one key, repeated ciphertext blocks become likely and can leak information in some modes. That is why modern ciphers use 128-bit blocks.

Real-life example 1, ATMs and bank cards: For decades, ATM networks and card PIN processing relied on DES and later 3DES to protect PIN blocks travelling from the ATM to the bank. As DES weakened, banks worldwide, including those whose ATMs you use in Bangladesh, migrated to 3DES and are moving to AES. Legacy systems last a long time, which is why understanding DES and 3DES still matters to engineers who maintain them.

Real-life example 2, a student's Feistel lab: A classic lab exercise is to implement a toy Feistel cipher in Python with 16-bit blocks, write any silly round function, and confirm that decryption with reversed keys always works, even when F throws away information. Then students change one plaintext bit and count how many ciphertext bits change after 1, 2, 4 and 8 rounds, watching diffusion grow round by round.

Common mistakes: Saying DES has a 64-bit key (effective 56). Thinking the Feistel round function must be invertible. Forgetting to reverse the round key order when decrypting. Believing double DES gives 112-bit security. Assuming 3DES with three keys gives 168-bit security. Confusing block size with key size.

What exams ask: Distinguish block and stream ciphers. Draw a Feistel round and prove that decryption works. Trace two rounds of a toy Feistel cipher. State DES parameters (block, key, rounds, round key size, S-boxes). Explain why DES became insecure. Explain meet-in-the-middle against double DES and the EDE structure of 3DES.

Recap: A block cipher is a keyed permutation on n-bit blocks; ideal random tables are impossible, so we build rounds of substitution and permutation with a key schedule. A Feistel network splits the block into halves, uses L_i = R_(i-1) and R_i = L_(i-1) xor F(R_(i-1), K_i), and decrypts with the same structure and reversed keys, even if F is not invertible. DES (1977) is a 16-round Feistel cipher with 64-bit blocks and 56-bit keys, broken by brute force in 1998. Double DES falls to meet-in-the-middle; 3DES gives about 112-bit strength but is retired. Next: AES.
key_points: A block cipher maps fixed-size n-bit blocks to n-bit blocks under a key; for each key it is a permutation.
A truly ideal block cipher would need an impossibly large table as key, so real ciphers use rounds and a key schedule.
Feistel round: L_i = R_(i-1), R_i = L_(i-1) xor F(R_(i-1), K_i); decryption uses the same structure with reversed round keys.
In a Feistel cipher the round function F does not need to be invertible.
DES (1977): 64-bit block, 56-bit effective key, 16 rounds, 48-bit round keys, eight 6-to-4-bit S-boxes.
DES fell to brute force: EFF's Deep Crack found a key in 56 hours in 1998.
Double DES gives only about 2^57 work because of meet-in-the-middle; 3DES (EDE) gives about 112-bit strength and is now retired.
Small 64-bit blocks become risky with large data under one key; modern ciphers use 128-bit blocks.
lessons.tip: Draw the Feistel diagram from memory until you can also explain decryption in two sentences. That single drawing answers many exam questions about DES.
lessons.task: Using paper or a few lines of Python, run the toy Feistel cipher from this lesson with a different plaintext and different keys. Then decrypt with the keys reversed and confirm you get the plaintext back. Try changing F to something that is not invertible, such as F(R, K) = (R AND K), and check that decryption still works.

quiz.q: What is the effective key length of DES?
quiz.explain: DES keys are written as 64 bits but 8 are parity bits, leaving 56 effective bits.

quiz.q: In a Feistel network, why can decryption work even when F is not invertible?
options: F is only ever recomputed in the forward direction and XOR cancels it
quiz.explain: Decryption recomputes F on a known half and XORs it away; F never runs backwards.

quiz.q: Toy Feistel round with F(R, K) = (R + K) mod 16: L0 = 1011, R0 = 0110, K1 = 0011. What is R1?
Why does double DES not give 112-bit security?
options: The meet-in-the-middle attack needs only about 2^57 operations plus memory
The second key is always equal to the first
quiz.explain: Encrypting forward from P and decrypting backward from C meet in a table, costing about 2 x 2^56 work.

quiz.q: What ended DES as a secure cipher in practice?
options: A backdoor found in its S-boxes
Brute-force key search with dedicated hardware
quiz.explain: Its 56-bit key was small enough for special machines like Deep Crack (1998) to try all keys.

lessons.title: AES: The Advanced Encryption Standard
lessons.content:
Imagine a lock that every bank in the world, every phone, every Wi-Fi router and every messaging app agrees to use. It must be fast enough to protect a 4K video stream, small enough to run on a cheap smart card, and strong enough that no government on Earth can pick it for decades. That is a tall order. In 1997 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) asked the world's cryptographers to design exactly such a lock, out in the open, and let everyone attack the candidates. The winner was a cipher called Rijndael, and today we call it AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard. When you open bKash, browse Daraz over HTTPS, or unlock an encrypted phone, AES is almost certainly doing the heavy lifting.

Where we are in the course: In lesson 07 we met block ciphers, the Feistel idea and DES. We saw that DES's 56-bit key became too short: special hardware searched the whole key space in days by 1998. Triple DES patched the problem but was slow and still used a small 64-bit block. The world needed a fresh design. In this lesson we look at AES at the concept level: what goes in, what comes out, what each round does and why. In lesson 09 we will learn how to use AES correctly on long messages (modes of operation), which is where most real mistakes happen.

The competition: NIST's process was itself a security lesson. It followed Kerckhoffs's principle from lesson 03: the design is public, only the key is secret. Fifteen candidate algorithms were submitted in 1998. After public analysis, five finalists remained: MARS, RC6, Rijndael, Serpent and Twofish. In October 2000 NIST announced Rijndael, designed by two Belgian cryptographers, Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. It became the standard FIPS 197 in November 2001. Rijndael won not because the others were broken, but because it combined strong security with excellent speed on everything from 8-bit chips to large servers.

The interface: AES is a block cipher. It takes a 128-bit block of plaintext (16 bytes) and a secret key, and outputs a 128-bit block of ciphertext. The key can be 128, 192 or 256 bits long, and the variants are called AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256. Decryption with the same key gives the plaintext back. Think of it as a keyed shuffling machine for exactly 16 bytes at a time: you cannot feed it 15 bytes or 17 bytes; longer messages are split into blocks and handled by a mode of operation.

Rounds: AES is built from rounds, the same idea we saw in DES: a simple step repeated many times becomes very strong. The number of rounds depends on the key size: 10 rounds for AES-128, 12 rounds for AES-192 and 14 rounds for AES-256. One important difference from DES: AES is not a Feistel network. In a Feistel cipher only half the block is changed per round. AES is a substitution-permutation network (SPN): every round transforms the whole 16-byte block. Because AES is not Feistel, decryption needs inverse versions of each step, run in reverse order.

The state: AES arranges the 16 bytes of a block into a 4 by 4 grid of bytes, called the state. The bytes are filled column by column: bytes 0 to 3 go into the first column, bytes 4 to 7 into the second, and so on. Every operation of the round works on this grid. Picture a 4 by 4 tray of eggs in a Dhaka bazar: some steps change each egg, some slide the rows, some mix the eggs within each column. Byte values are treated as elements of a special finite field with 256 elements, written GF(2^8). You do not need its full theory today; just know that it gives a way to add and multiply bytes so that every non-zero byte has an inverse.

Step 1, SubBytes: Each of the 16 bytes is replaced by another byte using a fixed lookup table called the S-box (substitution box). The S-box has 256 entries, one for each possible byte. It is built mathematically: take the multiplicative inverse of the byte in GF(2^8), then apply a fixed affine transformation. This makes the step strongly non-linear, which is the main source of confusion in Shannon's sense from lesson 06: the relationship between key and ciphertext becomes complicated. Without a non-linear step, the whole cipher would be a system of linear equations that an attacker could solve.

Step 2, ShiftRows: The rows of the state are rotated to the left. Row 0 does not move, row 1 rotates by 1 byte, row 2 by 2 bytes, and row 3 by 3 bytes. So the bytes of one column get spread into four different columns. On its own this is a trivial step, but it is essential teamwork: it makes sure that what happens in one column in this round affects all columns in the next round.

Step 3, MixColumns: Each column of 4 bytes is treated as a small vector and multiplied by a fixed 4 by 4 matrix, using GF(2^8) arithmetic. The result is a new column in which every output byte depends on all four input bytes. Change one input byte and all four output bytes change. ShiftRows spreads across columns and MixColumns spreads within columns; together they provide diffusion. After just two rounds, every byte of the state depends on every byte of the input. After ten rounds, the mixing is extremely thorough.

Step 4, AddRoundKey: The state is combined with a 128-bit round key using XOR, byte by byte. This is the only step that uses the key. Remember from lesson 06 that XOR with a secret value hides information perfectly when the value is random; here the round keys are not random, but they are derived from the secret key and change each round. Without this step all the other steps would be a fixed public scramble that anyone could undo.

Putting a full encryption together: AES-128 encryption looks like this in pseudo-code: state = plaintext; AddRoundKey(round key 0); then for rounds 1 to 9: SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey; then the final round 10: SubBytes, ShiftRows, AddRoundKey. Notice two details that exams love. First, there is an extra AddRoundKey at the very start, called key whitening, so that the attacker never sees an unkeyed step. Second, the last round skips MixColumns, which makes encryption and decryption more symmetric in structure without reducing security.

Key expansion: Where do the round keys come from? The key schedule (key expansion) stretches the original key into enough round keys. AES-128 needs 11 round keys of 16 bytes each, which is 176 bytes in total: one for the initial whitening plus one for each of the 10 rounds. The schedule works on 4-byte words: each new word is the XOR of the previous word and the word four positions earlier, and every fourth word is first rotated, passed through the S-box and XORed with a round constant. The details matter for implementers, but the concept is simple: one short secret key grows into a family of different round keys.

Decryption: Since every step is invertible, decryption runs the inverse steps in reverse order: InvShiftRows rotates rows to the right, InvSubBytes uses the inverse S-box, InvMixColumns multiplies by the inverse matrix, and AddRoundKey is its own inverse because XOR twice with the same key cancels out. The round keys are used from last to first. This is why AES implementations ship both an S-box and an inverse S-box.

Why AES is fast: Software implementations can merge SubBytes, ShiftRows and MixColumns into a few lookup tables, so each round becomes table lookups and XORs. Even better, most modern laptop, server and phone processors have dedicated AES instructions (on Intel and AMD chips they are called AES-NI, introduced around 2010; ARM processors have their own cryptography extensions). With hardware support, a single core can encrypt data at gigabytes per second. That is why turning on full-disk encryption on your laptop barely slows it down.

How strong is it: The best known attacks on full AES are only slightly better than brute force, nowhere near practical. So the security comes down to key size. A 128-bit key has 2^128 possible values, which is about 3.4 x 10^38. Suppose an attacker could test one trillion (10^12) keys per second. Then trying all keys takes about 1.08 x 10^19 years, which is close to a billion times the age of the universe. Even a fantasy machine testing 10^18 keys per second would need around 10^13 years. Compare DES: 2^56 keys at 10^12 per second takes about 20 hours. Every extra key bit doubles the work, which is why 72 more bits make such a difference.

AES-128 or AES-256: For ordinary use AES-128 is considered secure. AES-256 is chosen when organisations want an extra safety margin, for example against possible future quantum computers, which we discuss carefully in lesson 26. AES-256 is a little slower because it uses 14 rounds instead of 10. In practice, the strength of the key itself matters more: a 256-bit key derived from the password "123456" is only as strong as that password.

Side channels: A cipher can be mathematically sound and still leak its key through the way it runs. If a table-based implementation takes slightly different time depending on which memory location it reads, an attacker who measures timing or power use very precisely may learn key bits. These are called side-channel attacks. Hardware AES instructions and carefully written constant-time code avoid this. The lesson for programmers is simple: use a well-tested library, never write your own AES for real products.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet: When a Bangladeshi mobile wallet app talks to its server, the connection is protected by TLS (lesson 19), and in most connections the bulk data is encrypted with AES in GCM mode. Your PIN, the recipient's number and the amount travel as AES ciphertext. A person sharing the same cafe Wi-Fi in Dhanmondi sees only random-looking bytes. The app does not invent its own cipher; it relies on the platform's TLS library, which relies on AES.

Real-life example 2, an encrypted phone: Modern Android phones and iPhones encrypt the stored data with AES. The disk key is protected by a key derived from your screen lock and by secure hardware in the phone. If someone steals a locked phone at a busy bus stand in Gabtoli, pulling out the storage chip gives them only ciphertext. Here AES protects data at rest, while in the wallet example it protected data in transit.

Common mistakes: Saying AES is a Feistel cipher (it is a substitution-permutation network). Saying the block size changes with the key size (the block is always 128 bits; only the key and round count change). Forgetting the initial AddRoundKey or claiming MixColumns runs in the last round. Believing AES-256 is "twice as strong" as AES-128 (the brute-force work is 2^128 times larger, but both are far beyond reach). And the biggest real-world error: using AES correctly as a block cipher but incorrectly as a system, for example in ECB mode or with a reused nonce, which lesson 09 covers.

What exams ask: State the block size, key sizes and number of rounds of AES. Draw one AES round and explain the purpose of each of the four steps. Explain which steps provide confusion and which provide diffusion. Compare AES with DES (structure, block, key, rounds). Explain why the last round has no MixColumns and why there is an initial AddRoundKey. Compute how long brute force would take for a given key size and speed.

Recap: AES (Rijndael, FIPS 197, 2001) encrypts 128-bit blocks with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys using 10, 12 or 14 rounds. Each round does SubBytes (non-linear S-box), ShiftRows and MixColumns (diffusion), and AddRoundKey (the key). Round keys come from the key schedule. AES is fast, widely supported in hardware, and secure when used through a well-tested library and a proper mode. Next, we learn those modes.
key_points: AES (Rijndael by Daemen and Rijmen) won NIST's open competition and became FIPS 197 in 2001.
Block size is always 128 bits; keys are 128, 192 or 256 bits with 10, 12 or 14 rounds.
AES is a substitution-permutation network, not a Feistel cipher; the 16 bytes form a 4x4 state.
SubBytes gives non-linearity (confusion); ShiftRows and MixColumns give diffusion; AddRoundKey mixes in the key with XOR.
There is an initial AddRoundKey, and the final round has no MixColumns.
The key schedule expands one key into round keys (11 x 16 bytes for AES-128).
2^128 keys is about 3.4 x 10^38; brute force is hopeless, so real failures come from misuse and side channels.
Use AES through a trusted library with hardware support; never write your own for production.
lessons.tip: Draw the 4x4 state on paper and act out one round with coloured pens: change each cell, slide the rows, then mix each column. Once you can draw a round from memory, AES questions become easy marks.
lessons.task: Open Python and compute 2**128 and 2**56. Then calculate how many years brute force would take at 10**12 keys per second for each. Write one sentence explaining why 72 extra key bits make such a huge difference.

quiz.q: How many rounds does AES-256 use?
quiz.explain: AES-128 uses 10 rounds, AES-192 uses 12 and AES-256 uses 14.

quiz.q: What is the AES block size?
quiz.explain: The block is always 128 bits (16 bytes); only the key length and round count vary.

quiz.q: Which AES step is the main source of non-linearity (confusion)?
quiz.explain: SubBytes uses the S-box built from inverses in GF(2^8), which makes AES non-linear.

quiz.q: Which step is skipped in the final AES round?
quiz.explain: The last round does SubBytes, ShiftRows and AddRoundKey, but no MixColumns.

quiz.q: Which statement about AES structure is correct?
options: It is a Feistel network like DES
It is a substitution-permutation network that changes the whole block each round
It changes only half the block per round
quiz.explain: AES is an SPN; every round transforms all 16 bytes, unlike a Feistel round.

lessons.title: Modes of Operation: ECB, CBC, CTR and GCM
lessons.content:
Suppose you own the best padlock in the world, but you have a whole shop to protect, not a single box. If you put each item in its own box with the same lock and line the boxes up on the pavement, a thief cannot open any box, yet he can still learn a lot: which boxes are the same size, which ones look identical, and how many there are. A strong lock used in a careless way leaks information. AES from lesson 08 is that strong padlock, but it only locks exactly 16 bytes. Real messages are a PIN of 4 digits, a 300-byte JSON order, or a 2 GB video. The rules for applying a block cipher to data of any length are called modes of operation, and choosing the wrong mode is one of the most common real-world crypto mistakes.

What a mode must solve: A mode has to do three jobs. First, split a long message into 16-byte blocks and handle the last, shorter piece. Second, make sure that equal plaintext blocks do not produce equal ciphertext blocks, and that encrypting the same message twice gives different ciphertexts. Third, in modern designs, detect if anyone changed the ciphertext. The classic modes (ECB, CBC, CTR) handle only confidentiality. Modern authenticated modes such as GCM handle confidentiality and integrity together.

Notation: We write E(K, X) for encrypting one block X with AES under key K, and D(K, Y) for decrypting one block. P1, P2, P3 are plaintext blocks and C1, C2, C3 are ciphertext blocks. The symbol XOR is the bitwise exclusive-or from lesson 06.

ECB, Electronic Codebook: The simplest idea: encrypt each block on its own. C_i = E(K, P_i). Decryption is P_i = D(K, C_i). It looks innocent, but there is a deep flaw: the same plaintext block always becomes the same ciphertext block. It behaves like a giant codebook in which each 16-byte "word" has a fixed secret code. Anyone watching can see repeated blocks even without the key.

The penguin problem: The famous demonstration takes a picture of Tux, the Linux penguin, and encrypts its raw pixels with ECB. Areas of the same colour contain identical 16-byte blocks, so they encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks. The encrypted picture still clearly shows the outline of the penguin, just in strange colours. The cipher is strong, but the pattern leaks. A practical example: imagine an HR file where each employee's salary sits in its own 16-byte block, encrypted with ECB. Even without the key, a curious clerk can see which employees have the same salary as the boss. Rule: never use ECB for more than one block of real data.

CBC, Cipher Block Chaining: CBC fixes the pattern problem by mixing each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting: C_i = E(K, P_i XOR C_{i-1}). For the first block there is no previous ciphertext, so we use an initialisation vector, IV, as C_0. Decryption reverses it: P_i = D(K, C_i) XOR C_{i-1}. Now two equal plaintext blocks at different positions give different ciphertexts, because they are mixed with different previous blocks. If the IV is fresh and random for every message, encrypting the same message twice also gives totally different ciphertexts.

The IV rules for CBC: The IV is not secret; it is usually sent in front of the ciphertext. But it must be unpredictable, which in practice means freshly generated random bytes for every message. If an attacker can predict the next IV, chosen-plaintext attacks become possible; the BEAST attack of 2011 on old TLS 1.0 exploited predictable IVs. A fixed IV, such as sixteen zero bytes, makes the first block behave like ECB across messages.

CBC properties: Encryption is sequential: you need C1 before you can compute C2, so it cannot be parallelised. Decryption can run in parallel, because every C_{i-1} is already known. If one ciphertext bit is damaged in transit, the corresponding plaintext block decrypts to garbage and exactly one bit flips in the next block; the rest is fine. That last property also warns us: an attacker who flips a bit in C1 flips the same bit in P2. CBC provides no integrity on its own.

Padding with PKCS#7: ECB and CBC need the plaintext to be a whole number of blocks. PKCS#7 padding adds k bytes, each with the value k, where k = 16 minus (length mod 16). Worked example: the text "BKASH-ORDER" is 11 bytes long. 11 mod 16 = 11, so k = 16 - 11 = 5, and we add five bytes of value 05: BKASH-ORDER 05 05 05 05 05, exactly 16 bytes. When decrypting, the receiver reads the last byte (05), checks that the last five bytes are all 05, and removes them. What if the message is already exactly 16 bytes? Then k = 16 and a whole extra block of sixteen bytes of value 16 (0x10) is added, so the receiver never confuses data with padding. A 100-byte message gets 100 mod 16 = 4, so k = 12, total 112 bytes in 7 blocks.

Padding oracle, the idea only: Imagine a server that decrypts a CBC message and replies with one error for "bad padding" and a different error for "bad data". That tiny difference is called an oracle. Because flipping bits in C_{i-1} changes bits in P_i in a controlled way, an attacker who sends many modified ciphertexts and watches which error comes back can, step by step, learn the plaintext without ever learning the key. Serge Vaudenay described this in 2002 and it has hit real systems many times. We do not need the attack details; the lesson is that unauthenticated encryption plus detailed error messages is dangerous. The real cure is to authenticate the ciphertext before decrypting, as below.

CTR, Counter mode: CTR turns a block cipher into a stream cipher like the ones in lesson 06. You never encrypt the plaintext directly. Instead you encrypt a counter: keystream block i = E(K, nonce || i), where nonce is a unique value for this message and || means joining. Then C_i = P_i XOR keystream_i. Decryption is identical: XOR the same keystream again. Advantages: no padding is needed (just cut the last keystream block short), both encryption and decryption run in parallel, you can jump to block 1,000 directly, and only the encryption function E is needed.

The CTR golden rule: Never reuse a nonce with the same key. If two messages use the same nonce, they use the same keystream, and we are back to the two-time pad of lesson 06. Tiny worked example with one byte: P1 = 10110010, P2 = 01101100, shared keystream 11001010. Then C1 = 01111000 and C2 = 10100110. An eavesdropper computes C1 XOR C2 = 11011110, which is exactly P1 XOR P2: the key has cancelled out. With natural-language messages, P1 XOR P2 is often enough to recover both texts. Nonces can be counters or random, but they must never repeat under one key.

Other classic modes: You will also see CFB (cipher feedback) and OFB (output feedback) in textbooks. Both also make a block cipher behave like a stream cipher. They are mostly of historical interest today; CTR and the authenticated modes below have replaced them in new designs.

Why encryption alone is not enough: With CBC or CTR, an attacker who cannot read the message can still change it. In CTR, flipping bit 5 of the ciphertext flips bit 5 of the plaintext. If the attacker knows a payment message contains "amount=0100" at a certain position, they may turn it into a different amount without knowing the key. Confidentiality and integrity are different goals, as the CIA triad in lesson 01 told us. We need a check that detects any change.

Authenticated encryption and GCM: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) gives both in one step. Encryption takes a key, a nonce, the plaintext and optional associated data (for example a header that must stay readable but must not be changed) and outputs the ciphertext plus a short tag. Decryption checks the tag first and returns either the plaintext or a single error: "invalid". GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) is the most widely used AEAD with AES: it encrypts with CTR and computes the tag with a fast hash called GHASH over the ciphertext and associated data. Typical choices are a 96-bit nonce and a 128-bit tag. Nonce reuse in GCM is even worse than in CTR: besides leaking P1 XOR P2, it can let an attacker forge tags. MACs are explained properly in lesson 16.

ChaCha20-Poly1305: The other common AEAD combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher (lesson 06) with the Poly1305 authenticator. It is fast in pure software, so it is popular on phones and devices without AES hardware. TLS 1.3 (lesson 19) allows both AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, and it allows only AEAD ciphers.

Building it yourself, encrypt-then-MAC: If you must combine a classic mode with a MAC, the safe order is encrypt-then-MAC: encrypt the plaintext, then compute a MAC over the IV and the ciphertext, and on receipt verify the MAC before decrypting anything. This also kills padding oracles, because modified ciphertexts are rejected before the padding is ever checked. In practice, simply using an AEAD from a trusted library is easier and safer.

Real-life example 1, an e-commerce order API: A Chattogram-based online shop encrypts order records stored in its database. A junior developer first used AES-ECB because the library's default looked simple. A tester noticed that all orders for the same product and quantity had identical ciphertext prefixes, revealing what customers bought. The fix was AES-GCM with a fresh random 96-bit nonce per record, stored next to the ciphertext, with the order id as associated data so a record cannot be swapped into another order's row.

Real-life example 2, a messaging app on a budget phone: Many low-cost Android phones sold in Bangladesh have processors without AES instructions. A messaging app can choose ChaCha20-Poly1305 on those devices because it is fast in software, while using AES-GCM on phones with hardware support. Both give confidentiality and integrity; the choice is about speed and battery.

Common mistakes: Using ECB because it is the default. Using a constant or predictable IV in CBC. Reusing a nonce in CTR or GCM, for example after a device restarts its counter at zero. Encrypting without authentication and then returning detailed padding errors. Thinking the IV must be secret (it must be unique or unpredictable, not secret). Checking the tag after already using the decrypted data.

What exams ask: Draw the encryption and decryption diagrams for ECB, CBC and CTR and write their equations. Explain the ECB penguin. Compute PKCS#7 padding for a given length. Explain error propagation in CBC. State which modes can be parallelised. Explain why nonce reuse in CTR is fatal, using XOR. Explain what AEAD and GCM add over CBC.

Recap: A block cipher needs a mode. ECB leaks patterns and should not be used. CBC chains blocks with an unpredictable IV and needs padding such as PKCS#7. CTR makes a stream cipher from a counter and needs unique nonces. None of these alone protects integrity. Modern systems use AEAD, mainly AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, with unique nonces and tags checked before decryption.
key_points: A mode of operation tells how to use a 16-byte block cipher on data of any length.
ECB encrypts blocks independently, so equal blocks give equal ciphertext (the penguin problem); avoid it.
CBC: C_i = E(K, P_i XOR C_{i-1}) with a fresh unpredictable IV; it needs padding and encrypts sequentially.
PKCS#7 adds k bytes of value k; an 11-byte message gets five 05 bytes, a full block gets an extra block of 16s.
CTR: C_i = P_i XOR E(K, nonce || i); parallel and no padding, but a reused nonce gives a two-time pad.
CBC and CTR give confidentiality only; attackers can flip bits, and padding oracles can leak plaintext.
AEAD modes (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) give confidentiality and integrity with a tag checked before decryption.
IVs and nonces need not be secret, but must be unique (and for CBC unpredictable).
lessons.tip: For each mode, practise drawing the encryption diagram with boxes for E, circles for XOR and arrows. Then ask two questions: what happens if two plaintext blocks are equal, and what happens if a nonce repeats? Those two questions explain almost every mode.
lessons.task: On paper, compute PKCS#7 padding for messages of length 5, 15, 16 and 33 bytes with a 16-byte block. Then take two 8-bit plaintexts of your choice, XOR each with the same keystream byte, and verify that XORing the two ciphertexts gives the XOR of the plaintexts.

quiz.q: Why is ECB mode considered insecure for real data?
options: It cannot be decrypted in parallel
Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks
quiz.explain: ECB encrypts each block independently, so repeated blocks and patterns are visible, as in the penguin picture.

quiz.q: A 11-byte message is padded with PKCS#7 for a 16-byte block. What is added?
quiz.explain: k = 16 - (11 mod 16) = 5, so five bytes each with value 05 are added.

quiz.q: What happens if CTR mode reuses a nonce with the same key?
options: The XOR of the two ciphertexts equals the XOR of the two plaintexts
The key is printed in the ciphertext
quiz.explain: Same nonce means same keystream, which cancels out: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2, the two-time pad problem.

quiz.q: What does an AEAD mode like AES-GCM add compared to plain CBC?
options: An authentication tag that detects any change to ciphertext or associated data
quiz.explain: AEAD outputs a tag; decryption rejects any modified ciphertext or associated data before returning plaintext.

quiz.q: In CBC mode, which statement is correct?
options: Encryption is sequential, but decryption can run in parallel
Encryption can run in parallel, decryption cannot
quiz.explain: Each C_i needs C_{i-1} first when encrypting; when decrypting all ciphertext blocks are already known.

lessons.title: Number Theory for Crypto I: Modular Arithmetic, GCD and Inverses
lessons.content:
Look at a wall clock. If it is 9 o'clock now, what time will it be 5 hours later? Not 14, but 2. The clock "wraps around" after 12. You have been doing modular arithmetic since childhood without calling it that. The same thing happens with days of the week: if today is Friday, then 7 days later it is Friday again, and 100 days later it is Sunday. This wrap-around arithmetic sounds like a children's puzzle, but it is the engine of public-key cryptography. RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves all live inside "clock arithmetic" with clocks that have hundreds of digits. In this lesson and the next we build exactly the number theory those systems need, with every step worked by hand.

Recap and goal: In Discrete Mathematics (deep-cse-1-3, lessons 13-15) you met divisibility, mod, gcd and the modular inverse. Here we revisit them from the cryptographer's point of view and push to the exact calculations used later: the extended Euclidean algorithm that finds an RSA private key in lesson 12, and the groups of numbers that Diffie-Hellman uses in lesson 13. The goal is that, by the end, you can compute 17 to the power minus 1 modulo 3120 on paper and explain why the answer exists.

Division with remainder: For any integer a and any positive integer n, there are unique integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) with a = q x n + r and 0 <= r < n. We write r = a mod n. Examples: 38 = 3 x 12 + 2, so 38 mod 12 = 2 (38 hours after midnight the clock shows 2). 100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so 100 mod 7 = 2, which is why Friday plus 100 days is Sunday, two days after Friday. For negative numbers the remainder is still between 0 and n-1: -7 = (-1) x 26 + 19, so -7 mod 26 = 19. Be careful: some programming languages (C, Java) give -7 % 26 = -7, while Python gives 19. Crypto code must handle this correctly.

Congruence: We say a is congruent to b modulo n, written a ≡ b (mod n), when n divides a - b; equivalently, a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n. So 38 ≡ 2 (mod 12) because 38 - 2 = 36 = 3 x 12, and 17 ≡ -9 (mod 26). Congruence behaves like equality in many ways: it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it splits all integers into n classes. Modulo 12 the classes are "remainder 0", "remainder 1", up to "remainder 11".

The set Z_n: We collect one representative of each class: Z_n = {0, 1, 2, ..., n-1}. Arithmetic in Z_n means: do the normal operation, then reduce mod n. In Z_12, 9 + 5 = 2 and 5 x 5 = 1 (because 25 = 2 x 12 + 1). In Z_26, which matches the 26 letters of the English alphabet, Caesar's cipher from lesson 04 is just adding 3: E(x) = (x + 3) mod 26.

Rules that make big numbers manageable: The key fact is that you may reduce at any time. (a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n, and the same for subtraction and multiplication. Worked example: what is (123 x 456) mod 7? Instead of multiplying, reduce first: 123 = 17 x 7 + 4, so 123 mod 7 = 4; 456 = 65 x 7 + 1, so 456 mod 7 = 1. Then 4 x 1 = 4, so the answer is 4. Check: 123 x 456 = 56088 = 8012 x 7 + 4. Same answer, but with tiny numbers. This is how computers handle 2048-bit numbers without ever building gigantic intermediate results: they reduce after every multiplication.

What about division: In ordinary arithmetic, to divide by 7 we multiply by 1/7. In Z_n there are no fractions, so we look for a number that "acts like 1/7": an x with 7 x x ≡ 1 (mod n). That x is the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo n, written 7^-1 mod n. For example, modulo 26, 7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1, so 7^-1 ≡ 15 (mod 26). Some numbers have no inverse at all. Modulo 9, the multiples of 6 are 6 x 0, 6 x 1, ... which reduce to only 0, 6 and 3; the value 1 never appears, so 6 has no inverse mod 9. To know when inverses exist, and how to find them fast, we need the greatest common divisor.

GCD and the Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) is the largest integer dividing both a and b. Factoring to find it is slow for big numbers, but Euclid's algorithm (around 300 BCE) is fast. It uses one fact: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), because any number dividing a and b also divides a - q x b, and vice versa. Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd. Worked example, gcd(252, 105): 252 = 2 x 105 + 42; 105 = 2 x 42 + 21; 42 = 2 x 21 + 0. The last non-zero remainder is 21, so gcd(252, 105) = 21. In pseudo-code: while b != 0: (a, b) = (b, a mod b); return a.

Why Euclid is fast: The remainders shrink quickly; at least every two steps the larger number is cut by more than half. So the number of steps grows with the number of digits, not with the size of the number. For 2048-bit numbers that means at most a few thousand steps, done in microseconds. This speed is one of the quiet reasons public-key crypto is practical.

Bezout's identity: For any integers a and b, there are integers x and y with a x x + b x y = gcd(a, b). If gcd(a, n) = 1, then a x x + n x y = 1. Reduce both sides mod n: the n x y term disappears, leaving a x x ≡ 1 (mod n). So x is the inverse of a! This gives the rule every exam asks: a has an inverse modulo n exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1. That explains our examples: gcd(7, 26) = 1, so 7 has an inverse mod 26; gcd(6, 9) = 3, so 6 has none mod 9.

Extended Euclidean algorithm, worked: We find the inverse of 17 modulo 3120 (you will meet these exact numbers in RSA, lesson 12). First run Euclid and keep the quotients. 3120 = 183 x 17 + 9. Then 17 = 1 x 9 + 8. Then 9 = 1 x 8 + 1. Then 8 = 8 x 1 + 0. The gcd is 1, so an inverse exists. Now walk back up, writing 1 as a combination. From the third line: 1 = 9 - 8. From the second line, 8 = 17 - 9, so 1 = 9 - (17 - 9) = 2 x 9 - 17. From the first line, 9 = 3120 - 183 x 17, so 1 = 2 x (3120 - 183 x 17) - 17 = 2 x 3120 - 367 x 17. So x = -367. Reduce it: -367 + 3120 = 2753. Therefore 17^-1 ≡ 2753 (mod 3120). Check: 17 x 2753 = 46801 = 15 x 3120 + 1. Correct.

A table method: Many students prefer to carry two columns while running Euclid forward instead of substituting backward. Keep pairs (r, t) starting with (3120, 0) and (17, 1); for each quotient q compute new r = old r - q x r and new t = old t - q x t. The rows are (9, -183), (8, 184), (1, -367). When r reaches 1, t = -367, the same answer. In Python 3.8 and later, pow(17, -1, 3120) returns 2753 directly, which is handy for checking homework.

The group Z_n*: Collect the numbers in Z_n that do have inverses: Z_n* = {a in Z_n : gcd(a, n) = 1}. For n = 10 we get Z_10* = {1, 3, 7, 9}. This set is closed under multiplication mod 10: 3 x 7 = 21 ≡ 1, 3 x 9 = 27 ≡ 7, 7 x 9 = 63 ≡ 3, 9 x 9 = 81 ≡ 1. Every element has an inverse in the set (3 and 7 are inverses of each other; 9 is its own inverse). A set with an operation that is closed, associative, has an identity (1) and inverses is called a group. When n is a prime p, every non-zero number is coprime to p, so Z_p* = {1, 2, ..., p-1}, which is the group Diffie-Hellman uses. The number of elements of Z_n* is Euler's phi function, the star of lesson 11.

Real-life example 1, calendar and rotation: A Dhaka school runs a 6-day class routine and wants to know which routine day falls on the 45th school day. Since 45 = 7 x 6 + 3, 45 mod 6 = 3, so it is routine day 3 (counting day 0 as the first). Rotating duty rosters, weekly bazar schedules and ring buffers in programs all use exactly this arithmetic.

Real-life example 2, undoing an affine cipher: A classroom cipher encrypts letter x (A = 0, ..., Z = 25) as E(x) = (7x + 3) mod 26. The letter H (7) becomes 7 x 7 + 3 = 52 ≡ 0, which is A. To decrypt you must undo "multiply by 7", which means multiplying by 7^-1 = 15: D(y) = 15 x (y - 3) mod 26. Check: D(0) = 15 x (-3) = -45 ≡ 7 (mod 26), which is H again. If the teacher had chosen 6 instead of 7, decryption would be impossible, because 6 has no inverse mod 26 (gcd 2). That is the same reason RSA insists that e is coprime to phi(n).

Common mistakes: Forgetting that a mod n must be non-negative and getting -367 instead of 2753. Trying to "divide" in modular arithmetic instead of multiplying by an inverse. Assuming every non-zero number has an inverse mod n (only those coprime to n). In extended Euclid, mixing up which coefficient belongs to which number during back-substitution. Always finish with a check: multiply a by your answer and reduce; you must get 1.

What exams ask: Compute a mod n for positive and negative a. Use reduction rules to compute a product mod n. Find gcd with Euclid showing every step. Find a modular inverse with the extended Euclidean algorithm and verify it. State and explain the condition for an inverse to exist. List the elements of Z_n* for a small n and show it is closed under multiplication.

Recap: Modular arithmetic is clock arithmetic: reduce after every operation. Congruence a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a - b. Euclid's algorithm finds gcd quickly using gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b). The extended version writes the gcd as a x x + n x y, and when the gcd is 1, x is the inverse of a mod n; for example 17^-1 ≡ 2753 (mod 3120). The invertible elements form the group Z_n*. Next lesson: primes, Fermat, Euler and fast exponentiation.
key_points: a mod n is the remainder in a = q x n + r with 0 <= r < n; for example -7 mod 26 = 19.
a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a - b; you may reduce mod n after every addition or multiplication.
Euclid's algorithm uses gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); gcd(252, 105) = 21.
a has an inverse modulo n if and only if gcd(a, n) = 1 (Bezout's identity).
Extended Euclid writes 1 = 2 x 3120 - 367 x 17, so 17^-1 ≡ -367 ≡ 2753 (mod 3120).
Always check an inverse: 17 x 2753 = 46801 = 15 x 3120 + 1.
Z_n* is the set of invertible elements; Z_10* = {1, 3, 7, 9}, and Z_p* = {1, ..., p-1} for prime p.
lessons.tip: Never trust a modular inverse you have not checked. One multiplication and one reduction catch almost every slip in extended Euclid, and examiners give marks for the check line.

lessons.title: Number Theory for Crypto II: Fermat, Euler, Fast Powers and Primes
lessons.content:
Try this puzzle before reading on: what is the last digit of 7 to the power 222? A calculator gives up, because 7^222 has 188 digits. Yet after this lesson you will answer in ten seconds: the last digit is 9. RSA needs something much harder: numbers like m^e mod n where all three are hundreds of digits long, computed thousands of times per second on servers and in a fraction of a second on a cheap phone. It also needs to find enormous random primes quickly. Three ideas make this possible: Fermat's and Euler's theorems, which let us shrink exponents; fast modular exponentiation, which computes huge powers in a few thousand steps; and primality tests, which find big primes without factoring anything.

Where we are: Lesson 10 gave us modular arithmetic, Euclid, inverses and the group Z_n*. Here we add the theorems that explain why RSA decryption gives back the message (lesson 12) and why Diffie-Hellman works inside Z_p* (lesson 13).

Primes recap: A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and so on. Every integer above 1 factors uniquely into primes (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic), for example 3233 = 53 x 61. There are infinitely many primes; Euclid proved it over two thousand years ago. For cryptography the striking fact is an asymmetry: checking whether a large number is prime is easy, but splitting a large product of two primes back into its factors is, as far as anyone publicly knows, extremely hard. RSA is built on this gap.

How common are big primes: The prime number theorem says that around a number N, roughly 1 in ln N numbers is prime, where ln is the natural logarithm. For 1024-bit numbers (the size of each RSA-2048 prime), ln(2^1024) is about 710. So about 1 in 710 random 1024-bit numbers is prime, and if we only try odd numbers, about 1 in 355. A computer that can test a candidate quickly will find a prime after a few hundred tries. Primes are rare enough to be interesting but common enough to be found.

Fermat's little theorem: If p is prime and a is not a multiple of p, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Worked check with p = 17 and a = 3: we compute by repeated squaring. 3^2 = 9. 3^4 = 81 = 4 x 17 + 13, so 13. 3^8 = 13^2 = 169 = 9 x 17 + 16, so 16. 3^16 = 16^2 = 256 = 15 x 17 + 1, so 1. Exactly as promised, 3^16 ≡ 1 (mod 17). A useful corollary: a^(p-2) is the inverse of a mod p, because a x a^(p-2) = a^(p-1) ≡ 1. For example, 3^-1 mod 7 = 3^5 mod 7 = 243 mod 7 = 5, and indeed 3 x 5 = 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7).

Euler's phi function: For any n, phi(n) counts the numbers from 1 to n that are coprime to n; it is the size of Z_n* from lesson 10. Examples: phi(10) = 4 (the numbers 1, 3, 7, 9). For a prime p, phi(p) = p - 1, since every number below p is coprime to it, so phi(7) = 6. For two different primes p and q, phi(p x q) = (p - 1)(q - 1); for example phi(3233) = phi(53 x 61) = 52 x 60 = 3120. In general, phi(n) = n multiplied by (1 - 1/r) for each distinct prime r dividing n: phi(36) = 36 x (1 - 1/2) x (1 - 1/3) = 12.

Why phi(n) is easy only with the factors: If you know n = p x q, phi(n) is one multiplication away. If you only know n, computing phi(n) is as hard as factoring n. This one sentence is the secret of RSA: the owner knows p and q and can compute phi(n); everyone else sees only n.

Euler's theorem: If gcd(a, n) = 1, then a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Fermat's theorem is the special case n = p. Check with n = 10: 3^4 = 81 ≡ 1 and 7^4 = 2401 ≡ 1 (mod 10). The power of the theorem is that exponents can be reduced modulo phi(n). Back to the puzzle: the last digit of 7^222 is 7^222 mod 10. Since phi(10) = 4 and 222 = 55 x 4 + 2, we get 7^222 = (7^4)^55 x 7^2 ≡ 1^55 x 49 ≡ 9 (mod 10). The last digit is 9. In RSA we will choose e and d so that e x d = 1 + k x phi(n); then (m^e)^d = m x (m^phi(n))^k ≡ m, and decryption undoes encryption.

The problem with big powers: To compute m^e mod n naively you multiply m by itself e - 1 times. For e = 13 that is 12 multiplications, fine. But RSA private exponents have around 2048 bits, meaning e is about 10^616. Multiplying that many times would take far longer than the age of the universe. We need a smarter way.

Square-and-multiply: Write the exponent in binary. Every exponent is a sum of powers of two, and powers of two are easy to reach by repeated squaring: m, m^2, m^4, m^8, and so on, each one the square of the previous. Then multiply together the squares whose bits are 1. Reduce mod n after every step so the numbers stay small.

Worked example, 5^13 mod 23: In binary 13 = 1101, that is 8 + 4 + 1. The squares: 5^1 = 5. 5^2 = 25 ≡ 2. 5^4 = 2^2 = 4. 5^8 = 4^2 = 16. Now multiply the ones we need: 5^13 = 5^8 x 5^4 x 5^1 ≡ 16 x 4 x 5 = 320 = 13 x 23 + 21, so 5^13 ≡ 21 (mod 23). We used 3 squarings and 2 multiplications instead of 12 multiplications. In pseudo-code: result = 1; base = m mod n; while e > 0: if e is odd: result = result x base mod n; base = base x base mod n; e = e div 2. Tracing it for 13: e = 13 (odd) gives result 5; e = 6 (even), base becomes 4; e = 3 (odd) gives result 20; e = 1 (odd) gives result 20 x 16 = 320 ≡ 21. Same answer.

How fast is it: The number of squarings equals the number of bits of e, and the number of extra multiplications is at most that again. So a 2048-bit exponent needs at most about 4096 modular multiplications, which a modern processor does in milliseconds. This is why public keys often use e = 65537, which is 2^16 + 1 in binary 10000000000000001: only 16 squarings and 1 multiplication, so encrypting or verifying is very fast. Python's built-in pow(m, e, n) uses this kind of algorithm.

Primality testing, Fermat test: Trial division up to the square root of n is hopeless for 300-digit numbers. Instead we use Fermat's theorem backwards. Pick a random a and compute a^(n-1) mod n by square-and-multiply. If the result is not 1, n is definitely composite. If it is 1, n is probably prime. Example: n = 341 = 11 x 31 is composite, yet 2^340 mod 341 = 1, so base 2 is fooled; 341 is called a Fermat pseudoprime to base 2. Base 3 catches it: 3^340 mod 341 = 56, not 1, so 341 is composite. Worse, there are Carmichael numbers, such as 561 = 3 x 11 x 17, that pass the Fermat test for every base coprime to them.

Miller-Rabin: The Miller-Rabin test adds an extra check on square roots of 1 that defeats Carmichael numbers. For any composite n, a random base exposes it with probability at least 3/4. Running 40 independent rounds makes the chance of wrongly accepting a composite at most (1/4)^40 = 2^-80, smaller than the chance of a hardware fault. Real crypto libraries generate RSA primes this way: pick a random odd number of the right size, quickly remove small factors, then run Miller-Rabin rounds. A deterministic polynomial-time test, AKS, was published in 2002 and is a celebrated theoretical result, but Miller-Rabin is what practice uses.

Chinese Remainder Theorem in one paragraph: If n1 and n2 are coprime, a pair of congruences x ≡ a1 (mod n1) and x ≡ a2 (mod n2) has exactly one solution modulo n1 x n2. Example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5). Checking 0 to 14, only x = 8 works (8 = 2 x 3 + 2 = 1 x 5 + 3). RSA implementations use CRT to do decryption separately modulo p and modulo q with half-size numbers and then combine the results, which makes private-key operations several times faster.

Real-life example 1, generating a server key: When a bank's server in Motijheel generates a new RSA-2048 key, its library picks random 1024-bit odd numbers, discards those with small factors, and runs Miller-Rabin on the survivors. Following the density estimate, a few hundred candidates are usually enough, and the whole key generation finishes in a short moment. No one ever factors anything; the primes are found, never derived.

Real-life example 2, verifying on a cheap phone: When a budget Android phone in Rangpur checks a server certificate signed with RSA (lesson 18), it computes s^65537 mod n. Thanks to square-and-multiply with only 17 multiplications on 2048-bit numbers, this takes a tiny fraction of a second even on a slow processor. Without fast exponentiation, secure browsing on cheap phones would be impossible.

Common mistakes: Applying Fermat's theorem when a is a multiple of p, or Euler's theorem when gcd(a, n) is not 1. Using phi(n) = n - 1 for composite n (it is only true for primes). Reducing the exponent mod n instead of mod phi(n). Forgetting to reduce after each step in square-and-multiply and getting huge numbers. Thinking a Fermat test result of 1 proves primality.

What exams ask: State Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem and verify them on small numbers. Compute phi(n) for numbers like 36, 77 or 3233. Use Euler's theorem to find the last digit of a large power. Compute a^b mod n by square-and-multiply, showing the binary expansion and each square. Explain why the Fermat test can be fooled and what Miller-Rabin improves. Solve a small CRT system.

Recap: Primes are easy to find and test, products of primes are hard to factor. Fermat: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Euler: a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(a, n) = 1, with phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1), so exponents reduce mod phi(n). Square-and-multiply computes huge powers in about 2 x (number of bits) multiplications. Miller-Rabin finds big primes with tiny error. With these tools, RSA in the next lesson is just three short formulas.
key_points: Testing primality is easy; factoring a product of two large primes is believed to be hard.
About 1 in ln N numbers near N is prime; for 1024-bit numbers about 1 in 710 (1 in 355 odd numbers).
Fermat: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p not dividing a; for example 3^16 ≡ 1 (mod 17).
phi(n) counts numbers coprime to n; phi(p) = p - 1 and phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1), so phi(3233) = 3120.
Euler: a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) if gcd(a, n) = 1, so exponents reduce mod phi(n); 7^222 mod 10 = 9.
Square-and-multiply: 5^13 mod 23 = 5^8 x 5^4 x 5 ≡ 16 x 4 x 5 ≡ 21, using about 2 x bits multiplications.
Fermat test can be fooled (341, Carmichael 561); Miller-Rabin with many rounds is used in practice.
CRT combines results mod p and mod q, speeding up RSA private-key operations.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a big exponent, ask two questions: can I shrink the exponent with Fermat or Euler, and then can I finish with square-and-multiply? Writing the binary of the exponent first keeps your working tidy.
lessons.task: Compute 3^16 mod 17, 7^222 mod 10 and 5^13 mod 23 by hand using the methods of this lesson. Then open Python and check with pow(3, 16, 17), pow(7, 222, 10) and pow(5, 13, 23). Finally try pow(2, 340, 341) and pow(3, 340, 341) and explain the difference.

lessons.title: Public-Key Cryptography and RSA
lessons.content:
Imagine a post box outside the Gulshan post office. Anyone can drop a letter through the slot, but only the postmaster has the key that opens the box. You do not need to meet the postmaster, agree on a secret, or trust the road; you just drop the letter in. That is the dream of public-key cryptography: a lock that everyone can close but only one person can open. For thousands of years every cipher, from Caesar to AES, needed both sides to share the same secret key first. In the 1970s a few researchers realised that the closing key and the opening key could be different, and that one of them could be published to the whole world. RSA was the first practical system to do it, and it still protects a large part of the Internet today.

The key distribution problem: With symmetric ciphers like AES (lesson 08), Rahim and Karim must share a key before they can talk securely. How do they share it? Meeting in person does not scale. A company with 1,000 employees who all need private pairwise channels would need 1000 x 999 / 2 = 499,500 different keys. A web shop would need a secret shared in advance with every customer on Earth. Before public-key crypto, militaries and banks used couriers with locked briefcases. The Internet needed something better.

The public-key idea: Each person has a key pair. The public key is published, like a phone number; the private key never leaves its owner. Anything encrypted with Karim's public key can only be decrypted with Karim's private key. So Rahim can send Karim a secret without any earlier contact: he looks up Karim's public key and encrypts. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published this idea in 1976 (lesson 13), and in 1977 Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman at MIT designed RSA, named from their initials. It later emerged that Clifford Cocks at the British agency GCHQ had found an equivalent scheme in 1973, but it stayed classified until 1997.

One-way and trapdoor functions: A one-way function is easy to compute but hard to reverse. Multiplying two 1024-bit primes is instant; factoring their 2048-bit product is, as far as is publicly known, infeasible. A trapdoor one-way function is one-way for everyone except someone holding a secret hint, the trapdoor. In RSA, the function m -> m^e mod n is easy to compute for anyone, hard to reverse for strangers, and easy to reverse for whoever knows the factors of n. The factors are the trapdoor.

RSA key generation: Step 1, pick two large random primes p and q (lesson 11 showed how). Step 2, compute n = p x q; n is called the modulus. Step 3, compute phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1). Step 4, choose a public exponent e with 1 < e < phi(n) and gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1. Step 5, compute d = e^-1 mod phi(n) with the extended Euclidean algorithm (lesson 10). The public key is (e, n); the private key is d (and p, q, phi(n) are kept secret or destroyed). Encryption: c = m^e mod n. Decryption: m = c^d mod n. That is all of textbook RSA: three formulas.

Worked key generation: Take p = 61 and q = 53, tiny primes for learning. Then n = 61 x 53 = 3233 and phi(n) = 60 x 52 = 3120. Choose e = 17. Check gcd(17, 3120): 3120 = 2^4 x 3 x 5 x 13, and 17 is not among those factors, so the gcd is 1 and e is allowed. Now d = 17^-1 mod 3120. We already did this in lesson 10: 1 = 2 x 3120 - 367 x 17, so d = -367 + 3120 = 2753. Check: 17 x 2753 = 46801 = 15 x 3120 + 1. Public key: (e, n) = (17, 3233). Private key: d = 2753.

Worked encryption: Rahim wants to send the message m = 65 (in practice a number that encodes some bytes; it must be smaller than n). He computes c = 65^17 mod 3233 by square-and-multiply (lesson 11). 65^2 = 4225, and 4225 - 3233 = 992. 65^4 = 992^2 mod 3233 = 1232. 65^8 = 1232^2 mod 3233 = 1547. 65^16 = 1547^2 mod 3233 = 789. Since 17 = 16 + 1, c = 789 x 65 = 51285, and 51285 = 15 x 3233 + 2790, so c = 2790. Rahim sends 2790 over the open Internet.

Worked decryption: Karim computes 2790^2753 mod 3233, which gives 65. By hand that is a long but mechanical square-and-multiply. A neat shortcut is the Chinese Remainder Theorem from lesson 11: work modulo 61 and modulo 53 separately with smaller exponents. d mod 60 = 53 and d mod 52 = 49. Also 2790 mod 61 = 45 and 2790 mod 53 = 34. Then 45^53 mod 61 = 4 and 34^49 mod 53 = 12. The number below 3233 that leaves remainder 4 on division by 61 and 12 on division by 53 is 65 (65 = 61 + 4 = 53 + 12). Message recovered. Real libraries use exactly this CRT trick to speed up decryption.

Why decryption works: We chose e x d = 1 + k x phi(n); here 17 x 2753 = 1 + 15 x 3120. So c^d = (m^e)^d = m^(e x d) = m x (m^phi(n))^k. By Euler's theorem (lesson 11), m^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(m, n) = 1, so c^d ≡ m x 1^k = m. (With a little extra CRT reasoning the result holds even for the rare m that shares a factor with n.)

Why RSA is secure, as far as we know: An attacker sees n = 3233, e = 17 and c = 2790. To find d they need phi(n), and to get phi(n) they need p and q. For 3233 that is trivial, but for a 2048-bit n, which has 617 decimal digits, the best known classical factoring algorithm (the general number field sieve) would need an infeasible amount of computation. Public factoring records give a feel: in 2020 researchers factored RSA-250, an 829-bit number, using a very large amount of computing power. Today 2048-bit keys are the common minimum, and 3072-bit keys are recommended for longer-term security. Note the hedge: nobody has proved factoring is hard; it is believed hard because decades of effort have not broken it. Quantum computers would change this picture, as lesson 26 discusses.

Choosing e in practice: Most real keys use e = 65537 (2^16 + 1). It is prime, so it is coprime to phi(n) for almost all keys, and its binary form has only two 1 bits, which makes encryption and signature verification fast. The private exponent d is then large, around the size of n.

Textbook RSA is not safe as is: The three formulas alone have serious weaknesses. First, they are deterministic: the same m always gives the same c, so if an attacker suspects the message is "YES" or "NO", they encrypt both with the public key and compare. Second, small messages can be dangerous: if m^e is smaller than n, no reduction happens, and the attacker just takes an ordinary e-th root of c. Third, RSA is malleable: multiplying ciphertexts multiplies plaintexts. With our key, 2790 x 2^17 mod 3233 = 3017, and 3017 decrypts to 130, which is 2 x 65; an attacker changed the message without knowing it.

Padding with OAEP: The cure is to add structured randomness before encrypting. OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding, by Bellare and Rogaway, 1994) mixes the message with fresh random bytes using hash functions, so the same message encrypts differently each time and tampered ciphertexts are rejected. The older PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding suffered from an oracle attack published by Daniel Bleichenbacher in 1998, similar in spirit to the padding oracle in lesson 09. Modern guidance: use RSA-OAEP from a trusted library, never raw m^e mod n.

Hybrid encryption: RSA is slow compared with AES and can only encrypt a message smaller than n (minus padding). So real systems combine them. To send a 20 MB file, the sender generates a random 256-bit AES key, encrypts the file with AES-GCM (lesson 09), and encrypts only the small AES key with the receiver's RSA public key. The receiver decrypts the AES key with their private key and then decrypts the file. Public-key crypto solves key distribution; symmetric crypto does the bulk work. Almost every secure protocol, including TLS, email encryption and messaging apps, follows this pattern, although modern TLS 1.3 prefers Diffie-Hellman over RSA for the key exchange itself (lessons 13 and 19).

Real-life example 1, a government e-tender: Suppose a Bangladeshi e-tender portal lets contractors submit sealed bids. Each bid file is encrypted with a fresh AES key, and that key is encrypted with the tender committee's RSA public key. Competing contractors and even portal staff who copy the database before the opening time see only ciphertext. At opening time the committee's private key, kept on protected hardware, unlocks the AES keys. This is hybrid encryption serving confidentiality.

Real-life example 2, RSA signatures in daily life: RSA is used even more for signatures than for encryption: signing is "decrypting" a hash with the private key and verifying is "encrypting" with the public key. When your phone checks that an app update really came from the developer, or your browser checks a website certificate, there is a good chance an RSA signature is involved. Lesson 17 works through RSA signatures with these same small numbers.

Common mistakes: Using phi(n) = n - 1 instead of (p-1)(q-1). Choosing an e that is not coprime to phi(n). Computing d mod n instead of mod phi(n). Forgetting that m must be less than n. Saying "encrypt with the private key" for confidentiality (encryption for secrecy always uses the receiver's public key). Using textbook RSA without OAEP, or using RSA directly on large data instead of hybrid encryption. Reusing the same modulus n for different users.

What exams ask: Generate an RSA key pair from given small p, q and e, showing extended Euclid. Encrypt and decrypt a given m. Prove why decryption recovers m using Euler's theorem. Explain why RSA security depends on factoring. Explain why textbook RSA is insecure and what OAEP does. Explain hybrid encryption with a diagram.

Recap: Public-key crypto solves key distribution with key pairs. RSA: n = pq, phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1), e coprime to phi(n), d = e^-1 mod phi(n); c = m^e mod n and m = c^d mod n. With p = 61, q = 53, e = 17 we got n = 3233, d = 2753 and 65 -> 2790 -> 65. Security rests on the belief that factoring large n is hard. Use OAEP padding, at least 2048-bit keys, and hybrid encryption with AES.
key_points: Public-key crypto gives each user a key pair: the public key encrypts, only the private key decrypts.
RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977) is a trapdoor function; knowing the factors of n is the trapdoor.
Key generation: n = pq, phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1), gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1, d = e^-1 mod phi(n).
Worked: p = 61, q = 53 gives n = 3233, phi = 3120, e = 17, d = 2753; m = 65 encrypts to c = 2790.
Decryption works because ed = 1 + k x phi(n) and Euler's theorem gives m^(ed) ≡ m (mod n).
Security rests on factoring being hard; 2048 bits is the common minimum, 3072 for longer-term use.
Textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable; use OAEP padding from a trusted library.
Hybrid encryption: RSA (or DH) protects a random AES key; AES-GCM encrypts the actual data.
lessons.tip: Keep one tiny RSA example (61, 53, 17) memorised end to end. In the exam you can rebuild every formula from it, and you can sanity-check any new numbers by running pow(m, e, n) and pow(c, d, n) in Python while practising.
lessons.task: Build your own toy RSA key with p = 11, q = 17 and e = 7: compute n, phi(n) and d by extended Euclid. Encrypt m = 88 and decrypt the result. Check everything in Python with pow(7, -1, phi), pow(88, 7, n) and pow(c, d, n).

quiz.q: In RSA key generation, how is d computed?
quiz.explain: d is the inverse of e modulo phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1), found with the extended Euclidean algorithm.

quiz.q: With p = 61, q = 53, e = 17, what is the private exponent d?
Using public key (17, 3233), what is the ciphertext of m = 65?
Why is textbook RSA (no padding) unsafe?
options: It is deterministic and malleable, so equal messages and tampering can be exploited
Its keys are too short by definition
It needs a shared secret key
quiz.explain: Without randomised padding like OAEP, the same message always gives the same ciphertext and ciphertexts can be manipulated.

quiz.q: What does hybrid encryption do?
options: Encrypts the whole file with RSA twice
Uses only symmetric keys shared in person
Encrypts data with AES and protects the random AES key with public-key crypto
quiz.explain: Public-key crypto handles key distribution for a small random key; fast AES encrypts the bulk data.

lessons.title: Diffie-Hellman and the Discrete Logarithm
lessons.content:
Here is a magic trick that sounds impossible. Two students, Nadia in Sylhet and Tanvir in Khulna, have never met and share no secret. They talk only by shouting across a crowded classroom, so everyone hears every word. Yet at the end of the conversation both of them know the same secret number, and nobody else in the room can work it out. That is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, published by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976 in a paper called "New Directions in Cryptography", building on ideas of Ralph Merkle. It was the first public demonstration that two parties can agree on a secret over a completely public channel. Today, in its elliptic-curve form, it runs in almost every HTTPS connection you make.

Where this fits: In lesson 12, RSA solved key distribution by letting anyone encrypt to a public key. Diffie-Hellman (DH) solves it differently: instead of sending a secret, both sides compute a shared secret together. That shared secret then becomes the key for AES-GCM (lesson 09).
