quiz.explain: Browsers match the requested hostname against the names in the Subject Alternative Name extension.

quiz.q: Why is a root CA certificate self-signed yet still trusted?
options: It is trusted because it is pre-installed in the device's root store
Roots are signed by Let's Encrypt
quiz.explain: A self-signature proves nothing alone; trust comes from the root being in the root store chosen by the OS or browser vendor.

quiz.q: What does OCSP stapling do?
options: The server attaches a fresh signed revocation status to the handshake
It merges two certificates into one
quiz.explain: With stapling, the server fetches the CA's signed OCSP response and sends it along, so the client need not ask the CA.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of Certificate Transparency?
options: Publicly log certificates so mis-issued ones are quickly noticed
quiz.explain: CT puts every publicly trusted certificate in append-only public logs, so domain owners can spot certificates they did not request.

lessons.title: TLS from the Cryptographer's View
lessons.content:
Every time you open Facebook, pay a bill in a mobile-wallet app or log in to your university portal, a small miracle happens in less than a second. Your phone and a server that have never met agree on fresh secret keys over a network full of strangers, the server proves who it is, and from then on every byte is encrypted and protected against changes. That miracle is TLS, Transport Layer Security, the protocol behind the "S" in HTTPS. In Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3) and Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3) you saw TLS from outside: a padlock, port 443, an extra round trip. Now that you know Diffie-Hellman, signatures, certificates, HMAC and AEAD, we can open the box and see how each piece of this course fits into one handshake. We focus on TLS 1.3, the current version, and compare it with TLS 1.2.

Goals of TLS: TLS sits between TCP and the application, and gives three guarantees for the connection. Authentication: the client knows it is talking to the real server (and optionally the server can authenticate the client). Confidentiality: data is encrypted so eavesdroppers on the Wi-Fi, the ISP or any router cannot read it. Integrity: any modification, insertion, deletion or reordering of data is detected. It also aims for forward secrecy: if the server's long-term private key is stolen later, past recorded sessions still cannot be decrypted.

A short history: Netscape designed SSL in the mid-1990s; SSL 2.0 and SSL 3.0 both had serious flaws and are long dead. The IETF renamed it TLS: TLS 1.0 in 1999, TLS 1.1 in 2006, TLS 1.2 in 2008 and TLS 1.3 in 2018 (RFC 8446). TLS 1.0 and 1.1 were formally deprecated in 2021. Today, servers should support TLS 1.3 and 1.2 only. People still say "SSL certificate" out of habit, but the protocol in use is TLS.

Two phases: TLS has a handshake protocol and a record protocol. The handshake negotiates the version and algorithms, performs key exchange, authenticates the server, and derives keys. The record protocol then carries application data, such as HTTP requests, in encrypted and authenticated records. Think of the handshake as two people meeting, checking ID cards and agreeing on a secret code word, and the record protocol as all the conversation that follows in that code.

Step 1, ClientHello: The client opens the conversation with one message containing: a fresh 32-byte random value; the TLS versions it supports; a list of cipher suites, such as TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256; supported key-exchange groups such as X25519 and P-256; the signature algorithms it accepts; the server name it wants (SNI, so one IP address can host many sites); and, importantly, a key share: its ephemeral Diffie-Hellman public value, for example an X25519 public key computed as aG from a fresh secret a (lesson 14). The client guesses which group the server will like and sends the key share right away, which saves a round trip.

Step 2, ServerHello: The server picks one version, one cipher suite and one group, and replies with its own random value and its own key share, bG from a fresh secret b. Now both sides can compute the same ECDHE shared secret abG, while an eavesdropper who saw aG and bG cannot (ECDLP). If the client guessed a group the server does not support, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest naming a group, and the client tries again; this costs one extra round trip but is rare.

Step 3, deriving handshake keys: The shared secret is not used directly as an AES key. Both sides feed it into HKDF, an HMAC-based key derivation function (extract-then-expand), together with a hash of all handshake messages so far, called the transcript hash. The output is a set of separate keys: one for client-to-server handshake messages, one for server-to-client, and later others for application data. Using the transcript in the derivation binds the keys to exactly this conversation: if an attacker changed anything in the hello messages, the keys and later checks would not match.

Step 4, the encrypted server messages: Everything after ServerHello is already encrypted with the handshake keys, which is new in TLS 1.3 and hides the certificate from passive observers. The server sends EncryptedExtensions (other negotiated settings), then its Certificate chain (lesson 18), then CertificateVerify: a digital signature, made with the private key that matches the certificate, over the transcript hash so far. Finally it sends Finished: an HMAC over the transcript, keyed with a key derived from the handshake secret.

Why CertificateVerify is the heart of authentication: A certificate is public, so anyone can copy it and send it. What an impostor cannot do is sign the current transcript, which includes the fresh random values and key shares of this very handshake, with the private key. When the client verifies the certificate chain to a trusted root, checks the domain name, and then verifies the CertificateVerify signature with the certificate's public key, it knows the party who did this Diffie-Hellman exchange holds the real server's private key. That signature is exactly what defeats the man-in-the-middle attack on plain Diffie-Hellman from lesson 13.

Step 5, client Finished: The client checks the server's Finished HMAC; if it matches, nobody tampered with any handshake message. Then it sends its own Finished. At this point both sides derive application traffic keys from the secrets and transcript, and normal data starts flowing. Count the round trips: ClientHello goes out, ServerHello through server Finished comes back, which is one round trip, and the client can send its first HTTP request together with its Finished. That is a 1-RTT handshake. TLS 1.2 normally needed two round trips.

A small timing calculation: Suppose a student in Khulna opens a site whose server is about 100 ms round trip away. TCP's three-way handshake costs one RTT before TLS can start. With TLS 1.2: 1 RTT TCP + 2 RTT TLS + 1 RTT for the HTTP request and response = 4 RTT = 400 ms before the first byte of the page arrives. With TLS 1.3: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 RTT = 300 ms. Saving 100 ms on every new connection matters a lot on slow mobile networks. (HTTP/3 over QUIC goes further by combining the transport and TLS handshakes, as you saw in the Networks course.)

0-RTT resumption and its catch: When a client reconnects to a server it visited recently, TLS 1.3 can resume using a pre-shared key from the earlier session, and even lets the client send "early data" in its very first flight, with zero round trips of waiting. The catch: early data can be replayed by an attacker who records it and sends it again, because the server has not yet contributed fresh randomness. So 0-RTT should only be used for requests that are safe to repeat, like loading a page, never for "transfer 5000 taka". Many servers simply disable it for sensitive actions.

The record layer: After the handshake, data is split into records of up to 16 KB. Each record is protected with the negotiated AEAD cipher, AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 (lesson 09). The nonce for each record is built from a fixed IV and a 64-bit sequence number that counts records; the sequence number is not even sent, both sides just count. If an attacker deletes, repeats or reorders a record, the receiver uses the wrong sequence number, decryption fails authentication, and the connection is closed. This is the counter-based replay protection from lesson 16, built in.

Forward secrecy: In TLS 1.3 every full handshake uses fresh ephemeral (EC)DHE keys a and b that are deleted after use. The server's long-term certificate key is used only to sign, never to encrypt session secrets. So if, a year later, someone steals the server's private key, he still cannot decrypt traffic he recorded today, because the ephemeral secrets are gone. In TLS 1.2 there was also an option called static RSA key exchange, where the client encrypted the session secret with the server's RSA public key. That gave no forward secrecy: steal the key later, decrypt all old recordings. TLS 1.3 removed it.

What TLS 1.3 removed, and why: TLS 1.3 was a big cleanup. Gone are static RSA and static DH key exchange (no forward secrecy), CBC-mode cipher suites (source of padding-oracle style attacks), RC4, MD5 and SHA-1 in signatures, compression (which enabled the CRIME attack), renegotiation and custom DH groups. Every remaining cipher suite is an AEAD. The general lesson: fewer options means fewer ways to misconfigure, and many past TLS attacks lived in rarely used, old options.

Downgrade protection: An active attacker might try to edit the ClientHello so both sides fall back to an older, weaker version. TLS 1.3 resists this in two ways. The Finished messages and the CertificateVerify signature cover the whole transcript, so any edit to the hellos is detected. And if a TLS 1.3 server is pushed to negotiate TLS 1.2, it puts a special marker in the last bytes of its random value; a TLS 1.3 client that sees this marker knows something is wrong and aborts.

What TLS does not protect: TLS protects data in transit between two endpoints, nothing more. An observer can still see IP addresses, the timing and sizes of messages, and usually the server name in SNI (an extension called Encrypted Client Hello is being deployed to hide it). TLS does not protect data stored on the server, does not help if the phone or server is infected with malware, and does not stop phishing: a fake site with its own valid certificate gets a perfect TLS connection to the victim. And the first plain-HTTP visit can be attacked by stripping the redirect to HTTPS, which is why sites use HSTS (recap from deep-cse-5-3) to tell browsers to always use HTTPS.

Real-life example 1, mobile banking on café Wi-Fi: A customer in a Dhanmondi café uses free Wi-Fi to check her bank balance. Anyone on that Wi-Fi can capture her packets. Inside the app, TLS 1.3 runs: X25519 key shares, the bank's certificate chained to a trusted root and checked for the right domain, a CertificateVerify signature, and then AES-GCM records. The snooper sees only that she connected to the bank's IP address and roughly how much data moved. If he tries to impersonate the bank, he cannot produce a valid CertificateVerify, and the app, especially if it uses certificate pinning, refuses to continue.

Real-life example 2, servers talking to servers: When an online shop's server calls a payment gateway's API, both sides may require mutual TLS: the client server also presents a certificate and signs a CertificateVerify, so the gateway knows exactly which merchant is calling, not just that the connection is encrypted. Inside large systems, the same idea is used between internal services. Strong TLS here protects card and wallet data between data centres, while HMAC-signed callbacks (lesson 16) add another layer on top.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include saying TLS encrypts with the server's public key (in TLS 1.3 the public key only verifies signatures; encryption uses AEAD keys from ECDHE), thinking HTTPS means the site is safe or honest, disabling certificate verification in code "just for testing" and shipping it, and enabling 0-RTT for non-idempotent requests. Exams ask you to draw the TLS 1.3 handshake with message names and which crypto each uses, explain forward secrecy and why static RSA lacked it, compare TLS 1.2 and 1.3, explain how the record layer prevents replay and reordering, and explain how CertificateVerify stops man-in-the-middle.

Recap: TLS 1.3 combines this whole course. ClientHello and ServerHello exchange randoms and ephemeral ECDHE key shares. HKDF turns the shared secret and transcript hash into keys. The server proves its identity with a certificate chain (PKI) and a CertificateVerify signature; Finished HMACs confirm nobody tampered. Records are protected with AEAD and implicit sequence numbers. The result is a 1-RTT handshake with forward secrecy and a much smaller, safer set of options than TLS 1.2. Next lesson we move from protecting channels to protecting accounts: authentication.
key_points: TLS gives server authentication, confidentiality and integrity for data in transit, plus forward secrecy in TLS 1.3.
ClientHello and ServerHello carry randoms, cipher suite choices and ephemeral (EC)DHE key shares such as X25519.
HKDF derives separate handshake and traffic keys from the shared secret and the transcript hash.
The server sends its certificate chain and a CertificateVerify signature over the transcript; this stops man-in-the-middle.
Finished messages are HMACs over the transcript, proving the handshake was not modified.
TLS 1.3 needs 1 RTT (TLS 1.2 needed 2); 0-RTT early data is replayable, so use it only for safe requests.
Records use AEAD (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with nonces from implicit sequence numbers, stopping replay and reordering.
TLS 1.3 removed static RSA, CBC suites, RC4, SHA-1 signatures and compression; TLS does not hide metadata or stop phishing.
lessons.tip: Draw the TLS 1.3 handshake as a two-column diagram and next to each message write which earlier lesson it uses: ECDHE, HKDF/HMAC, certificate chain, signature, AEAD. If you can label every arrow, you understand the whole course so far.
lessons.task: Open any HTTPS website in Chrome or Firefox on a computer, open DevTools, go to the Security tab (Chrome) or the padlock's connection details (Firefox), and write down the TLS version, key exchange group and cipher suite. Then calculate how many milliseconds TLS 1.3 saves compared with TLS 1.2 if the round-trip time is 150 ms.

quiz.q: In TLS 1.3, what does the server's CertificateVerify message contain?
options: An encrypted copy of the certificate
The list of supported cipher suites
A signature over the handshake transcript made with the certificate's private key
quiz.explain: CertificateVerify proves possession of the certificate's private key by signing the transcript of this exact handshake.

quiz.q: Why does TLS 1.3 provide forward secrecy?
options: Every handshake uses fresh ephemeral (EC)DHE keys that are deleted after use
It encrypts session keys with the server's RSA key
It changes the certificate every session
quiz.explain: Ephemeral key shares mean a later theft of the long-term key cannot recover old session keys.

quiz.q: If the round-trip time is 100 ms, how long until the first page byte with TCP + TLS 1.3 + one HTTP request?
quiz.explain: 1 RTT for TCP, 1 RTT for the TLS 1.3 handshake and 1 RTT for the request and response: 3 x 100 = 300 ms.

quiz.q: Why should 0-RTT early data not be used for a money transfer request?
options: It can be replayed by an attacker
quiz.explain: Early data is sent before the server adds fresh randomness, so a recorded copy can be replayed.

quiz.q: Which of these was removed in TLS 1.3?
quiz.explain: Static RSA key transport gave no forward secrecy, so TLS 1.3 removed it; AES-GCM, X25519 and certificates remain.

lessons.title: Authentication: Passwords, MFA, OTP and Biometrics
lessons.content:
Imagine you walk into your bank branch in Motijheel to withdraw money. The officer does not just take your word that you are Rahim. She asks for your cheque book, checks your signature against the one on file, and maybe looks at your NID card. Only when she is convinced do you get the cash. A computer system faces the same problem a million times a day, but it cannot see your face across the counter. All it receives is a stream of bytes over a network. Authentication is the science of turning those bytes into a confident answer to one question: is this really the person (or program) it claims to be?

Identification vs authentication: These two words are often mixed up. Identification is when you claim an identity: typing your username, phone number or email. Authentication is when you prove that claim: typing the password, scanning a finger, approving a prompt on your phone. A third step, authorization, decides what you may do once you are in, and that is the topic of the next lesson. A useful order to remember is: identify, authenticate, authorize, and then keep a log so actions can be traced back (accountability, from lesson 01).

The three factors: Every authentication method proves one of three kinds of things. Something you know: a password, a PIN, the answer to a security question. Something you have: a phone that receives a code, a hardware key, a smart card, a SIM. Something you are: a fingerprint, a face, an iris, a voice. Some textbooks add somewhere you are (location) and something you do (typing rhythm), but the classic three are what exams ask about. Each factor fails in a different way: secrets can be guessed or phished, objects can be stolen, and body features cannot be changed if they leak. That is exactly why combining factors is so powerful.

Passwords are still everywhere: Passwords are cheap, need no special hardware and every user understands them. Their weakness is people. Humans choose short, memorable, predictable passwords and reuse them across many sites. To measure how hard a password is to guess, we use entropy, measured in bits. If a password is chosen truly at random from an alphabet of N symbols and has length L, the number of possible passwords is N to the power L, and the entropy is L times log2(N) bits. Every extra bit doubles the attacker's work.

Entropy worked: Take 8 random lowercase letters. The number of possibilities is 26^8 = 208,827,064,576, about 2.09 x 10^11, which is about 37.6 bits. Now take 8 random characters from upper case, lower case and digits (62 symbols): 62^8 is about 2.18 x 10^14, about 47.6 bits. Take 12 random characters from all 94 printable keyboard symbols: 12 x log2(94) is about 78.7 bits. A 4-digit PIN has only 10^4 = 10,000 possibilities, about 13.3 bits, and a 6-digit PIN has about 19.9 bits. Notice the big catch: these numbers are only true if the password is chosen at random. "Dhaka@2024" looks complex but appears in guessing lists, so its real entropy is far lower than the formula suggests.

Online vs offline attacks: In an online attack, the attacker types guesses into the real login page or API. The server can defend itself: rate limiting, temporary lockout, CAPTCHA after several failures, and alerts. That is why a 4-digit PIN can still be acceptable on a bank card: after 3 wrong tries the card is blocked, so the attacker gets 3 guesses out of 10,000, a 0.03% chance. In an offline attack, the attacker has stolen the database of password hashes and guesses on his own machines with no limit. Here only the hashing method protects users.

Offline cracking worked: Suppose the database stored a fast, unsalted hash, and the attacker's GPU rig computes 10^10 hashes per second (a realistic order of magnitude for fast hashes). Every 8-letter lowercase password falls in 2.09 x 10^11 / 10^10, about 21 seconds. Even the 62-symbol 8-character space falls in about 6 hours. If the site instead used a deliberately slow password hash tuned so that one guess costs much more, say only 10^4 guesses per second for the attacker, the same 8-letter lowercase space takes about 242 days. Same password, wildly different safety, only because of how the server stored it.

Storage recap: Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3, lesson 21) covered this from the developer's side, so here is the short version. Never store passwords in plain text, and never encrypt them with a key the server holds. Store a salted, slow hash. The salt is a random value, unique per user, stored next to the hash. It makes identical passwords produce different hashes and makes precomputed rainbow tables useless, because the attacker must attack each user separately. A slow, memory-hard function such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 makes each guess expensive. A secret "pepper" kept outside the database adds one more layer. The hash functions themselves are the subject of lesson 15.

Credential stuffing and reuse: The biggest real-world password problem is not cracking at all. Big websites get breached, and lists of email plus password pairs are traded online. Attackers then try those exact pairs on other services, from email to shopping to banking apps. If you used the same password everywhere, one leak opens every door. Defences on the server side are rate limits, checking new passwords against known-breached lists, detecting unusual login locations and, above all, a second factor. On the user side, the answer is a password manager that creates a long random password for every site.

Good password policy today: Modern guidance, such as NIST's digital identity guidelines, moved away from old rules like "change every 30 days" and "must contain a symbol", because those rules pushed people toward predictable patterns like Password1!, Password2!. The current direction is: allow long passphrases, set a reasonable minimum length, block common and breached passwords, do not force periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise, allow paste so password managers work, and add multi-factor authentication.

Multi-factor authentication: MFA means using factors from two or more different categories. A password plus a PIN is not MFA, because both are something you know. A password plus a code from your phone is MFA, because the phone is something you have. The point is that the attacker must now defeat two different kinds of protection. A stolen password from a breach list is useless without the phone, and a stolen phone is useless without the PIN.

One-time passwords, HOTP: A one-time password is valid for a single login and then dies, so a stolen one is worth little. HOTP (HMAC-based OTP, RFC 4226) works like this. The server and your token share a secret key K and a counter C. To make a code, compute HMAC(K, C) (you met HMAC in lesson 16), cut the result down to a number, and keep the last 6 digits. Each time you press the button the counter goes up by one, and the server does the same. Since only someone with K can compute the right code, the code proves possession of the token.

TOTP, the time version: TOTP (RFC 6238) replaces the counter with time. Both sides compute T = floor(current Unix time / 30), so the counter ticks once every 30 seconds by default, and the code is HOTP with C = T. Worked example: at Unix time 1,700,000,000 seconds, T = floor(1,700,000,000 / 30) = 56,666,666, with 20 seconds already used in that window, so the code on screen will change in 10 seconds. Authenticator apps on your phone do exactly this offline: no network needed, only the shared secret (usually delivered once through a QR code) and a reasonably correct clock. Servers often accept the neighbouring time step too, to tolerate small clock drift.

Why SMS OTP is weaker: Many Bangladeshi services send a 6-digit code by SMS. It is far better than a password alone, but it has known weaknesses. A criminal can trick a mobile operator into issuing a new SIM for your number (SIM swap), malware on the phone can read SMS, and, most commonly, a scammer can simply phone you and persuade you to read the code aloud. The code itself is fine; the human channel is the weak point. That is why every bank and wallet repeats: never share your OTP or PIN with anyone, including someone claiming to be from the company. Lesson 24 looks at these scams in detail.

Biometrics: A fingerprint or face scan is convenient: you cannot forget it and it is fast. But biometric matching is never exact. Each scan is a little different, so the system compares a score against a threshold. Two error rates matter. The false accept rate (FAR) is how often an impostor is wrongly accepted; the false reject rate (FRR) is how often the real user is wrongly rejected. Worked example: in a test with 10,000 impostor attempts, 3 were accepted, so FAR = 3/10,000 = 0.03%. In 1,000 genuine attempts, 20 were rejected, so FRR = 20/1,000 = 2%. Raising the threshold lowers FAR but raises FRR. The point where the two rates are equal is the equal error rate (EER), a common single number for comparing systems.

Biometric cautions: You cannot reset your fingerprint if a template leaks, so templates must be protected, ideally stored only on the device in secure hardware. On modern phones, the fingerprint usually does not travel to the bank at all; it only unlocks a key stored in the phone's secure chip, and that key does the real authentication. Liveness detection tries to stop photos and fake fingers. Biometrics work best as one factor among several, not as a secret.

Passkeys and FIDO2: The newest approach removes the shared secret altogether. With FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys, your device creates a public and private key pair for each website. The website stores only the public key. To log in, the site sends a random challenge, your device signs it with the private key after you unlock it with a fingerprint or PIN, and the site checks the signature (lesson 17). There is no password to steal from the server and nothing to type into a fake site. The signature is also bound to the real website's domain, so a lookalike phishing site cannot use it. That makes passkeys strongly resistant to phishing, which neither passwords nor SMS codes are.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet login: Think of a typical Bangladeshi mobile wallet app. On first install, it verifies your SIM by sending an OTP (something you have), then asks for your PIN (something you know). It also binds the account to that device, so logging in from a new phone triggers extra checks. Daily, you may unlock with your fingerprint, which really just unlocks a device key. Sending money asks for the PIN again. Each layer covers a gap in another: the PIN protects a stolen phone, the device binding protects a leaked PIN, and limits plus alerts protect against both.

Real-life example 2, a university portal: Suppose your university's result and registration portal uses student ID plus password. A sensible upgrade path is: hash passwords with Argon2 or bcrypt and a per-user salt; rate-limit login attempts per account and per IP address; block the most common passwords; offer TOTP through any authenticator app for students and make it mandatory for teachers and staff who can change grades. Staff accounts deserve stronger protection because the damage from their compromise is much larger, a direct application of the risk idea from lesson 02.

Common mistakes: Thinking that two passwords make two factors. Believing a complex-looking password is strong when it follows a common pattern. Storing passwords with a fast hash like plain SHA-256 and calling it secure. Giving detailed login errors such as "wrong password" vs "no such user", which helps attackers find valid accounts. Treating a biometric as a secret. Forgetting that account recovery ("forgot password") is also an authentication path, often the weakest one.

What exams ask: Define authentication and distinguish it from identification and authorization. List the three factors with examples and explain why MFA must combine different factors. Calculate password entropy for a given alphabet and length. Explain the role of salt and slow hashing. Describe how HOTP and TOTP generate codes. Define FAR, FRR and EER and explain the effect of changing the threshold. Explain why passkeys resist phishing.

Recap: Authentication proves a claimed identity using something you know, have or are. Password strength is measured in bits of entropy, but only randomly chosen passwords achieve the formula. Online attacks are slowed by rate limits; offline attacks are slowed only by salted, slow hashing. MFA combines different factor types; TOTP codes come from HMAC of a shared secret and the current 30-second time step. SMS codes are better than nothing but can be swapped or talked out of people. Biometrics trade FAR against FRR and cannot be reset. Passkeys replace secrets with signatures and resist phishing.
key_points: Identification claims an identity, authentication proves it, authorization decides what is allowed.
Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are; MFA must mix different factors.
Entropy of a random password = L x log2(N) bits; 8 random lowercase letters give about 37.6 bits.
Online guessing is limited by rate limits and lockout; offline cracking is limited only by salted, slow hashing.
HOTP = HMAC of a shared secret and a counter; TOTP uses T = floor(Unix time / 30) as the counter.
SMS OTP can be defeated by SIM swap, malware or simply talking the victim into sharing the code.
Biometrics trade false accept rate against false reject rate; the crossing point is the equal error rate.
Passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) sign a challenge with a device-held private key and resist phishing.
lessons.tip: When you study authentication, always ask two questions about any method: how does an attacker get it, and what happens after it leaks? That pair of questions explains almost every design choice in this lesson.
lessons.task: Open the security settings of your email account and one social media account. Write down which factors each one uses right now, turn on an authenticator-app based second factor if it is offered, and save the backup codes somewhere safe offline.

quiz.q: Which pair is a real two-factor combination?
options: Password and a TOTP code from your phone
quiz.explain: MFA needs different categories. A TOTP code proves something you have (the phone with the secret), the password is something you know.

quiz.q: What is the entropy of a 12-character password chosen at random from 94 printable symbols?
quiz.explain: Entropy = L x log2(N) = 12 x log2(94), which is about 12 x 6.55 = 78.7 bits.

quiz.q: In TOTP with a 30-second step, what is T at Unix time 1,700,000,000?
quiz.explain: T = floor(1,700,000,000 / 30) = 56,666,666, and this T is fed into HMAC as the counter.

quiz.q: A fingerprint system raises its matching threshold. What usually happens?
quiz.explain: A stricter threshold rejects more impostors (lower FAR) but also rejects more genuine users (higher FRR).

quiz.q: Why do passkeys resist phishing better than SMS OTP?
options: They are longer than six digits
The signature is bound to the real site's domain and no secret is typed
They are sent by email instead of SMS
quiz.explain: The device signs a challenge only for the registered domain; there is no code a fake site can collect and replay.

lessons.title: Access Control: Matrix, ACLs, DAC, MAC and RBAC
lessons.content:
Think of a hospital in Dhaka. The receptionist can see your name and appointment time but not your test reports. Your doctor can read and update your medical file. The pharmacist can see prescriptions but not the doctor's private notes. The accounts office sees bills, not diagnoses. Nobody wrote "Rahim may read file 4,512" on a wall; there is a system of rules deciding who may do what to which thing. In a computer that system is called access control, and it is the part of security that turns "we know who you are" into "here is exactly what you are allowed to touch".

Where access control sits: The last lesson ended with authentication: proving who you are. Authorization comes next: deciding whether an authenticated user may perform a requested action. Access control is the set of models and mechanisms that make this decision on every request. Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1, lesson 25) introduced protection, the access matrix and Unix rwx bits from an OS point of view; here we look at the models more formally and add the security policies used in military, business and modern cloud systems.

Subjects, objects and rights: Every access control decision has three parts. A subject is the active party asking to do something: a user, or a process running on behalf of a user. An object is the passive thing being accessed: a file, a database row, a printer, an API endpoint, even another process. A right (or permission, or access mode) is the operation: read, write, execute, append, delete, own, approve. A request is then a triple (subject, object, right), and the system answers allow or deny. Nearly every model in this lesson is a different way of storing and reasoning about these triples.

The access matrix: The simplest complete model, from Lampson in the early 1970s, is a table. Rows are subjects, columns are objects, and each cell lists the rights that subject has on that object. Example: three users Anika, Babu and Chitra; three objects salary.xlsx, notice.txt and backup.sh. Anika (the accountant) has read and write on salary.xlsx, read on notice.txt, nothing on backup.sh. Babu (an ordinary staff member) has nothing on salary.xlsx, read on notice.txt, nothing on backup.sh. Chitra (the admin) has read on notice.txt and write on it too, plus execute on backup.sh, but nothing on salary.xlsx. Checking a request is just looking up a cell: may Babu write notice.txt? The cell says only read, so deny.

Why not store the whole matrix: In a real system with thousands of users and millions of files, almost every cell is empty. Storing the full table wastes huge memory. So systems store it in one of two compressed ways. Cut the matrix by columns and you get, for each object, a list of who may do what: an access control list (ACL). Cut it by rows and you get, for each subject, a list of what it may access: a capability list. Same information, different shape, different strengths.

ACLs: An ACL is attached to the object. notice.txt carries the list "Anika: read; Babu: read; Chitra: read, write". ACLs make it easy to answer "who can access this file?" and easy to revoke everyone's access to one object: just edit its list. They make it hard to answer "what can Babu access?" because you must scan every object. Most file systems (Windows NTFS, Unix permission bits as a tiny ACL, cloud storage buckets) use ACLs.

Capabilities: A capability is like a ticket held by the subject: an unforgeable token that says "the holder may read notice.txt". Whoever presents a valid ticket gets in, a bit like a movie ticket at Star Cineplex. Capabilities make it easy to pass rights along and to see everything a subject can do, and they fit naturally with least privilege: give a process only the tickets it needs. They make revocation harder, because tickets may have been copied or passed on. Unix file descriptors behave like capabilities: once a process has opened a file, it holds a handle and later reads are not rechecked against the file's permissions. Signed access tokens in web APIs follow the same idea.

Discretionary access control (DAC): In DAC, the owner of an object decides who else may access it, at their own discretion. When you create a file on your laptop you own it, and you can share it with anyone. Unix permissions, Windows file sharing and Google Drive sharing are DAC. It is flexible and natural for personal data. Its big weakness: a program you run acts with your rights. If a trojan horse program runs under your account, it can read your private file and quietly copy it into a file your enemy can read, and DAC sees nothing wrong, because you (the owner) technically "allowed" it.

Unix permissions recap: Each Unix file has an owner, a group and three sets of rwx bits for owner, group and others. Mode 754 means owner rwx (4+2+1=7), group r-x (4+1=5), others r-- (4). Mode 640 is rw-r-----: owner reads and writes, group reads, others nothing. Mode 700 is rwx------, private to the owner. A private key file for a server should be 600 or stricter. The root user bypasses these checks, which is why running everything as root breaks least privilege (lesson 03).

Mandatory access control (MAC): In MAC, a central policy set by the system, not the owner, decides access, and users cannot override it. Every subject gets a clearance and every object gets a classification, for example Unclassified < Confidential < Secret < Top Secret. The classic confidentiality model is Bell-LaPadula (1970s, for the US military). It has two rules. Simple security property, "no read up": a subject may read an object only if its clearance is at least the object's level. Star property, "no write down": a subject may write to an object only if the object's level is at least the subject's level. The second rule is the clever one: it stops a Secret-level process (perhaps a trojan) from copying Secret data into an Unclassified file. That is exactly the leak DAC could not prevent.

Bell-LaPadula worked: Officer Karim has clearance Secret. Can he read a Confidential report? Yes, Confidential is below Secret, so reading down is allowed. Can he read a Top Secret plan? No, no read up. Can he write into the Confidential report? No: writing down could leak Secret knowledge. Can he write into a Top Secret log? Yes, writing up is allowed (he cannot read it back, but he can append). Many students find "write up allowed" surprising; remember the model protects only confidentiality, so information flowing upward is harmless for secrecy.

Biba, the integrity mirror: Bell-LaPadula keeps secrets but does nothing for integrity. The Biba model flips the rules to protect trustworthiness: "no read down" (a high-integrity process must not read low-integrity data, which could corrupt its decisions) and "no write up" (a low-integrity subject must not modify high-integrity objects). Example: a random downloaded script (low integrity) must not overwrite system binaries (high integrity). Modern systems use a form of this: Windows integrity levels stop a low-integrity browser sandbox from writing to normal user files. SELinux and AppArmor on Linux are practical MAC systems.

Role-based access control (RBAC): In businesses, permissions follow jobs, not individuals. RBAC assigns permissions to roles, and users to roles. In a bank branch, roles might be Teller, Officer, Manager and Auditor. The Teller role has "create deposit" and "view balance"; the Manager role adds "approve large withdrawal". When a new teller joins, the admin just assigns the Teller role; when someone changes job, swap their role; when they leave, remove it. No hunting through thousands of individual permissions.

RBAC worked: Suppose a company has 500 users and 40 distinct permissions. If permissions were assigned directly, the worst case is 500 x 40 = 20,000 user-permission entries to manage and audit. With 4 roles, each user gets one role (500 entries) and each role lists at most 40 permissions (4 x 40 = 160 entries), so at most 660 entries. Fewer entries means fewer mistakes and easier audits. RBAC also supports separation of duty: the policy can forbid one user from holding both "create payment" and "approve payment", so fraud needs two people to collude.

ABAC: Attribute-based access control decides using attributes of the subject, object, action and environment, written as rules. Example: "a doctor may read a patient record if the doctor's department equals the patient's ward and the time is within their shift". It is very flexible, which suits cloud platforms and large organisations, but rules can become hard to understand and test. Many real systems mix RBAC for the big picture with a few attribute rules on top.

The reference monitor: Whatever the model, enforcement should happen in a reference monitor: the component that checks every access. Classic requirements say it must be always invoked (complete mediation, no way around it), tamper-proof (attackers cannot modify it), and small enough to be verified (economy of mechanism). The OS kernel's permission checks and a web application's central authorization middleware are both reference monitors. A common web bug, insecure direct object reference (IDOR, deep-cse-5-3 lesson 22), is exactly a missing mediation: the app checks that you are logged in but not that order 1043 is yours.

Real-life example 1, a mobile financial service back office: Customer care agents can view a customer's recent transactions to help with complaints but cannot move money. Agents can raise a refund request; a supervisor role must approve it (separation of duty). Developers have no access to production customer data at all; they work with masked test data. Auditors have read-only access to everything plus the logs. Every action is logged with the user, role and time, so a dispute can be traced. This is RBAC with least privilege and accountability working together.

Real-life example 2, a university server: On a shared Linux server in a CSE lab, each student's home folder is mode 700 so classmates cannot copy assignments. The course folder is owned by the teacher with group "cse62" and mode 750: the teacher writes, enrolled students in the group can read and enter, others see nothing. The grade sheet is mode 600. A student account is never added to the administrators group "just to install something"; instead the admin installs the package system-wide.

Common mistakes: Confusing authentication with authorization. Checking permissions only in the user interface by hiding buttons instead of on the server. Granting broad admin rights because fine-grained roles feel like effort. Forgetting to remove rights when people change jobs (privilege creep). Mixing up the Bell-LaPadula rules: it is no read up and no write down for secrecy, and Biba reverses both for integrity.

What exams ask: Draw an access matrix for a given scenario and derive the ACLs and capability lists from it. Compare ACLs and capabilities. Define DAC, MAC and RBAC with examples and explain the trojan horse weakness of DAC. State the two Bell-LaPadula properties and decide allow or deny for given read and write requests. Explain Biba and how it differs. Convert Unix modes like 754 into rwx form. Describe the reference monitor's three properties.

Recap: Access control answers whether a subject may perform a right on an object. The access matrix is the full model; ACLs store it by object and capabilities by subject. DAC lets owners decide and is flexible but weak against trojans. MAC enforces central labels: Bell-LaPadula (no read up, no write down) for confidentiality, Biba (no read down, no write up) for integrity. RBAC groups permissions into job roles and supports separation of duty; ABAC uses attribute rules. A reference monitor must check every access, resist tampering and stay small enough to verify.
key_points: Access control decides (subject, object, right) requests: allow or deny, after authentication.
The access matrix has subjects as rows and objects as columns; ACLs are its columns, capabilities its rows.
DAC lets the owner decide; it is flexible but cannot stop a trojan running with the owner's rights.
Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality: no read up (simple security) and no write down (star property).
Biba protects integrity with the mirror rules: no read down and no write up.
RBAC assigns permissions to roles and roles to users; it simplifies administration and supports separation of duty.
Unix mode 754 means rwxr-xr--; 600 or 700 keeps a file private to its owner.
A reference monitor must mediate every access, be tamper-proof and be small enough to verify.
lessons.tip: For Bell-LaPadula questions, draw the levels as floors of a building with the subject standing on one floor. Secrets must never flow down the stairs: so no reading from upper floors and no writing to lower floors.
lessons.task: Pick a small organisation you know, such as a coaching centre or a family shop. List 4 roles, 6 resources and fill in an access matrix on paper. Then write the ACL for one resource and the capability list for one role, and mark any pair of permissions that should be separated between two people.

quiz.q: Storing the access matrix column by column, one list per object, gives what?
quiz.explain: Each column belongs to one object and lists which subjects have which rights on it: that is an ACL.

quiz.q: Under Bell-LaPadula, a Secret-cleared user wants to write into a Confidential file. What happens?
options: Denied, because writing down could leak secret data
Denied, because reading up is forbidden
quiz.explain: The star property forbids writing down, so secret information cannot flow into a lower-classified object.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of discretionary access control?
options: It needs security labels on every file
A trojan running with the owner's rights can leak the owner's data
Owners cannot share their own files
quiz.explain: In DAC, programs act with the user's rights, so malicious code can copy data anywhere the user can write.

quiz.q: A company has 500 users, 40 permissions and 4 roles (one role per user). What is the maximum number of assignments with RBAC?
quiz.explain: 500 user-role entries plus at most 4 x 40 = 160 role-permission entries gives 660, compared with up to 20,000 direct entries.

quiz.q: Which Unix mode gives the owner read and write, the group read, and others nothing?

lessons.title: Software Security: Memory Safety, Overflows and Input Validation
lessons.content:
Imagine a row of letter boxes outside a building in Dhanmondi, one per flat. The box for flat 3A is small, but the postman is told to push in whatever arrives, without checking size. A thick parcel goes in, does not fit, and spills into the box of 3B next door, covering 3B's letters. If someone wanted to, they could prepare a parcel shaped so that its overflow lands in 3B as a fake instruction: "give the spare key to the bearer". That is the core idea of a buffer overflow, the most famous bug class in software security. Cryptography from earlier lessons is useless if the program holding the keys can be tricked into doing something its author never intended.

Bugs vs vulnerabilities: Every large program has bugs. A vulnerability is a bug that an attacker can trigger on purpose to break a security goal: read data they should not (confidentiality), change something (integrity), crash or freeze a service (availability), or run their own code. Software security is about writing, building and running programs so that ordinary mistakes do not turn into such weaknesses. This lesson explains the main bug classes at the concept level and focuses on defences; hands-on exploitation belongs to Advanced Cyber Security (deep-cse-9-5) and is done only in legal lab settings.

Memory layout recap: When a C program runs, its memory is divided into regions you met in Operating Systems and Computer Architecture. The text segment holds machine code. The data and BSS segments hold global variables. The heap holds memory requested at run time with malloc or new. The stack holds function call frames: each frame contains the function's local variables, saved registers and, crucially, the return address, which tells the CPU where to continue when the function finishes. On common systems the stack grows downward, and a local array sits close to that saved return address.

Buffer overflow, the concept: A buffer is a fixed-size block of memory, like char name[16], room for 16 bytes. C and C++ do not check array bounds automatically. If code copies user input into the buffer with a function that does not respect its size, and the user sends 40 bytes, the first 16 fill the buffer and the remaining 24 bytes overwrite whatever lies next to it in memory. On the stack, that neighbouring memory includes other local variables, the saved frame pointer and the return address. Overwriting a variable such as is_admin can change program logic; overwriting the return address can make the CPU jump somewhere the attacker chose when the function returns. That is how a simple length mistake can become "run attacker code". We stop at this concept; the important lesson is that the root cause is a missing length check.

Classic dangerous functions: The old C function gets() reads a line into a buffer with no way to know the buffer's size; it was so dangerous that it was removed from the C language in the C11 standard. strcpy and strcat copy until a terminating zero byte, again ignoring the destination size. sprintf can write more than the buffer holds. Safer patterns pass the size: fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin), snprintf with the buffer length, or library functions designed for bounded copying. Better still, use higher-level string types that track their own length.

Heap and other memory errors: Overflows also happen on the heap, where they can corrupt neighbouring objects or the allocator's bookkeeping. Other memory-safety bugs include out-of-bounds reads (reading past the end, leaking secrets), use-after-free (using memory after it was released, when it may already belong to something else), double free, and uninitialised reads. All share one theme: the program touches memory it does not legitimately own at that moment.

Heartbleed, a real over-read: In 2014 a bug called Heartbleed was found in OpenSSL, the library behind a large share of HTTPS servers. The TLS heartbeat feature let a client send a small message plus a stated length, and the server echoed the message back. The code trusted the stated length without checking it against the real message size. A client could send 1 byte but claim 64 kilobytes (65,536 bytes was the maximum), and the server would copy back nearly 64 KB of whatever happened to sit in its memory, sometimes including passwords, session cookies or even private keys. Defenders had to patch, revoke and reissue certificates, and change passwords. The fix was a single bounds check. One missing comparison, worldwide impact.

How big is the problem: Large vendors have reported that memory-safety bugs make up a large share of their serious vulnerabilities; figures around 70 percent have been published by both Microsoft (for its products) and the Chromium project (for high-severity browser bugs). That is why governments and companies now recommend memory-safe languages for new code.

Memory-safe languages: In Java, C#, Python, Go, JavaScript, Kotlin, Swift and Dart (the language of Flutter), array accesses are bounds-checked at run time and memory is managed automatically, so the classic overflow and use-after-free bugs cannot happen in ordinary code. An out-of-range index throws an exception instead of silently corrupting memory. Rust goes further: it gives C-like speed without a garbage collector, and its compiler's ownership and borrowing rules reject use-after-free and data races at compile time. Memory safety does not make code secure by itself; logic bugs and injection still happen, but an entire class of disasters disappears.

System defences, defence in depth: Because huge amounts of C and C++ remain, operating systems and compilers add layers that make exploitation much harder even when a bug exists. Stack canaries: the compiler places a secret random value between local buffers and the return address and checks it before returning; if an overflow changed it, the program aborts instead of jumping. Non-executable memory (NX bit, called DEP on Windows): pages used for data, like the stack and heap, are marked non-executable, so injected bytes cannot simply be run as code. ASLR (address space layout randomisation): the positions of the stack, heap and libraries change every run, so the attacker cannot know where to jump. Control-flow integrity checks that indirect jumps only go to valid targets. Each layer can sometimes be bypassed, but together they turn many bugs into crashes rather than takeovers.

Integer overflow: Numbers in programs have fixed sizes. An 8-bit unsigned value holds 0 to 255, so 250 + 10 wraps around to 260 mod 256 = 4. A 32-bit signed int holds up to 2,147,483,647; adding 1 wraps to -2,147,483,648 in typical machine arithmetic (and in C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour, which is even worse). Why does this matter for security? Imagine code that computes size = count x item_size and allocates that many bytes. With 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, 70,000 x 70,000 should be 4,900,000,000 but wraps to 605,032,704. The program allocates about 605 MB, then writes 4.9 GB of data, overflowing the buffer. Defences: check for overflow before multiplying, use wider types, and use language features or libraries that detect overflow.

Input validation: Almost every attack begins with input the program did not expect: too long, wrong type, negative, special characters, or a crafted file. The rule is to validate all input that crosses a trust boundary, on the side you control (the server, not just the app). Prefer allow-lists over deny-lists: define exactly what is valid (for a Bangladeshi mobile number, 11 digits starting with 01) and reject everything else, rather than trying to list every bad character. Check length, type, range and format. Canonicalise before checking, for example decode a URL fully before you look for "../" in a file path, otherwise an encoded form slips through.

Injection recap: Injection happens when data is mixed into a command or query and the interpreter treats part of the data as code. SQL injection, OS command injection, LDAP injection and cross-site scripting are all this pattern. Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3, lesson 22) showed the web forms in detail. The universal fix is to keep code and data separate: parameterised queries, APIs that take argument lists instead of a shell string, and context-aware output encoding. Validation helps, but separation is the real defence.

Race conditions and TOCTOU: A time-of-check to time-of-use bug happens when a program checks a condition and then acts on it, but the situation changes in between. Classic example: a privileged program checks that a user may write to a file path, and a moment later opens that path, but in that gap the path was swapped to point to a protected system file. In a wallet app, two simultaneous withdrawal requests might both check "balance is 1,000 taka, enough for 800" before either deducts, ending with minus 600. Fixes: make check and use one atomic operation, use database transactions and row locks, and operate on already-opened file handles rather than names.

Secure coding habits: Use well-tested libraries for crypto, parsing and authentication instead of writing your own. Handle errors explicitly and fail safe (lesson 03): if a permission check throws an error, deny. Do not leak details in error messages. Run with least privilege. Keep secrets out of source code. Keep dependencies updated, since much modern code is third-party. Treat compiler warnings as errors. Code review with a security checklist catches many issues early.

Finding bugs before attackers do: Static application security testing (SAST) analyses source code for risky patterns. Dynamic testing (DAST) probes the running program. Fuzzing feeds huge numbers of random or mutated inputs and watches for crashes; tools such as AFL and libFuzzer, and sanitizers like AddressSanitizer, have found thousands of memory bugs. Software Testing (deep-cse-5-8, lesson 23) covers these tools from the testing side.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi payment gateway's C module: Suppose an old module parses transaction messages in C. The team adds AddressSanitizer to its test builds, fuzzes the parser with mutated messages every night, replaces strcpy with bounded copies, enables stack protectors, ASLR and NX in the build, and plans to rewrite the parser in a memory-safe language. Each step is cheap compared with a breach.

Real-life example 2, a Flutter app: A student builds a Flutter shop app. Dart is memory-safe, so no buffer overflows in her code. But she still validates phone numbers and quantities on the server, uses parameterised queries in the backend, checks that a user can only see their own orders, and keeps the payment API key on the server rather than inside the app, because anything inside an app can be extracted.

Common mistakes: Thinking a crash is "just a bug" and not a security issue. Trusting client-side validation. Believing a memory-safe language makes the whole system secure. Using deny-lists of bad characters. Ignoring integer sizes in length calculations. Checking a file or balance and acting later without atomicity.

What exams ask: Explain a stack buffer overflow with a diagram of the stack frame. List and explain defences: canaries, NX/DEP, ASLR, bounds checking, memory-safe languages. Give an integer overflow example with numbers. Distinguish allow-list from deny-list validation. Explain TOCTOU with an example. Describe Heartbleed and its root cause.

Recap: A vulnerability is a bug an attacker can trigger to break a security goal. Buffer overflows happen when data is written past a fixed-size buffer, possibly overwriting the return address; the root cause is a missing length check. Memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes; canaries, NX and ASLR make exploitation harder in unsafe code. Integer overflows silently produce wrong sizes. Validate input with allow-lists on the server, keep code and data separate against injection, make check and use atomic, and use SAST, fuzzing and code review to find bugs first.
key_points: A vulnerability is a bug an attacker can trigger deliberately to break confidentiality, integrity or availability.
A buffer overflow writes past a fixed-size buffer and can overwrite neighbours such as the saved return address.
Heartbleed (OpenSSL, 2014) was a missing bounds check that leaked up to about 64 KB of server memory per request.
Memory-safe languages (Java, Python, Go, Dart, Rust and others) remove overflows and use-after-free in ordinary code.
Stack canaries, NX/DEP and ASLR are layered defences that make memory bugs much harder to exploit.
Integer overflow wraps values (8-bit 250 + 10 = 4) and can produce wrong buffer sizes.
Validate input on the server with allow-lists; keep code and data separate to stop injection.
TOCTOU races appear when check and use are separate steps; make them atomic.
lessons.tip: Whenever you read code that copies or sizes something, ask: who controls this length, and where is it checked? That one habit finds a surprising number of real vulnerabilities.
lessons.task: Write a tiny Python function that computes a 32-bit unsigned product the way C would (use % 2**32) and test it with 70,000 x 70,000 and a few other values. Then write a safe version that refuses to continue when the true product exceeds 2**32 - 1.

quiz.q: What is the root cause of a classic stack buffer overflow?
options: Writing more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, without a length check
Encrypting data with a weak key
quiz.explain: The program copies input past the end of the buffer because no one checked the length.

quiz.q: An 8-bit unsigned counter holds 250. What is its value after adding 10?
quiz.explain: 8-bit unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 256: 260 mod 256 = 4.

quiz.q: Which defence randomises where the stack, heap and libraries are placed in memory?
quiz.explain: Address space layout randomisation changes addresses each run so attackers cannot predict jump targets.

quiz.q: What was the root cause of Heartbleed?
options: The server trusted a length field without checking it against the real data
quiz.explain: The heartbeat code copied as many bytes as the client claimed, reading past the real message into server memory.

quiz.q: Which input validation approach is generally safer?
options: Allow-list: accept only what matches a precise valid format
Validate only in the mobile app
Skip validation if HTTPS is used
quiz.explain: Defining exactly what is valid rejects unexpected inputs that a deny-list would miss.

lessons.title: Malware: Viruses, Worms, Trojans, Ransomware and Defences
lessons.content:
Picture the dengue season in Dhaka. A mosquito bites one person, then another, and soon a whole neighbourhood is sick. Some infections spread by themselves, some need a carrier, some hide quietly for days before symptoms show. Doctors fight them with knowledge of how each one spreads, with early detection, and with prevention like clearing standing water. Malicious software behaves remarkably similarly, which is why so much of its vocabulary, virus, worm, infection, quarantine, comes from medicine. Malware is any software intentionally designed to harm a computer, its data or its user, or to act against the user's interests.

What makes something malware: The key word is intent. A buggy program that crashes is not malware; a program written to secretly copy your contacts and send them to a stranger is. Malware is described along three axes: how it spreads (propagation), what it does once inside (payload), and how it avoids being noticed (concealment). The common names you will hear mix these axes, so one sample can be a trojan, a keylogger and part of a botnet at the same time.

Virus: A virus attaches itself to a host, such as a program file, a document with macros or, historically, the boot sector of a disk. When the host runs, the virus code runs too and copies itself into other hosts. The key feature is that a virus needs the host to be executed, usually by a user action like opening a file. One of the first PC viruses, Brain (1986), spread through infected floppy disks. Macro viruses later spread through office documents, which is why modern office software disables macros in files from the Internet by default.

Worm: A worm is self-contained and spreads on its own across networks, exploiting vulnerabilities or weak passwords with no user action needed. That makes worms extremely fast. Imagine each infected machine infects two new ones every hour: starting from one, after 10 hours there are 2^10 = 1,024 infected machines, and after 20 hours 2^20 = 1,048,576, over a million. Real spread slows as vulnerable machines run out, but the early growth is exponential, which is why patching speed matters so much.

The Morris worm, 1988: In November 1988 a Cornell graduate student, Robert Tappan Morris, released a worm that exploited known weaknesses in Unix services and weak passwords. A bug in its replication logic made it reinfect machines repeatedly, overloading them. It disabled thousands of computers, a large fraction of the Internet of that time. It led to the first conviction under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and to the creation of CERT, the first computer emergency response team. Its lesson still stands: one flaw replicated automatically across many identical systems causes outsized damage.

Trojan horse: Named after the wooden horse of the Greek legend, a trojan pretends to be something useful, a free game, a cracked version of paid software, a "battery booster" app, a fake invoice, while secretly carrying a harmful payload. It does not replicate by itself; it relies on the victim installing it willingly. In Bangladesh, pirated software, cracked games and APK files downloaded from random websites or shared in groups are a common way trojans arrive. A remote access trojan (RAT) gives the attacker remote control of the device.

Ransomware: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files with strong cryptography (the same algorithms from this course, used for harm) and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the decryption key. Many modern groups also steal data first and threaten to publish it, called double extortion. Paying gives no guarantee and funds more crime. The real defence is prevention plus offline or immutable backups (lesson 26), so you can restore without paying.

WannaCry, 2017: In May 2017 the WannaCry ransomware spread as a worm through a vulnerability in the Windows SMB file-sharing protocol. Microsoft had released a patch (MS17-010) in March, about two months earlier, but many organisations had not applied it, and some ran old unsupported Windows versions. It hit hundreds of thousands of computers in over 150 countries, including hospitals in the UK's National Health Service, where appointments were cancelled. A researcher found a "kill switch" domain that slowed its spread. The single biggest lesson: a patch available for two months would have prevented most of the damage.

Spyware and stalkerware: Spyware secretly collects information: browsing habits, messages, location, passwords. A keylogger is spyware that records keystrokes, capturing passwords and PINs as they are typed. Stalkerware is spyware installed on a partner's or family member's phone to monitor them without consent; it is a real problem in many countries and a serious privacy and safety issue. Warning signs include unknown apps with accessibility or device admin permissions, unusual battery drain and data use.

Adware, rootkits and fileless malware: Adware floods the user with ads or redirects searches to earn money for its author; it is often bundled with free software. A rootkit is designed to hide itself and other malware by modifying the operating system, sometimes the kernel or even the boot process, so normal tools cannot see the malicious files or processes. Detecting kernel rootkits may require booting from clean media. Fileless malware avoids writing a normal program file to disk, instead living in memory and abusing legitimate system tools and scripts, which makes signature scanning harder.

Botnets: A bot is an infected machine that quietly obeys commands from the attacker's command-and-control (C2) server. Thousands or millions of bots form a botnet. Botnets send spam, run distributed denial-of-service attacks (lesson 25), mine cryptocurrency, try stolen passwords at scale and rent themselves out to other criminals. Internet of Things devices, routers and cameras with default passwords, have been recruited into huge botnets such as Mirai (2016).

Targeted malware: Most malware is opportunistic, trying everyone. Some is highly targeted. Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, was crafted to sabotage industrial control systems in Iran's uranium enrichment programme and showed that malware can cause physical damage. Closer to home, in February 2016 attackers placed malware on systems at Bangladesh Bank and used them to send fraudulent payment instructions through the SWIFT network; about 81 million US dollars was lost. These cases show that well-funded attackers patiently study one target, a theme for Advanced Cyber Security (deep-cse-9-5).

Infection vectors: How does malware get in? Email attachments and links (often combined with social engineering, lesson 24). Malicious or compromised websites and fake download buttons. Unpatched services exposed to the Internet, which worms love. Pirated software and APKs from outside official stores. Infected USB drives, still common in shared computer shops and offices. Compromised software updates or dependencies (supply-chain attacks). Weak or default passwords on remote access services.

Detection, signatures: Traditional antivirus keeps a database of signatures: hashes of known malicious files and characteristic byte patterns. Scanning compares files against it. Signatures are precise and fast with very few false alarms, but they only catch what has been seen before, and attackers repack or slightly modify malware (polymorphism) to change its signature.

Detection, heuristics and behaviour: Heuristic analysis looks for suspicious features in code, such as packing or self-modification. Behavioural detection watches what programs do: a process that suddenly encrypts hundreds of files per second, disables backups or injects code into other processes is suspicious whatever its hash. Sandboxing runs an unknown file in an isolated virtual environment and observes it. Modern endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools combine these with central logging. The trade-off is false positives: a detector that wrongly flags 0.1% of clean files will raise about 5 false alarms when scanning 5,000 clean files, and too many false alarms teach people to ignore alerts.

Defences that work: Patch quickly, especially Internet-facing systems (WannaCry). Use least privilege: daily work in a non-admin account limits what malware can do. Install apps only from official stores and check their permissions; keep Android's install-from-unknown-sources off. Do not use pirated software. Keep macros disabled. Use reputable security software with automatic updates. Segment networks so one infected PC cannot reach everything. Keep tested backups offline. Train people, since many infections start with a click.

Why people write malware: In the early days many viruses were pranks or experiments. Today almost all malware is about money or power. Criminal groups steal banking credentials, run ransomware as a business (some even rent it out to affiliates, "ransomware as a service"), sell stolen data and rent out botnets. Other actors spy on governments, companies or activists. Knowing the motive helps you guess the target: money-driven malware goes where payments are, which is why mobile wallets, online banking and e-commerce accounts attract so much attention.

Backdoors and logic bombs: A backdoor is a hidden way into a system that bypasses normal authentication, left by malware or sometimes by a careless or malicious developer. A logic bomb is code that stays dormant until a condition is met, such as a date or an employee's name disappearing from the payroll, and then deletes or corrupts data. Both are reasons to review code, control who can deploy to production and keep audit logs.

Mobile malware: On phones, malicious apps typically ask for powerful permissions: reading SMS (to steal OTPs), accessibility services (to read the screen and tap buttons by themselves), drawing over other apps (to show fake login screens on top of a real banking app) and device administrator rights (to resist removal). An app that does not obviously need these powers but asks for them is a red flag.

Real-life example 1, a cyber cafe or computer shop: A shop in a district town lets customers plug in USB drives to print documents. Infections pass from drive to drive. Fixes: disable autorun, scan removable media automatically, run printing on a locked-down standard account, keep the OS updated, and reinstall from a clean image regularly.

Real-life example 2, a small office hit by ransomware: An accounts office finds all its files renamed with a strange extension and a ransom note. The right response: disconnect affected machines from the network, do not pay quickly or delete evidence, report to management and, where appropriate, to the national incident response team (BGD e-GOV CIRT in Bangladesh), identify the entry point, wipe and rebuild, then restore from offline backups. If backups were on a drive permanently connected to the same PC, they are probably encrypted too, which is exactly why backups must be offline or immutable.

Common mistakes: Calling every malware a virus. Thinking Android phones or Macs cannot get malware. Believing an antivirus alone is enough. Installing "cracked" software to save money. Keeping the only backup on a drive that stays connected. Paying the ransom as the first response.

What exams ask: Define and compare virus, worm and trojan. Explain ransomware and double extortion. Describe a botnet and its uses. Explain rootkits. Compare signature-based and behaviour-based detection with pros and cons. Describe a famous incident (Morris worm, WannaCry) and the lesson it teaches. List infection vectors and defences.

Recap: Malware is software designed to harm. Viruses need a host and user action; worms spread by themselves through vulnerabilities; trojans trick users into installing them. Ransomware encrypts and often steals data; spyware and keyloggers steal information; rootkits hide; botnets are armies of infected machines. Signatures catch known malware precisely, while heuristics, behaviour monitoring and sandboxes catch new variants at the cost of false positives. Patching, least privilege, official app stores, no pirated software, network segmentation and offline backups are the defences that matter most.
key_points: Malware is software intentionally designed to harm or act against the user; it is described by propagation, payload and concealment.
A virus needs a host and usually a user action; a worm spreads by itself across networks; a trojan disguises itself as useful.
Worm spread is exponential early on: doubling each hour turns 1 machine into 1,024 after 10 hours.
Ransomware encrypts files for ransom and often steals data too; offline or immutable backups are the real defence.
WannaCry (2017) used an SMB flaw patched about two months earlier: fast patching would have prevented most damage.
Rootkits hide malware by modifying the OS; botnets are infected machines controlled through a C2 server.
Signature detection is precise but misses new variants; behaviour and sandbox detection catch more but give false positives.
Key defences: patching, least privilege, official app stores, no pirated software, segmentation and tested offline backups.
lessons.tip: Learn malware types as a table with three columns: how it spreads, what it does, how it hides. Exam questions that compare virus, worm and trojan are just asking you to read one row of that table.
lessons.task: On your phone, open the app list and the special access settings (device admin apps, accessibility, install unknown apps). Write down any app that has these powers and decide whether it really needs them. Remove or restrict anything you do not recognise.

quiz.q: What mainly distinguishes a worm from a virus?
options: A worm spreads by itself over networks without needing a host file or user action
quiz.explain: Viruses attach to hosts and need them to run; worms are self-contained and propagate automatically.

quiz.q: A worm starts on one machine and each infected machine infects one new machine every hour (doubling). How many are infected after 10 hours?
quiz.explain: Doubling 10 times gives 2^10 = 1,024.

quiz.q: Which practice would most directly have prevented WannaCry infections?
options: Installing the security patch released two months earlier
quiz.explain: WannaCry exploited an SMB vulnerability that Microsoft had already patched in March 2017.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of signature-based detection?
options: It misses new or modified malware it has not seen before
It needs internet to run every scan
quiz.explain: Signatures match known samples; repacked or brand-new malware has a different signature.

quiz.q: Why must ransomware-proof backups be offline or immutable?
options: Ransomware can encrypt backups that stay connected to the infected system
quiz.explain: A backup drive permanently attached to the infected PC is just another set of files for the ransomware to encrypt.

lessons.title: Social Engineering and Phishing
lessons.content:
Your phone rings. A polite, confident voice says: "Assalamu alaikum, I am calling from your mobile wallet's customer service. Your account has been flagged and will be blocked in 30 minutes. To verify that you are the real owner, please tell me the 6-digit code we just sent you." A code really does arrive by SMS. You panic a little, the caller sounds official, and in that moment it feels helpful to cooperate. If you read the code out, the caller completes a login or PIN reset on their own phone and empties your balance. No encryption was broken, no server was hacked. The attacker simply persuaded the one component nobody can patch with software: a human being. This is social engineering.

What social engineering is: Social engineering is manipulating people into performing actions or revealing information that benefits the attacker. It targets trust, fear, helpfulness, curiosity and greed rather than code. Security people often say that humans are the weakest link, but a fairer view is that attackers go wherever it is cheapest. When TLS, AES and good password hashing make technical attacks expensive, tricking one person becomes the easiest path.

Why it works, the psychology: Researchers of persuasion, notably Robert Cialdini, describe principles that influence everyone. Attackers abuse them. Authority: we obey people who seem official, a "bank officer", "police", "your boss". Urgency and scarcity: "within 30 minutes", "last chance", so we act before thinking. Liking and familiarity: a friendly voice, a message that appears to come from a friend's account. Social proof: "everyone in your area has already updated". Reciprocity: someone does you a small favour, then asks for one. Fear and greed: account blocked, or prize won. Almost every scam message combines two or three of these.

Phishing: Phishing is sending fraudulent messages, mainly email, that look like they come from a trusted source, to make the victim click a link, open an attachment or enter credentials on a fake page. A classic phishing email says your account is suspended and links to a page that looks exactly like the real login page, but the address is slightly different: yourbank-verify-login.com instead of yourbank.com.bd. Whatever you type goes to the attacker.

Spear phishing and whaling: Mass phishing goes to millions of people with a generic message. Spear phishing is aimed at a specific person, using details gathered from social media, the company website or LinkedIn: your name, your manager's name, a project you are working on. It is much more convincing. Whaling targets senior executives. Business email compromise (BEC) is a close cousin: the attacker impersonates (or actually takes over) a manager's or supplier's email and asks the accounts team to pay an "urgent invoice" to a new bank account.

Smishing and vishing: Smishing is phishing by SMS or messaging apps: "Your parcel is held, pay 50 taka customs fee at this link." Vishing is voice phishing by phone call, like the opening story. Attackers can spoof caller ID so the number looks familiar. Messaging apps add voice notes, fake profile photos and hijacked accounts of real friends asking to "borrow" money urgently.

Pretexting, baiting and tailgating: Pretexting is inventing a believable story (the pretext) to get information: posing as IT support who needs your password to "fix your mailbox", or as a researcher doing a survey. Baiting offers something tempting: a USB drive labelled "Salary list 2025" left in the office parking area, which installs malware when plugged in. Tailgating (piggybacking) is physically following an authorised person through a secured door. Quid pro quo offers a service in exchange for information: "free internet package if you install this app".

Mobile money scam patterns: In Bangladesh, where mobile financial services are used by millions of people, several scam patterns repeat. We keep them generic because they target customers of every provider. The fake blocking call: the caller claims your account will be blocked and asks for the OTP or PIN. The wrong-send trick: you receive an SMS that looks like a money-received alert, then a call: "I sent you 5,000 taka by mistake, please send it back." The SMS was fake, sent from an ordinary number, and your real balance never increased. The prize or lottery message: "You won a prize, pay a processing fee first."
