The fake customer care number advertised on social media pages. The remote-help trick: "install this screen-sharing app so I can fix your problem", after which the scammer watches you type your PIN.

The golden rule: Real providers never need your PIN or OTP. The OTP is how the system checks that you, holding your phone, approve an action; anyone asking for it is trying to perform that action in your name. Always check balances inside the official app, never trust an SMS alone, and call back using the official number printed on the card or shown in the app, not the number that called you.

Fake apps and fake pages: Scammers also publish lookalike apps and social media pages. A fake "wallet update" APK shared through a link, a page with the real logo offering "double cashback", or a "job" group that asks for a registration fee. The fake app may show a perfect copy of a login screen and forward everything typed to the attacker. Install financial apps only from the official store, check the developer name and download count, and never install an app because a caller told you to.

Oversharing feeds the attacker: Spear phishing works because attackers can learn so much about us for free. Your Facebook profile may reveal your workplace, your manager's name, your phone number, your birthday, your school and where you are travelling this week. Each detail makes a pretext more believable and may even answer security questions. Reviewing privacy settings and thinking before posting are real security measures, not just etiquette.

Voice and video can be faked: Tools that imitate a person's voice or face from a short recording are becoming easier to use, and there are reported cases of fraud using cloned voices of family members or executives. You do not need to know how they work to defend against them: a family code word, or calling back on a known number before sending money, defeats even a perfect imitation.

Red flags checklist: Urgency or threats. A request for a PIN, OTP, password or card details. A link whose domain is not exactly the official one (check the part just before the first single slash; yourbank.com.bd.secure-login.net belongs to secure-login.net). Messages from an ordinary mobile number claiming to be a company. Unexpected attachments, especially archives, documents asking to "enable content", and APK files. Spelling mistakes and odd greetings. Requests to keep things secret. Offers that are too good to be true. Any request to move money to a new account.

The numbers game: Why do attackers bother when most people ignore their messages? Because they only need one success. Suppose an office of 200 employees receives a phishing email and each person independently has just a 1% chance of clicking. The probability that nobody clicks is 0.99^200, about 0.134, so the probability that at least one person clicks is about 87%. Training that cuts the click rate helps, but the organisation must also assume someone will eventually click, and design defences for that moment.

Technical defences, email: Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3, lesson 07) introduced SPF and DKIM. SPF lets a domain list which servers may send its mail; DKIM adds a digital signature (lesson 17) over the message; DMARC tells receivers what to do when these checks fail (none, quarantine or reject) and sends reports to the domain owner. Together they make it much harder to send mail that truly appears to come from yourbank.com.bd, though they do nothing against lookalike domains. Mail gateways also scan links and attachments, and many organisations add a banner like "External sender" to outside email.

Technical defences, accounts and browsers: MFA (lesson 20) means a stolen password alone is not enough. Phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys and hardware security keys go further, because they will not sign in to a lookalike domain at all. Password managers help too: they fill passwords only on the exact domain they were saved for, so on a fake site the autofill stays empty, a useful warning. Browsers and DNS filters block known phishing sites. Transaction limits, cooling-off periods for new payees and alerts for every transaction limit the damage.

Organisational defences: Clear rules help people say no: "we never ask for passwords by phone", "any change of supplier bank details must be confirmed by calling a known number". Verification steps for money transfers, two-person approval above a limit, awareness training with real examples, simulated phishing exercises, and an easy way to report suspicious messages. A culture where reporting a mistake quickly is praised, not punished, is crucial: the faster a click is reported, the less damage it does.

If you have been scammed: Act fast. Call your provider's official helpline from the number in the app or on the card and ask them to block or freeze the account. Change your PIN and passwords, starting with email, since email resets everything else. Log out of other sessions and remove unknown devices. Keep evidence: screenshots, numbers, transaction IDs, times. Report to the police; Bangladesh Police has cyber crime units that handle such complaints, and lessons on the legal side come in Professional Ethics & Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6). Warn friends if your account was used to message them.

Real-life example 1, the university office: The accounts section of a private university receives an email that appears to be from a regular furniture supplier, saying their bank account has changed and asking for the pending payment of 4 lakh taka to the new account. The officer follows the rule: call the supplier on the phone number in the existing contract, not the one in the email. The supplier never sent it; their email had been compromised. A simple out-of-band check saved the money.

Real-life example 2, a family WhatsApp message: Your aunt receives a message from her nephew's account: "Khala, I am in trouble, please send 10,000 taka to this number, I will explain later, don't tell anyone." Urgency, secrecy, a new number and an unusual request all appear together. She calls her nephew directly, discovers his account was hijacked, and he recovers it and turns on two-step verification.

Common mistakes: Believing only foolish people fall for scams; skilled attackers fool experts. Trusting caller ID or sender names. Checking only that a page has HTTPS, since phishing sites use HTTPS too. Thinking an OTP is harmless to share because it "expires soon". Blaming and shaming victims, which makes others hide incidents.

What exams ask: Define social engineering and explain why it works. Distinguish phishing, spear phishing, whaling, smishing, vishing, pretexting, baiting and tailgating with examples. List red flags of a phishing message. Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC and their limits. Describe organisational and technical controls against social engineering. Explain why passkeys resist phishing.

Recap: Social engineering attacks people instead of code, using authority, urgency, liking, social proof, reciprocity, fear and greed. Phishing comes by email, smishing by SMS, vishing by phone; spear phishing and BEC are targeted. In mobile money, never share PIN or OTP and verify only through official channels. Red flags are urgency, secrecy, credential requests and lookalike links. Defend with SPF/DKIM/DMARC, MFA and passkeys, password managers, transaction controls, clear verification rules, training and a no-blame reporting culture.
key_points: Social engineering manipulates people into giving information or taking actions that help the attacker.
Attackers exploit authority, urgency and scarcity, liking, social proof, reciprocity, fear and greed.
Phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice); spear phishing, whaling and BEC are targeted forms.
Real providers never need your PIN or OTP; verify balances in the official app and call back on official numbers.
With 200 people each 1% likely to click, the chance that at least one clicks is about 87%.
SPF, DKIM and DMARC make spoofing a real domain hard but do not stop lookalike domains.
Passkeys, hardware keys and password managers resist phishing because they are bound to the exact domain.
Clear verification rules, training and a no-blame reporting culture limit damage when someone does click.
lessons.tip: Train yourself to pause for ten seconds whenever a message makes you feel urgent fear or excitement. That feeling is the attacker's tool, and the pause is the cheapest security control there is.
lessons.task: Collect three suspicious SMS or emails you or your family have received (hide personal details). For each, list the persuasion principles used and the red flags you can spot, then write the one-line correct response, such as calling the official number.

quiz.q: A caller says your wallet account will be blocked in 30 minutes unless you share the code just sent to you. Which principles is the caller mainly using?
options: None, this is a technical attack
quiz.explain: Posing as official staff is authority; the 30-minute deadline is urgency, designed to stop you thinking.

quiz.q: What is spear phishing?
options: Phishing sent to millions with a generic message
Phishing aimed at a specific person using personal details
Phishing done only over phone calls
A firewall rule that blocks phishing
quiz.explain: Spear phishing is targeted and uses gathered details to look convincing.

quiz.q: In 200 employees each with an independent 1% chance of clicking a phishing link, about how likely is at least one click?
quiz.explain: P(no one clicks) = 0.99^200, about 0.134, so P(at least one) is about 0.866.

quiz.q: What does DMARC add on top of SPF and DKIM?
options: A policy telling receivers what to do when checks fail, plus reports
A second password for the mailbox
quiz.explain: DMARC publishes a policy (none, quarantine, reject) and reporting for mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment.

quiz.q: Which login method is most resistant to phishing?
options: A passkey bound to the real website's domain
quiz.explain: A passkey only signs challenges for the registered domain, so a fake site gets nothing usable.

lessons.title: Network Security: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, VPNs, DDoS and Wi-Fi
lessons.content:
Think of a big apartment complex in Bashundhara. At the main gate a guard checks who enters: residents walk in, delivery riders must say which flat, strangers are turned away. Inside, the CCTV room watches for unusual behaviour, someone trying every door handle on the fifth floor. Residents who work from home use a private, locked corridor to reach the office building across the road. Each of these ideas has a twin in network security: the gate is a firewall, the CCTV room is an intrusion detection system, and the private corridor is a VPN. This lesson looks at how these defences work, what they can and cannot stop, and how attacks like denial of service and Wi-Fi cracking fit in.

Where this lesson sits: Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3) taught you IP addresses, ports, TCP and UDP, NAT and the TCP three-way handshake, and lesson 26 there gave a short tour of network security. TLS from lesson 19 protects one connection between two programs. Here we protect whole networks: deciding which traffic is allowed in and out, watching for attacks, connecting remote sites safely and keeping services available.

Firewalls, the idea: A firewall is a device or program that sits between networks of different trust, typically your internal network and the Internet, and allows or blocks traffic according to a rule set. It enforces a policy such as "the outside world may reach our web server on port 443, our staff may browse the web, nothing else gets in". It implements least privilege and fail-safe defaults (lesson 03) at the network level: the last rule should be deny everything not explicitly allowed.

Packet filters: The simplest firewall, a stateless packet filter, looks at each packet on its own: source and destination IP address, protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP), source and destination port, and sometimes TCP flags. Each rule says: if the packet matches these fields, allow or deny. Rules are usually checked in order and the first match wins. Packet filters are fast and are built into routers, but they see no context: they cannot tell whether an incoming packet is a reply to a connection we opened or an unsolicited probe.

Firewall rules worked: Suppose an office network uses the documentation range 203.0.113.0/24 and has a public web server. The rules are: Rule 1, allow TCP to port 443 (HTTPS) from any source. Rule 2, allow TCP to port 22 (SSH) only if the source is in 203.0.113.0/24. Rule 3, deny everything. Now test four packets. A customer's browser sends TCP to port 443: Rule 1 matches, allowed. An unknown address on the Internet tries TCP port 22: Rule 1 does not match (wrong port), Rule 2 does not match (source not in the office range), Rule 3 matches, denied. The office admin at 203.0.113.25 connects to port 22: Rule 2 matches, allowed. A UDP packet to port 53 arrives: only Rule 3 matches, denied. Now notice the ordering trap: if someone moved "deny everything" to the top, every packet would be blocked, because the first match wins.

Stateful inspection: A stateful firewall remembers connections in a state table. When an internal user opens a TCP connection to a website, the firewall records (internal IP, internal port, external IP, external port, state). Reply packets that match this entry are allowed back automatically; unexpected packets that claim to be replies but match no entry are dropped. This makes rules simpler ("allow outbound web browsing" without opening all high ports inbound) and blocks many tricks that fool stateless filters. Home routers doing NAT behave in a similar stateful way.

Application-level gateways and next-generation firewalls: An application proxy (application-level gateway) understands a specific protocol such as HTTP or SMTP. The client connects to the proxy, which inspects the request and makes its own connection to the server. It can block particular URLs, file types or commands, and log in detail, at the cost of more processing. A web application firewall (WAF) is a proxy specialised for HTTP that looks for patterns of SQL injection, XSS and similar attacks in front of a web app; it is a useful extra layer but never a substitute for fixing the app. Next-generation firewalls combine stateful filtering with application identification, user identity, intrusion prevention and sometimes TLS inspection.

Network design, DMZ and segmentation: Servers that must be reachable from the Internet, such as the public web server or mail server, are placed in a separate zone called the DMZ (demilitarised zone), between an outer and an inner firewall, or on a separate firewall interface. If a DMZ server is compromised, the attacker still faces another firewall before reaching the internal network with employee PCs and databases. More generally, segmentation splits a network into zones (staff, guests, servers, payment systems, cameras) with rules between them, so that a single infected laptop cannot reach everything. Guest Wi-Fi on a separate network is a simple example.

Zero trust: Traditional designs trusted anything inside the firewall, a "castle and moat" model. But attackers often get inside through phishing, and many users now work from outside. Zero trust means no device or user is trusted just because of its network location: every request is authenticated and authorised, devices are checked, and access is granted per application with least privilege. Firewalls still matter, but identity becomes the main perimeter.

Intrusion detection systems: An IDS monitors traffic or host activity and raises alerts about suspected attacks. A network IDS (NIDS) watches packets at a key point, for example behind the firewall; a host IDS (HIDS) watches logs, file changes and processes on one machine. Detection uses two main methods. Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns, such as a byte sequence used by a known exploit: precise, but blind to new attacks. Anomaly-based detection learns what normal traffic looks like and flags deviations, such as a PC that suddenly sends data to hundreds of addresses at 3 a.m.: it can catch new attacks but produces more false alarms. Snort, Suricata and Zeek are well-known open-source tools.

IDS vs IPS: An IDS only watches and alerts; it usually sits on a copy of the traffic. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline, in the traffic path, and can drop malicious packets or block connections automatically. The trade-off: an IPS can stop attacks in real time, but a false positive in an IPS blocks legitimate users, and if it fails it can cut off the network unless designed to fail open or fail closed deliberately.

The base-rate problem worked: Why do security teams drown in alerts? Suppose a network sees 1,000,000 events per day and only 10 are real attacks. The IDS detects 99% of attacks and wrongly flags just 0.1% of normal events. True alerts: 10 x 0.99 = 9.9, about 10. False alerts: 999,990 x 0.001, about 1,000. So of roughly 1,010 alerts per day, only about 1% are real. A detector that sounds very accurate still produces mostly false alarms when attacks are rare. That is why tuning, correlation of alerts in a SIEM (security information and event management) system, and good triage matter as much as the detector itself.

VPNs: A virtual private network creates an encrypted, authenticated tunnel across an untrusted network, so remote users or branch offices can use the internal network as if they were directly connected. Site-to-site VPNs connect two offices, for example a head office in Dhaka and a branch in Chattogram, through their gateways. Remote-access VPNs connect individual laptops or phones. A VPN protects traffic between the device and the VPN gateway; after the gateway, traffic is as exposed as any other.

IPsec: IPsec secures traffic at the IP layer. Its Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol provides confidentiality and integrity; the older Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity only. In transport mode only the payload is protected; in tunnel mode the whole original IP packet is encrypted and wrapped in a new IP header, which is what site-to-site VPNs use. Keys are negotiated with IKE (Internet Key Exchange), which uses Diffie-Hellman (lesson 13) and certificates or pre-shared keys for authentication.

TLS VPNs and WireGuard: Many remote-access VPNs run over TLS, which passes easily through firewalls and NAT because it looks like ordinary HTTPS traffic. WireGuard is a newer VPN protocol with a deliberately small codebase and a fixed set of modern algorithms, including Curve25519 for key exchange and ChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption (lessons 06, 09 and 14), now included in the Linux kernel. Note that consumer "VPN apps" mainly move your trust from your ISP to the VPN company; they are not a magic privacy shield.

Denial of service: A DoS attack aims at availability: it makes a service unusable for legitimate users. A distributed DoS (DDoS) uses many machines, usually a botnet (lesson 23). Volumetric attacks fill the bandwidth: 10,000 bots each sending 2 Mbps produce 20 Gbps, twenty times what a 1 Gbps link can carry, so legitimate packets are crowded out. Protocol attacks exhaust state, such as a SYN flood filling a server's half-open connection table (Computer Networks lesson 15). Application-layer attacks send expensive requests, like searches, that look legitimate. Reflection and amplification attacks send small requests with a forged source address to open servers (some DNS or NTP servers) that reply with much larger answers to the victim.

DDoS defences: You cannot stop a 20 Gbps flood at the end of a 1 Gbps link; it must be absorbed upstream. Defences include ISP filtering, cloud scrubbing services and CDNs with huge capacity and anycast addresses that spread the load, SYN cookies for SYN floods, rate limiting and caching for application attacks, and ingress filtering by ISPs so that forged source addresses cannot leave their networks. Having a plan and a contact at your ISP before an attack is part of preparation (lesson 26).

Wi-Fi security: Wireless traffic can be received by anyone nearby, so encryption at the link layer is essential. WEP, the original scheme, used RC4 with a 24-bit initialisation vector. With only 2^24 = 16,777,216 possible IVs, by the birthday effect (lesson 15) a repeated IV becomes likely after about 4,800 packets, and other design flaws made WEP keys recoverable within minutes. WPA was an interim fix, then WPA2 (2004) brought AES-based CCMP encryption. WPA2-Personal's weakness is that anyone who captures a handshake can try password guesses offline, so a short Wi-Fi password is a real risk. WPA3 (2018) replaces that handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline dictionary attacks. WPA2-Enterprise and WPA3-Enterprise authenticate each user individually through a server, which suits universities and offices. Disable WPS PIN pairing, which has had serious weaknesses.

Real-life example 1, a small e-commerce company: The company in Dhaka places its web server in a DMZ, allows only ports 80 (redirect) and 443 from the Internet, allows SSH only through a VPN, keeps the database in an internal zone reachable only from the app server, uses a CDN for DDoS absorption, runs an IDS on the internal segment with alerts sent to the on-call engineer, and puts the office guest Wi-Fi on a separate network with WPA3.

Real-life example 2, a university campus: Student hostels, labs, administration and the exam server sit in different segments. The exam server accepts connections only from the exam office segment. Wi-Fi uses enterprise authentication with each student's own account, so a leaked password affects one person and abuse can be traced. A site-to-site VPN connects the main campus with a second campus in another city.

Common mistakes: Thinking a firewall makes a network secure by itself. Putting "deny all" before the allow rules or leaving a temporary "allow any" in place. Trusting everything inside the network. Treating IDS alerts as either all true or all noise. Believing a VPN encrypts traffic all the way to the website. Using short Wi-Fi passwords with WPA2-Personal.

What exams ask: Compare packet filter, stateful and application-level firewalls. Evaluate a given rule list against packets (first-match). Explain a DMZ with a diagram. Distinguish IDS from IPS and signature from anomaly detection, including false positives and negatives. Explain IPsec ESP vs AH and tunnel vs transport mode. Classify DoS attacks and defences. Explain why WEP failed and what WPA2 and WPA3 improved.

Recap: Firewalls enforce which traffic may pass; packet filters judge single packets, stateful firewalls track connections, proxies understand applications. Order matters: first match wins, and the default should be deny. DMZs and segmentation contain damage; zero trust stops trusting location. IDS detect and IPS block, using signatures or anomalies, and rare attacks mean most alerts are false. VPNs tunnel traffic with IPsec, TLS or WireGuard. DDoS attacks availability and must be absorbed upstream. Wi-Fi moved from broken WEP to WPA2 and WPA3, where SAE resists offline guessing.
key_points: A firewall enforces a traffic policy between trust zones; the final rule should deny everything not allowed.
Rules are usually first-match: putting deny-all at the top blocks everything.
Stateless filters judge single packets; stateful firewalls track connections; application proxies and WAFs understand protocols.
A DMZ and segmentation limit how far an attacker gets; zero trust stops trusting network location.
IDS alerts, IPS blocks inline; signature detection finds known attacks, anomaly detection finds new ones with more false alarms.
With rare attacks, even a 0.1% false positive rate makes most alerts false (about 1% real in the worked example).
VPNs tunnel traffic using IPsec (ESP, tunnel mode, IKE), TLS or WireGuard; protection ends at the VPN gateway.
DDoS must be absorbed upstream (CDN, scrubbing, ISP); Wi-Fi went from broken WEP to WPA2 (AES-CCMP) and WPA3 (SAE).
lessons.tip: For firewall questions, always walk each packet through the rules from the top and write down which rule matched first. Most exam marks are lost by students who jump to the rule that looks most relevant instead of the first one that matches.
lessons.task: Open your home router's admin page (the address is usually printed on the router). Check which Wi-Fi security mode it uses (prefer WPA3 or WPA2 with AES), whether WPS is on, whether remote administration is enabled, and whether the admin password is still the default. Fix what you safely can and write down the settings.

quiz.q: A rule list reads: 1) allow TCP 443 from any, 2) allow TCP 22 from 203.0.113.0/24, 3) deny all. What happens to a TCP packet to port 22 from 198.51.100.7?
quiz.explain: Rule 1 is for port 443, rule 2 needs a source in 203.0.113.0/24, so the first match is rule 3: deny.

quiz.q: What does a stateful firewall add over a stateless packet filter?
options: It tracks connections so replies to internal requests are allowed automatically
quiz.explain: A state table lets the firewall recognise legitimate replies and drop unsolicited packets pretending to be replies.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: IDS uses signatures, IPS uses anomalies
An IDS only alerts, while an IPS sits inline and can block traffic
An IPS works only on hosts
quiz.explain: Both can use either detection method; the IPS is in the traffic path and can drop packets.

quiz.q: 10,000 bots each send 2 Mbps toward a server on a 1 Gbps link. What is the attack volume?
quiz.explain: 10,000 x 2 Mbps = 20,000 Mbps = 20 Gbps, twenty times the link capacity.

quiz.q: Which Wi-Fi feature specifically resists offline password guessing from a captured handshake?
quiz.explain: SAE is designed so that capturing the handshake does not let an attacker test password guesses offline.

lessons.title: Security in Practice, the Quantum Future and Capstone
lessons.content:
A new building in Gulshan can have the best locks money can buy, but if nobody changes the guard's shift, checks the fire extinguishers, keeps spare keys in a safe place or knows what to do when the alarm rings, the locks will not save it. The same is true of everything in this course. AES, RSA, TLS, MFA and firewalls are the locks. Security in practice is the daily routine around them: patching, backups, logging, responding to incidents and preparing for the future. The security expert Bruce Schneier summed it up in a line often quoted: security is a process, not a product. This final lesson covers that process, takes an honest look at the quantum future, and then pulls the whole course together in a capstone: securing a Bangladeshi mobile-wallet style app from end to end.

Know what you have: You cannot protect what you do not know exists. The first practical step is an inventory: every server, laptop, phone, cloud account, domain name, application, database and third-party service, with an owner for each. Forgotten test servers, old admin panels and unused cloud buckets are a classic way in. With the inventory, you can apply the risk thinking from lesson 02: which assets matter most, what threatens them and what is already in place.

Patching and vulnerability management: Software vulnerabilities are discovered every day and published with CVE identifiers (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), such as CVE-2014-0160 for Heartbleed (lesson 22). Each usually gets a CVSS score from 0 to 10: in version 3, 0.1 to 3.9 is low, 4.0 to 6.9 medium, 7.0 to 8.9 high and 9.0 to 10.0 critical. Organisations cannot patch everything instantly, so they prioritise: Internet-facing systems, vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild, and critical scores first. A typical policy might say critical Internet-facing issues are patched within days, others within a month. Remember WannaCry (lesson 23): the patch existed two months before the outbreak. Automatic updates on phones and laptops, and dependency scanning in software projects, close most of the gap for free.

Configuration and hardening: Many breaches need no vulnerability at all, only a bad setting: a default admin password, a database open to the Internet, a storage bucket readable by anyone, debug mode left on in production, unnecessary services running. Hardening means removing what is not needed, changing defaults, enabling security features and following published baselines (for example CIS Benchmarks). It is boring work, which is exactly why it is often skipped and why it pays off.

Backups and the 3-2-1 rule: Backups protect availability and integrity against ransomware, hardware failure, mistakes and disasters. The 3-2-1 rule says: keep at least 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy off-site. Against ransomware add a fourth idea: at least one copy offline or immutable (cannot be changed or deleted for a set period), so malware with admin rights cannot destroy it. Two numbers define a backup plan. Recovery point objective (RPO): how much data you can afford to lose. If backups run daily at 2 a.m. and the server dies at 5 p.m., up to 15 hours of work is lost. Recovery time objective (RTO): how long you can afford to be down while restoring. And the golden rule: a backup that has never been test-restored is only a hope.

Logging and monitoring: Logs are the security camera footage of IT. Record authentication successes and failures, privilege changes, admin actions, access to sensitive data, configuration changes and errors. Send logs to a central place the attacker cannot easily erase, keep clocks synchronised so events can be put in order, and keep logs long enough to investigate incidents discovered weeks later. Never log secrets such as passwords, full card numbers, PINs or OTPs. A SIEM correlates logs and raises alerts (lesson 25), but someone must actually look at them; a security operations centre (SOC) is the team that does this around the clock.

Incident response: Despite everything, incidents happen. The classic NIST incident handling lifecycle (SP 800-61) has four phases. Preparation: a plan, contact list, tools, backups and practice drills before anything goes wrong. Detection and analysis: noticing something is wrong, confirming it, deciding its scope and severity. Containment, eradication and recovery: isolating affected systems to stop the spread, removing the attacker's access and malware, restoring from clean backups and watching closely. Post-incident activity: a blameless review of what happened, why, and what to change. Preserve evidence during the process, communicate honestly with affected users, and follow legal reporting duties; in Bangladesh, the national CIRT (BGD e-GOV CIRT) coordinates incident response, and the legal side is covered in Professional Ethics & Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6).

People and policy: Most of this course has been technical, but policies decide whether the technology is used: acceptable use, password and MFA rules, who approves access, how suppliers are vetted, how data is classified and how long it is kept. Regular awareness training (lesson 24) and simulated drills turn policy into habit.

The quantum question: A large, fault-tolerant quantum computer would change public-key cryptography. In 1994 Peter Shor published a quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms efficiently. That would break RSA (lesson 12), Diffie-Hellman (lesson 13) and elliptic-curve cryptography (lesson 14). Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speed-up for brute-force search, which roughly halves the effective security of symmetric keys: a 128-bit AES key would offer about 64-bit security against such an attacker, so AES-256 is the conservative choice. Hash functions are affected similarly and are handled with longer outputs.

How worried should we be: Nobody can say when, or whether, a quantum computer large and reliable enough to break 2048-bit RSA will exist; today's machines are far too small and noisy, and expert estimates differ widely. But there is a reason to act now: "harvest now, decrypt later". An adversary can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it years later if such a machine appears. Data that must stay secret for a long time, such as health records or state secrets, is already at risk in that sense.

Post-quantum cryptography: Post-quantum cryptography means classical algorithms, running on ordinary computers, built on mathematical problems believed to be hard even for quantum computers. After a public competition that began in 2016, the US NIST published its first post-quantum standards in August 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from the CRYSTALS-Kyber design) for key establishment, FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) for signatures and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+, based only on hash functions) for signatures. Some major browsers and services have already started using hybrid key exchange in TLS, combining a classical method like X25519 with ML-KEM so the connection stays safe if either one holds. The lesson for engineers is crypto agility: design systems so algorithms can be replaced without rebuilding everything.

Capstone, the setting: Now let us use the whole course. Imagine you join the small team building "TakaPay", a fictional mobile wallet for Bangladesh: users register with their phone number, keep a balance, send money to other users, pay merchants by QR code and cash out at agents. There is an Android and iOS app, a back-end API, a database, an admin back office and links to banks and payment networks.

Capstone, assets and threats: Assets are customer money, balances and transaction records, personal data (NID, phone number, contacts), credentials and keys, and the service's availability. Threat actors include scammers who trick users, criminals stealing credentials at scale, malicious insiders, and attackers who want to disrupt the service. Using STRIDE (lesson 02): spoofing a user's identity, tampering with amounts, repudiating a payment, disclosing personal data, denying service on salary day, and elevating a customer account to admin powers. The risk ranking puts account takeover and fraudulent transfers at the top.

Capstone, identity and authentication: Registration verifies the SIM with an OTP and binds the account to the device by generating a key pair in the phone's secure hardware (Android Keystore or iOS Secure Enclave); the server stores the public key. Daily login uses a PIN or biometric that unlocks that device key, which signs a server challenge (lessons 17 and 20). A 5-digit PIN has only 100,000 possibilities, so it is protected not by entropy but by rate limiting: after 3 wrong tries the account locks, giving an attacker a 3 in 100,000 (0.003%) chance. The PIN is never stored in plain text, and even a salted hash is not enough on its own, because 100,000 possibilities are cracked offline in moments; so it is verified with a keyed hash whose key lives inside a hardware security module. Moving the account to a new phone requires stronger verification and a cooling-off period with reduced limits.

Capstone, cryptography: All traffic uses TLS 1.3 with forward secrecy (lesson 19), with HSTS for web pages. Each transaction request carries the device signature plus a nonce and timestamp so it cannot be replayed (lesson 16). Sensitive fields in the database are encrypted with AES-GCM (lesson 09), with keys kept in a key management service or hardware security module rather than in code, and rotated on a schedule. Webhooks from partner banks are verified with HMAC or signatures. Passwords for staff accounts use Argon2 or bcrypt. Algorithms are configurable to allow a future post-quantum migration.

Capstone, access control and software: Every API call checks that the authenticated user owns the account being debited, preventing IDOR-style bugs. Money movements run inside database transactions with row locks, preventing the double-spend TOCTOU race from lesson 22, and each transfer carries an idempotency key so a retried request is not paid twice. The back office uses RBAC with separation of duty: agents raise refunds, supervisors approve, developers have no production data access, auditors are read-only (lesson 21). Services are written in memory-safe languages, inputs are validated with allow-lists on the server, queries are parameterised, dependencies are scanned, and the pipeline runs SAST and fuzzing.

Capstone, network and operations: Public APIs sit behind a CDN and WAF with DDoS protection, in a DMZ separated from internal databases; admin access requires VPN plus MFA (lesson 25). Logs of every login, PIN failure and transfer flow to a SIEM, with alerts for unusual patterns such as many new-device logins from one location. Backups follow 3-2-1 with an immutable copy, restores are tested monthly, and an incident response plan has named people and a 24-hour contact at the ISP and the national CIRT.

Capstone, the human layer: The app never asks for a PIN or OTP over calls or SMS, and says so on every OTP message. It shows warnings when a user sends money to a new number for the first time, applies limits and a short delay on large first-time transfers, provides an in-app way to report scam calls, and offers easy account freezing from the helpline. Clear in-app balance views reduce the power of fake "money received" SMS (lesson 24). Privacy by design keeps only the data that is needed, for as long as needed.

Course recap: You started with the goals, confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity and non-repudiation, and learned to think in threats, vulnerabilities and risk. You saw why classical ciphers fell to frequency analysis, why the one-time pad is perfect but impractical, how block ciphers like AES and modes like GCM protect data, how number theory powers RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves, and how hashes, MACs and signatures provide integrity and authenticity. PKI and TLS put it together on the Internet. Authentication and access control decide who gets in and what they may do; software security, malware, social engineering and network defences showed where real attacks happen; and this lesson turned it all into a routine.

What next: Professional Ethics & Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) covers the law, privacy and responsibilities that come with this knowledge. Blockchain (deep-cse-9-2) builds directly on hashes and signatures. Advanced Cyber Security (deep-cse-9-5) goes into penetration testing, forensics and advanced attacks, always within legal and ethical limits. Practise legally: capture-the-flag competitions, intentionally vulnerable lab apps on your own machine and bug bounty programmes with clear rules. Careers include security analyst in a SOC, application security engineer, penetration tester, cloud security engineer and cryptography engineer.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Treating security as a one-time project. Keeping backups that were never restored. Logging passwords or OTPs. Panicking about quantum computers or ignoring them completely. Exams ask: explain the 3-2-1 backup rule, RPO and RTO; list and explain the incident response phases; explain patch prioritisation and CVSS; explain the impact of Shor's and Grover's algorithms and name the 2024 NIST post-quantum standards; and design security controls for a given system, exactly like the capstone.
key_points: Security is a process: inventory, patching, hardening, backups, logging, incident response and training.
Prioritise patches by exposure, active exploitation and CVSS severity (9.0-10.0 is critical in CVSS v3).
3-2-1 backups: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site, plus an offline or immutable copy; test restores.
RPO is how much data you can lose (daily 2 a.m. backup, 5 p.m. failure = up to 15 hours); RTO is how long you can be down.
Incident response phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.
Shor's algorithm would break RSA, DH and ECC on a large quantum computer; Grover halves effective symmetric key strength.
NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), 204 (ML-DSA) and 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024; design for crypto agility.
Securing a wallet app combines device-bound keys, rate-limited PINs, TLS 1.3, ownership checks, transactions, RBAC, monitoring and scam-aware design.
lessons.tip: When an exam asks you to secure a system, walk through it in the order of this course: goals and threats, cryptography, authentication, access control, software, network, operations and people. That structure turns a vague question into a full-marks answer.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily, such as a wallet, bank or university portal. On one page, write its main assets, three top threats, and for each threat two controls you can see from the outside (for example PIN lockout or transaction alerts) and one control you would expect behind the scenes. Finally, write a 3-2-1 backup plan for your own photos and documents.

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule require?
options: 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 off-site
3 backups per day, 2 per week, 1 per month
quiz.explain: At least three copies of the data, on two types of media, with one copy stored off-site.

quiz.q: Backups run daily at 2 a.m. The server fails at 5 p.m. How much data could be lost?
quiz.explain: Everything created after the 2 a.m. backup, up to 5 p.m., is lost: 15 hours. This is what RPO measures.

quiz.q: Which phase of the NIST incident response lifecycle includes isolating infected machines and restoring from clean backups?
quiz.explain: Containment stops the spread, eradication removes the threat and recovery restores normal service.

quiz.q: What would a large fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm mainly break?
quiz.explain: Shor's algorithm solves factoring and discrete logarithms efficiently, the problems behind RSA, DH and ECC.

quiz.q: In the TakaPay capstone, why is a 5-digit PIN acceptable despite low entropy?
options: Because it is encrypted with AES
Because rate limiting and lockout after 3 tries give an attacker only a 3 in 100,000 chance
quiz.explain: Online guessing is limited by lockout, so the attacker gets 3 guesses out of 100,000 possibilities.
